Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

For every smooth Riemannian metric on the two sphere whose Gaussian curvature is bounded below by one, we prove that each positive Laplace eigenvalue, counted with multiplicity, is no smaller than the corresponding eigenvalue of the unit round sphere. Equality at any positive position in the ordered spectrum forces the metric to be isometric to the unit round metric.

We further establish a sharp finite spectral counting comparison for Alexandrov two spheres with curvature bounded below by one. At every positive spectral threshold of the unit round sphere, the number of Laplace eigenvalues below or at that threshold, counted with multiplicity, does not exceed the corresponding number for the round sphere. Equality at any such threshold forces the Alexandrov sphere to be isometric to the unit round sphere.

As an application, we obtain the sharp Euclidean dimension bound for spaces of polynomial growth harmonic functions on complete three dimensional manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature and positive asymptotic volume ratio, together with rigidity in the equality case.

1. Introduction

Throughout the paper we use the conventions

ℤ+={1,2,…},ℤ≥0={0,1,2,…}.\displaystyle\mathbb{Z}^{+}=\{1,2,\ldots\},\qquad\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.

For a nonnegative self-adjoint operator PP with compact resolvent and eigenvalues λ0​(P)≤λ1​(P)≤⋯\lambda_{0}(P)\leq\lambda_{1}(P)\leq\cdots, counted with multiplicity, we use the operator-subscript notation

NP<​(Λ)\displaystyle N_{P}^{<}(\Lambda) :=#⁡{j≥0:λj​(P)<Λ},\displaystyle:=\#\{j\geq 0:\lambda_{j}(P)<\Lambda\},
𝒩P​(Λ)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{P}(\Lambda) :=#⁡{j≥0:λj​(P)≤Λ}.\displaystyle:=\#\{j\geq 0:\lambda_{j}(P)\leq\Lambda\}.
Notation 1.1 (Spectral conventions).

We use

Δg=divg∇,−Δg≥0.\Delta_{g}=\operatorname{div}_{g}\nabla,\qquad-\Delta_{g}\geq 0.

For a compact Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g), define

λj​(M,g):=λj​(−Δg),j∈ℤ≥0.\lambda_{j}(M,g):=\lambda_{j}(-\Delta_{g}),\qquad j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

For a compact Alexandrov space XX carrying its canonical nonnegative Laplacian, define

λj​(X):=λj​(−ΔX).\lambda_{j}(X):=\lambda_{j}(-\Delta_{X}).

All eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity and indexed from 00.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be a complete Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature. For d≥0d\geq 0, denote by ℋd​(Mn)\mathscr{H}_{d}(M^{n}) the vector space of harmonic functions on MnM^{n} with polynomial growth of degree at most dd. Yau’s original finite-dimensionality question [37, Problem 48, pp. 275–319] asks whether

dimℋd​(Mn)<∞\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(M^{n})<\infty

for every fixed growth degree d≥0d\geq 0. That formulation also asks whether ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} has the maximal dimension of polynomial-growth harmonic functions.

In 19981998, Colding and Minicozzi proved the following Weyl-type bound [11].

Theorem 1.2 (Colding–Minicozzi).

If (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) is complete and Rc≥0\Rc\geq 0, then there exists C⁡(n)>0C(n)>0 such that, for every d≥1d\geq 1,

dimℋd​(Mn)≤C⁡(n)​dn−1.\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(M^{n})\leq C(n)d^{n-1}.

The same circle of ideas includes Colding–Minicozzi’s work on harmonic functions with polynomial growth and their work on harmonic sections [9, 8, 10], also see [21]. Together with Theorem 1.2, these results give the correct Weyl growth exponent in the following sense.

Here “Weyl growth exponent” means only the power-law exponent predicted by Weyl’s law, not the sharp leading Weyl constant. Let (Nn−1,h)(N^{n-1},h) be a closed Riemannian manifold with Riemannian metric hh and suppose Rc⁡(h)≥(n−2)​h\Rc(h)\geq(n-2)h. On the punctured metric cone

C⁡(N)=(0,∞)×N,hC=d​r2+r2​h,\displaystyle C(N)=(0,\infty)\times N,\qquad h_{C}=dr^{2}+r^{2}h,

the Ricci tensor is nonnegative.

If −Δh​φi=λi​(−Δh)​φi-\Delta_{h}\varphi_{i}=\lambda_{i}(-\Delta_{h})\varphi_{i}, then a separated function rα​φi​(θ)r^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}(\theta) is harmonic on the cone if and only if

(1.1) α⁡(α+n−2)=λi​(−Δh).\displaystyle\alpha(\alpha+n-2)=\lambda_{i}(-\Delta_{h}).

By (1.1), we have

(1.2) dimℋk​(C⁡(N))=𝒩−Δh​(k⁡(k+n−2)).\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{H}_{k}(C(N))=\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{h}}\big(k(k+n-2)\big).

Note Weyl’s law gives

limΛ→∞𝒩−Δh​(Λ)Λn−12=ωn−1​Vol⁡(N)(2​π)n−1,\displaystyle\lim_{\Lambda\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{h}}(\Lambda)}{\Lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}}=\frac{\omega_{n-1}\operatorname{Vol}(N)}{(2\pi)^{n-1}},

where ωn−1\omega_{n-1} is the Euclidean volume of the unit ball in ℝn−1\mathbb{R}^{n-1}. Thus the Weyl order of the counting function is Λn−12\Lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.

In the cone discussion above, evaluating at the round thresholds Λ=k⁡(k+n−2)∼k2\Lambda=k(k+n-2)\sim k^{2} gives the order kn−1k^{n-1} for 𝒩−Δh​(k⁡(k+n−2))\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{h}}(k(k+n-2)), equivalently for the cone dimension in (1.2). Therefore Theorem 1.2 has the sharp Weyl growth exponent dn−1d^{n-1}.

The sharp comparison part of Yau’s question asks whether the Euclidean model gives the sharp upper bound at the integer degrees.

Question 1.3 (Yau’s sharp dimension question).

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be complete with Rc≥0\Rc\geq 0. Is it true that

(1.3) dimℋd​(Mn)≤dimℋd​(ℝn),∀d∈ℤ+​?\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(M^{n})\leq\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\quad\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}?

Moreover, if equality holds for some d∈ℤ+d\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, must MnM^{n} be isometric to ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}?

Remark 1.4.

When n=2n=2, Li–Tam give an affirmative answer to the corresponding surface question [19, Theorem 4.2]. For d=1d=1 and general nn, the inequality follows from Li–Tam [18], and the rigidity is due to Cheeger–Colding–Minicozzi [6].

Donnelly [12] showed, for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0 there is a complete manifold (M5,g)(M^{5},g) with Rc≥0\Rc\geq 0 such that

dimℋ2−ϵ​(M5)>dimℋ2−ϵ​(ℝ5).\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{H}_{2-\epsilon}(M^{5})>\dim\mathscr{H}_{2-\epsilon}(\mathbb{R}^{5}).

This does not disprove the integer-degree version (1.3), and the integer-degree problem remains a natural sharp form of the question.

For the Euclidean cone ℝn=C⁡(𝕊n−1)\mathbb{R}^{n}=C(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}), (1.2) gives the usual dimension of harmonic polynomials of degree at most kk. Hence the sharp integer-degree form of Yau’s question suggests the following question, which can be viewed as a compact cross-section version of Question 1.3.

Question 1.5.

Assume (Nn−1,h)(N^{n-1},h) has Rc⁡(h)≥(n−2)​h\Rc(h)\geq(n-2)h, do we have

(1.4) 𝒩−Δh​(k⁡(k+n−2))≤𝒩−Δ𝕊n−1​(k⁡(k+n−2)),∀k∈ℤ≥0​?\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{h}}\big(k(k+n-2)\big)\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}\big(k(k+n-2)\big),\qquad\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}?

And if the equality in (1.4) holds for some k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, must Nn−1N^{n-1} be isometric to 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}?

Remark 1.6.

This point of view is already present in [11, pp. 260–262]. Colding and Minicozzi [11, Page 261261] (also see [24, Conjecture 33]) pointed out that

“it has been a long standing open problem whether for a closed manifold Nn−1N^{n-1} with Ricci curvature greater or equal to n−2n-2,

(1.5) λi​(𝕊n−1)≤λi​(Nn−1),i≥1,\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})\leq\lambda_{i}(N^{n-1}),\qquad i\geq 1,

with equality for some positive integer i=max⁡{j≥i|λj​(𝕊n−1)=λi​(𝕊n−1)}i=\max\{j\geq i|\lambda_{j}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})=\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1})\} if and only if Nn−1N^{n-1} is isometric to 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}.”

Aryan’s recent work gives counterexamples to (1.5) in the conjecture for n≥5n\geq 5 [2]. We show that (1.5) does not hold for n=4n=4 in Section 16.

Note that the rigidity part of the above open problem is equivalent to the rigidity part of Question 1.5, and Question 1.5 remains open for n≥3n\geq 3. In this paper, we answer Question 1.5 affirmatively in the case n=3n=3 and prove (1.5) in this dimension.

This inequality (1.4) should be understood as a spectral counting rigidity statement. It compares entire eigenvalue distributions rather than individual eigenvalues.

The estimate (1.4) is also a Pólya-type spectral comparison. Pólya’s classical conjecture asks that the Dirichlet and Neumann eigenvalue counting functions of a Euclidean domain be bounded from above and from below, respectively, by the leading Weyl term [28, 29]; here the comparison model is the round sphere rather than a Euclidean domain.

Thus, in the present paper the phrase “Pólya-type” is meant in this precise finite-counting sense: one asks for a non-asymptotic comparison at the exact round thresholds k⁡(k+n−2)k(k+n-2), not merely for this Weyl-order growth exponent.

Remark 1.7.

Weyl’s law and Bishop–Gromov volume comparison imply that a non-round metric with the relevant Ricci lower bound has fewer eigenvalues than the round sphere at sufficiently high energy, but this asymptotic information does not decide the exact finite thresholds in (1.4). The difficulty is precisely finite-index spectral comparison.

One main result of this paper is the full finite-index comparison when the cross-section dimension is two.

Theorem 1.8.

Let (S2,g)(S^{2},g) be a smooth Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1. Then

(1.6) λi​(S2,g)≥λi​(𝕊2,ground),i≥1.\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{2},g)\geq\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}}),\qquad i\geq 1.

Moreover, if equality holds in (1.6) for some i0≥1i_{0}\geq 1, then (S2,g)(S^{2},g) is isometric to (𝕊2,ground)(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}}).

One corollary of the above theorem is the following counting comparison result, which answers Question 1.5 affirmatively.

Corollary 1.9.

Let (S2,g)(S^{2},g) be a smooth Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1. Then

(1.7) 𝒩−Δg​(k⁡(k+1))≤𝒩−Δ𝕊2​(k⁡(k+1)),∀k∈ℤ≥0.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{g}}\big(k(k+1)\big)\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}}\big(k(k+1)\big),\qquad\forall k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

And if the equality in (1.7) holds for some k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, then (S2,g)(S^{2},g) is isometric to (𝕊2,ground)(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}}).

To study Question 1.3 for (M3,g)(M^{3},g), we establish the following strengthening of Corollary 1.9.

Theorem 1.10.

Let XX be one Alexandrov two-sphere with curvature ≥1\geq 1. Then

(1.8) 𝒩−ΔX​(l⁡(l+1))≤𝒩−Δ𝕊2​(l⁡(l+1)),∀l∈ℤ≥0.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{X}}\big(l(l+1)\big)\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{2}}}\big(l(l+1)\big),\qquad\forall l\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Moreover, if equality holds in (1.8) for some l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, then XX is isometric to (𝕊2,ground)(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}}).

Remark 1.11.

Well-known example 17.3 shows that a nonround Alexandrov two-sphere XX with curvature ≥1\geq 1 may still satisfy λ1​(X)=λ1​(𝕊2)=2\lambda_{1}(X)=\lambda_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{2})=2. Thus the rigidity part in Theorem 1.8 does not hold for Alexandrov spheres; the correct hypothesis is equality of the whole finite counting function at a round cluster threshold.

As a consequence of Theorem 1.10, we obtain the following sharp dimension estimate for polynomial growth harmonic functions on three-dimensional manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature and positive asymptotic volume ratio.

Theorem 1.12.

Let (M3,g)(M^{3},g) be a complete Riemannian manifold with Kg≥0K_{g}\geq 0 and AVR⁡(M)>0\operatorname{AVR}(M)>0. Then

(1.9) dimℋd​(M)≤dimℋd​(ℝ3)=(d+1)2,d∈ℤ≥0.\displaystyle\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\leq\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{3})=(d+1)^{2},\qquad d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Moreover, if equality holds in (1.9) for some d∈ℤ+d\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, then (M3,g)(M^{3},g) is isometric to ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Remark 1.13.

From [36], we know dimℋd​(M3)≥2\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(M^{3})\geq 2, i.e. there exists a non-constant harmonic function of polynomial growth on such (M3,g)(M^{3},g).

The paper is written deliberately as a progression of languages. The underlying algebra is always the same: one constructs a first-order operator, compares the two partner operators

T∗​T+candT​T∗+c,\displaystyle T^{*}T+c\quad\text{and}\quad TT^{*}+c,

uses curvature to obtain a one-sided inequality, and then converts the kernel dimension of TT into a finite counting recursion by min–max. What changes from one stage to the next is not the formal spectral mechanism, but the language needed to make the objects canonical. This general mechanism is discussed in Section 2.

  1. Part 11

    . It contains section 3−−63--6, and it deals with rotationally symmetric metrics on Sn−1S^{n-1}.

    For a rotationally symmetric metric, spherical-harmonic decomposition reduces the Laplacian to a family of one-dimensional radial operators. A first-order factorization, together with the curvature inequalities, the identity

    dim⁡(ker⁡𝐁m)=1,ker⁡𝐁m∗={0},\mathrm{dim}(\ker\mathbf{B}_{m})=1,\qquad\ker\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}=\{0\},

    and min–max yields a counting recursion in the angular degree. Summing over the spherical-harmonic multiplicities gives the sharp comparison with the round sphere, as well as the corresponding rigidity statement. When n=3n=3, this is precisely the usual Fourier-mode decomposition on circles.

    Section 3 sets up the rotationally symmetric model and fixes the real Hilbert-space conventions. Sections 4–6 prove the rotationally symmetric model. Section 4 constructs the separated radial operators and the radial ladder identity. Section 5 proves the one-dimensional kernel identity dimℝker⁡𝐁m=1\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\ker\mathbf{B}_{m}=1 and the adjoint-kernel vanishing ker⁡𝐁m∗={0}\ker\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}=\{0\}. Section 6 applies min–max, sums the angular multiplicities, and proves the rotational comparison and rigidity theorem.

  2. Part 22

    . It contains Sections 7–10 and treats arbitrary smooth metrics on S2S^{2}.

    Without rotational symmetry, the angular modes are replaced by the line bundles

    Em=(T1,0​S2)⊗m.E_{m}=(T^{1,0}S^{2})^{\otimes m}.

    The associated first-order operators

    Bm:L2​(Em)⟶L2​(Em+1)B_{m}:L^{2}(E_{m})\longrightarrow L^{2}(E_{m+1})

    satisfy a global curvature-dependent ladder identity. The kernel formulas

    dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1,ker⁡Bm∗={0},\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1,\qquad\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\},

    then give, through spectral pairing and min–max, a recursion for

    Am=Bm∗​Bm+m⁡(m+1)​I.A_{m}=B_{m}^{*}B_{m}+m(m+1)I.

    Iteration yields the sharp finite counting inequalities, and the equality case is handled by a strict min–max argument.

    Section 7 constructs the global two-dimensional ladder on the bundles EmE_{m}, defines BmB_{m} and its formal adjoint, identifies B0∗​B0B_{0}^{*}B_{0} with −Δg-\Delta_{g}, and proves the Riemannian ladder identity. Section 8 proves

    dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1,ker⁡Bm∗={0}.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1,\qquad\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\}.

    Section 9 applies the abstract counting mechanism to the shifted operators AmA_{m}, proves the ordered eigenvalue comparison, and obtains smooth rigidity from the strict form of the ladder inequality.

    Section 10 reformulates the same construction on the Riemann surface (S2,J)(S^{2},J). The bundles are identified with powers of the anticanonical bundle, and the operators BmB_{m} become Dolbeault operators through

    Λ0,1​T∗​S2⊗K−m≃K−m−1.\Lambda^{0,1}T^{*}S^{2}\otimes K^{-m}\simeq K^{-m-1}.

    Riemann–Roch and Serre duality give the kernel dimensions, while the Bochner–Kodaira identity supplies the curvature-dependent ladder inequality. This provides a shorter structural explanation of the smooth counting argument and, more importantly, introduces the language that continues to make sense for singular conformal metrics.

  3. Part 33

    . It contains Sections 11– 15 and extends the comparison and rigidity argument to Alexandrov 22-spheres with curvature at least 11.

    After fixing a conformal identification of the Alexandrov sphere with ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1}, the smooth Gaussian curvature is replaced by the curvature measure ωX\omega_{X}, and the lower curvature bound is encoded by the nonnegative defect measure

    νX:=ωX−d​AX≥0.\nu_{X}:=\omega_{X}-dA_{X}\geq 0.

    The singular argument separates the comparison statement from the equality case. Smooth approximation and Mosco convergence preserve the one-sided ladder inequality, whereas rigidity requires recovering more precise information about the defect measure.

    Section 11 fixes the conformal parametrization

    F:ℂ​ℙ1⟶X,F:\mathbb{CP}^{1}\longrightarrow X,

    represents the metric by a singular conformal factor

    gX=e2​u​g0,g_{X}=e^{2u}g_{0},

    and introduces the curvature measure, the defect measure, the singular Hermitian bundle metrics, the Hilbert spaces HmXH_{m}^{X}, and the maximal operators BmXB_{m}^{X}. It also constructs the heat-regularized metrics gτg_{\tau}, proves that Kgτ≥1K_{g_{\tau}}\geq 1, and records the metric and spectral convergence needed to pass from the smooth theorem to XX.

    Section 12 places the smooth and singular operators in fixed Hilbert spaces and proves Mosco convergence of their graphs, adjoint graphs, and shifted quadratic forms. Passing the smooth Bochner–Kodaira identity to the limit gives the weak singular form order

    Dom⁡(𝔠mX)⊂Dom⁡(𝔞m+1X),𝔠mX≥𝔞m+1X.\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}^{X})\subset\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}^{X}),\qquad\mathfrak{c}_{m}^{X}\geq\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}^{X}.

    The same section proves the holomorphic kernel bound

    ker⁡BmX⊂H0​(ℂ​ℙ1,Kℂ​ℙ1−m),dimℂker⁡BmX≤2​m+1,\ker B_{m}^{X}\subset H^{0}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},K_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}^{-m}),\qquad\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}^{X}\leq 2m+1,

    and establishes the compact-resolvent properties required by the abstract counting recursion.

    Section 13 analyzes the atomic case. Equality in a round counting threshold first saturates every rung of the singular ladder and produces a top-rung space of dimension 2​l+12l+1. If the curvature-defect measure had an atom at pp, the maximal adjoint-domain condition would force every section in that top-rung space to vanish at pp. The resulting loss of one holomorphic degree of freedom contradicts the saturated dimension. Consequently, equality at a round counting threshold forces νX\nu_{X} to be atomless.

    Section 14 treats the complementary case. When the curvature measure is atomless, the weak form inequality can be sharpened on the saturated top rung to the exact defect identity

    𝔠l−1X​(s,s)−𝔞lX​(s,s)=2​l​∫X|s|hl,X2​d​νX,s∈VlX.\mathfrak{c}_{l-1}^{X}(s,s)-\mathfrak{a}_{l}^{X}(s,s)=2l\int_{X}|s|_{h_{l,X}}^{2}\,d\nu_{X},\qquad s\in V_{l}^{X}.

    The proof recovers the curvature term directly from the maximal adjoint domain, using the Poincaré–Lelong formula, truncation, and the vanishing of the boundary fluxes around the zeros of the holomorphic section.

    Section 15 assembles these ingredients. Smooth approximation gives the ordered eigenvalue comparison, while the singular ladder gives the finite counting inequalities at the round thresholds. In the equality case, Section 13 first eliminates atoms. The exact identity from Section 14, together with saturation of the holomorphic top rung, then forces

    νX=0.\nu_{X}=0.

    Gauss–Bonnet and the equality case of Alexandrov volume comparison finally show that XX is isometric to the unit round sphere.

  4. Part 44

    . It contains Sections 16 and 17 and describes both the higher-dimensional limitation of the spectral comparison and its three-dimensional harmonic-growth application.

    Section 16 shows that the two-dimensional ordered eigenvalue comparison does not extend directly to higher-dimensional cross-sections. It constructs an explicit smooth conformal perturbation of the round metric on S3S^{3} satisfying

    Ricg≥2​g\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 2g

    for which a sufficiently high eigenvalue lies strictly below the corresponding round eigenvalue. Thus the success of the line-bundle ladder on S2S^{2} reflects a genuinely two-dimensional structure rather than a general consequence of a Ricci lower bound.

    Section 17 applies the Alexandrov counting theorem to complete three-manifolds with nonnegative sectional curvature and positive asymptotic volume ratio. It first obtains the unique tangent cone at infinity

    C⁡(X),C(X),

    shows that the cross-section XX is an Alexandrov two-sphere with curvature at least 11, and applies the finite-dimensional comparison theorem for polynomial-growth harmonic functions together with the counting estimate of Section 15. This gives

    dimℋd​(M)≤𝒩−ΔX​(d⁡(d+1))≤(d+1)2=dimℋd​(ℝ3).\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(M)\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{X}}\bigl(d(d+1)\bigr)\leq(d+1)^{2}=\dim\mathscr{H}_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{3}).

    If equality holds at a positive integer degree, Alexandrov counting rigidity makes XX the unit round sphere. The tangent cone is therefore ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, and the equality case of Bishop–Gromov comparison forces MM itself to be isometric to ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. The section also explains, through the spherical-football example, why equality of a single Alexandrov eigenvalue is insufficient for rigidity, and concludes with a discussion of the collapsed regime AVR⁡(M)=0\operatorname{AVR}(M)=0.

Thus the paper proceeds from the abstract ladder-counting mechanism to a rotational model, then to an invariant smooth construction and its complex-geometric reformulation, and finally to the singular Alexandrov setting required by the tangent-cone application. The last part records both the sharp three-dimensional consequence and the obstruction to a straightforward higher-dimensional extension.

Proof flowchart for the main conclusions

Each diagram below has a unique terminal node. The first diagram ends at Theorem 1.8, and the second ends at Theorem 1.12. Every solid arrow records a direct logical dependence. The rotational model and the independent S3S^{3} counterexample are not included, since neither is an input to these two final conclusions.

2. The abstract ladder-counting mechanism

The purpose of this section is to isolate the functional-analytic mechanism that is common to all the geometric realizations used below. The geometry determines the Hilbert spaces, the closed first-order operators, their domains, their kernel dimensions, and the form inequality between consecutive levels. Once those facts have been verified, the remaining spectral argument is independent of whether the operators arise from a rotational decomposition, a smooth Riemannian bundle, a Dolbeault complex, or a singular Alexandrov metric.

The common mechanism has six steps.

  1. (1)

    The positive spectra of the partner operators T∗​TT^{*}T and T​T∗TT^{*} agree, including multiplicity.

  2. (2)

    The space ker⁡T\ker T gives an unpaired block at the bottom of T∗​TT^{*}T and therefore produces an index shift.

  3. (3)

    The condition ker⁡T∗={0}\ker T^{*}=\{0\} removes the corresponding unpaired block on the T​T∗TT^{*} side.

  4. (4)

    A quadratic-form inequality compares the T​T∗TT^{*} partner at one level with the T∗​TT^{*}T operator at the next level.

  5. (5)

    The min–max principle converts this comparison into a recursion for strict and closed counting functions.

  6. (6)

    The recursion terminates when the shift at the final level reaches the prescribed round threshold.

This is precisely the spectral mechanism behind the different geometric stages of the proof.

All Hilbert spaces in this section may be real or complex. We write 𝔽∈{ℝ,ℂ}\mathbb{F}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\} for the ground field, and all dimensions and spectral multiplicities are taken over 𝔽\mathbb{F}.

Notation 2.1.

Let {Hm}m≥0\{H_{m}\}_{m\geq 0} be Hilbert spaces, and let

Bm:Dom⁡(Bm)⊂Hm⟶Hm+1,m≥0,\displaystyle B_{m}:\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m})\subset H_{m}\longrightarrow H_{m+1},\qquad m\geq 0,

be closed densely defined operators. Let

0≤α0<α1<α2<⋯.\displaystyle 0\leq\alpha_{0}<\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\cdots.

Define the closed quadratic forms

𝔞m​(u,v)\displaystyle\mathfrak{a}_{m}(u,v) :=⟨Bm​u,Bm​v⟩Hm+1+αm​⟨u,v⟩Hm,\displaystyle:=\langle B_{m}u,B_{m}v\rangle_{H_{m+1}}+\alpha_{m}\langle u,v\rangle_{H_{m}}, Dom⁡(𝔞m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m}) =Dom⁡(Bm),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}),
𝔠m​(s,t)\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}(s,t) :=⟨Bm∗​s,Bm∗​t⟩Hm+αm​⟨s,t⟩Hm+1,\displaystyle:=\langle B_{m}^{*}s,B_{m}^{*}t\rangle_{H_{m}}+\alpha_{m}\langle s,t\rangle_{H_{m+1}}, Dom⁡(𝔠m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}) =Dom⁡(Bm∗).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{*}).

Let AmA_{m} and CmC_{m} be the associated self-adjoint operators. Equivalently,

Am=Bm∗​Bm+αm​Iin ​Hm,Cm=Bm​Bm∗+αm​Iin ​Hm+1.\displaystyle A_{m}=B_{m}^{*}B_{m}+\alpha_{m}I\quad\text{in }H_{m},\qquad C_{m}=B_{m}B_{m}^{*}+\alpha_{m}I\quad\text{in }H_{m+1}.

We assume that, for every m≥0m\geq 0, both AmA_{m} and CmC_{m} have compact resolvent. Since Am,Cm≥0A_{m},C_{m}\geq 0, this is equivalent to requiring the bounded operators

(Am+I)−1:Hm⟶Hm,(Cm+I)−1:Hm+1⟶Hm+1\displaystyle(A_{m}+I)^{-1}:H_{m}\longrightarrow H_{m},\qquad(C_{m}+I)^{-1}:H_{m+1}\longrightarrow H_{m+1}

to be compact.

Set

rm:=dim𝔽ker⁡Bm,sm:=dim𝔽ker⁡Bm∗.\displaystyle r_{m}:=\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\ker B_{m},\qquad s_{m}:=\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\ker B_{m}^{*}.

These dimensions are finite because the eigenspaces of AmA_{m} and CmC_{m} at αm\alpha_{m} are finite dimensional.

Lemma 2.2.

In the setting of Notation 2.1, the positive spectra of Bm∗​BmB_{m}^{*}B_{m} and Bm​Bm∗B_{m}B_{m}^{*} agree, including multiplicity. More precisely, for every λ>0\lambda>0, the map BmB_{m} gives an isomorphism

Bm:ker⁡(Bm∗​Bm−λ​I)⟶ker⁡(Bm​Bm∗−λ​I),\displaystyle B_{m}:\ker(B_{m}^{*}B_{m}-\lambda I)\longrightarrow\ker(B_{m}B_{m}^{*}-\lambda I),

whose inverse is λ−1​Bm∗\lambda^{-1}B_{m}^{*}. Consequently,

(2.1) λj+rm(Am)=λj+sm(Cm),j=0,1,2,…,\displaystyle\lambda_{j+r_{m}}(A_{m})=\lambda_{j+s_{m}}(C_{m}),\qquad j=0,1,2,\ldots,
NAm<​(Λ)−NCm<​(Λ)=rm−sm,∀Λ>αm,\displaystyle N_{A_{m}}^{<}(\Lambda)-N_{C_{m}}^{<}(\Lambda)=r_{m}-s_{m},\quad\quad\forall\Lambda>\alpha_{m},
(2.2) 𝒩Am​(Λ)−𝒩Cm​(Λ)=rm−sm,∀Λ≥αm,.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{A_{m}}(\Lambda)-\mathcal{N}_{C_{m}}(\Lambda)=r_{m}-s_{m},\quad\quad\forall\Lambda\geq\alpha_{m},.
Proof.

Suppose that u∈Dom⁡(Bm∗​Bm)u\in\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{*}B_{m}) and

Bm∗​Bm​u=λ​u,λ>0.\displaystyle B_{m}^{*}B_{m}u=\lambda u,\qquad\lambda>0.

Then Bm​u≠0B_{m}u\neq 0. Moreover, Bm​u∈Dom⁡(Bm∗)B_{m}u\in\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{*}), and Bm∗​(Bm​u)=λ​u∈Dom⁡(Bm)B_{m}^{*}(B_{m}u)=\lambda u\in\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}). Hence

Bm​Bm∗​(Bm​u)=λ​Bm​u.\displaystyle B_{m}B_{m}^{*}(B_{m}u)=\lambda B_{m}u.

Conversely, if v∈Dom⁡(Bm​Bm∗)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}B_{m}^{*}) and

Bm​Bm∗​v=λ​v,λ>0,\displaystyle B_{m}B_{m}^{*}v=\lambda v,\qquad\lambda>0,

then Bm∗​v≠0B_{m}^{*}v\neq 0 and

Bm∗​Bm​(Bm∗​v)=λ​Bm∗​v.\displaystyle B_{m}^{*}B_{m}(B_{m}^{*}v)=\lambda B_{m}^{*}v.

The two maps are inverse after multiplication by λ−1\lambda^{-1}. Thus the positive eigenspaces have the same dimensions.

The eigenspace of AmA_{m} at αm\alpha_{m} is ker⁡Bm\ker B_{m}, while the eigenspace of CmC_{m} at αm\alpha_{m} is ker⁡Bm∗\ker B_{m}^{*}. Removing these two bottom eigenspaces leaves the same ordered sequence of shifted positive eigenvalues. This proves (2.1). The two counting identities in (2.2) follow by counting the bottom eigenspaces and the paired positive spectrum separately. ∎

The quadratic-form order Cm≥Am+1C_{m}\geq A_{m+1} will always mean both the form-domain inclusion and the inequality displayed below. On a singular space, the formal commutator identity on smooth sections of the regular set does not by itself determine the closed realizations of the two operators. Thus both the domain inclusion and the form inequality must be established at the level of the closed quadratic forms.

Lemma 2.3.

Fix m≥0m\geq 0. Assume that the consecutive forms satisfy

Dom⁡(𝔠m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}) ⊂Dom⁡(𝔞m+1),\displaystyle\subset\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}),
(2.3) 𝔠m​(v,v)\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}(v,v) ≥𝔞m+1​(v,v),v∈Dom⁡(𝔠m).\displaystyle\geq\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}(v,v),\qquad v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}).

Then ker⁡Bm∗={0}\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\}.

Proof.

Let v∈ker⁡Bm∗v\in\ker B_{m}^{*}. Then v∈Dom⁡(𝔠m)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}), so (2.3) gives v∈Dom⁡(𝔞m+1)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}) and

αm+1​‖v‖Hm+12\displaystyle\alpha_{m+1}\|v\|_{H_{m+1}}^{2} ≤𝔞m+1​(v,v)≤𝔠m​(v,v)=αm​‖v‖Hm+12.\displaystyle\leq\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}(v,v)\leq\mathfrak{c}_{m}(v,v)=\alpha_{m}\|v\|_{H_{m+1}}^{2}.

Since αm+1>αm\alpha_{m+1}>\alpha_{m}, one has v=0v=0. ∎

Proposition 2.4.

Fix m≥0m\geq 0 and assume (2.3). Then, for every j≥0j\geq 0,

(2.4) λj+rm​(Am)=λj​(Cm)≥λj​(Am+1).\displaystyle\lambda_{j+r_{m}}(A_{m})=\lambda_{j}(C_{m})\geq\lambda_{j}(A_{m+1}).

Consequently, for every Λ∈ℝ\Lambda\in\mathbb{R},

(2.5) NAm<​(Λ)\displaystyle N_{A_{m}}^{<}(\Lambda) ≤rm+NAm+1<​(Λ),𝒩Am​(Λ)\displaystyle\leq r_{m}+N_{A_{m+1}}^{<}(\Lambda),\quad\quad\mathcal{N}_{A_{m}}(\Lambda) ≤rm+𝒩Am+1​(Λ).\displaystyle\leq r_{m}+\mathcal{N}_{A_{m+1}}(\Lambda).
Proof.

Lemma 2.3 gives ker⁡Bm∗={0}\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\}. Therefore Lemma 2.2 gives the equality in (2.4).

The form inequality (2.3) and the min–max principle give

λj​(Cm)≥λj​(Am+1),j≥0.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(C_{m})\geq\lambda_{j}(A_{m+1}),\qquad j\geq 0.

This proves (2.4).

Equivalently, the number of eigenvalues of CmC_{m} below, or below and at, a fixed threshold does not exceed the corresponding number for Am+1A_{m+1}, this proves (2.5). ∎

Proposition 2.5.

Let 0≤q≤l0\leq q\leq l, and assume that (2.3) holds for m=q,q+1,…,l−1m=q,q+1,\ldots,l-1. Then

NAq<​(αl)\displaystyle N_{A_{q}}^{<}(\alpha_{l}) ≤∑m=ql−1rm,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{m=q}^{l-1}r_{m},
(2.6) 𝒩Aq​(αl)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{A_{q}}(\alpha_{l}) ≤∑m=qlrm.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{m=q}^{l}r_{m}.

Since

Al=Bl∗​Bl+αl​I≥αl​I,\displaystyle A_{l}=B_{l}^{*}B_{l}+\alpha_{l}I\geq\alpha_{l}I,

one has

NAl<​(αl)=0,𝒩Al​(αl)=dim𝔽ker⁡Bl=rl.\displaystyle N_{A_{l}}^{<}(\alpha_{l})=0,\qquad\mathcal{N}_{A_{l}}(\alpha_{l})=\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\ker B_{l}=r_{l}.

Iterating the two inequalities in (2.5) from level qq to level ll gives (2.6). ∎

Proposition 2.6.

Let l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, and assume that (2.3) holds for m=0,1,…,l−1m=0,1,\ldots,l-1. Suppose that

rm≤ρm,0≤m≤l,\displaystyle r_{m}\leq\rho_{m},\qquad 0\leq m\leq l,
(2.7) 𝒩A0​(αl)=∑m=0lρm.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{A_{0}}(\alpha_{l})=\sum_{m=0}^{l}\rho_{m}.

𝒩Am​(αl)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{A_{m}}(\alpha_{l}) =rm+𝒩Am+1​(αl),\displaystyle=r_{m}+\mathcal{N}_{A_{m+1}}(\alpha_{l}),

Then

Set

nm:=𝒩Am​(αl),qm:=𝒩Cm​(αl).\displaystyle n_{m}:=\mathcal{N}_{A_{m}}(\alpha_{l}),\qquad q_{m}:=\mathcal{N}_{C_{m}}(\alpha_{l}).

𝔠l−1​(s,s)=αl​‖s‖Hl2.\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{l-1}(s,s)=\alpha_{l}\|s\|_{H_{l}}^{2}.

αl​‖s‖Hl2\displaystyle\alpha_{l}\|s\|_{H_{l}}^{2} ≤𝔞l​(s,s)≤𝔠l−1​(s,s)=αl​‖s‖Hl2.\displaystyle\leq\mathfrak{a}_{l}(s,s)\leq\mathfrak{c}_{l-1}(s,s)=\alpha_{l}\|s\|_{H_{l}}^{2}.

El⊂Vl⊂ker⁡Bl.\displaystyle E_{l}\subset V_{l}\subset\ker B_{l}.

The first and last spaces have the same dimension rlr_{l}, so all three spaces coincide. This proves (2.10), and the same argument gives (2.11). ∎

Corollary 2.7.

Assume that

αm=m⁡(m+1),rm≤2​m+1,m≥0,\displaystyle\alpha_{m}=m(m+1),\qquad r_{m}\leq 2m+1,\qquad m\geq 0,

and that (2.3) holds at every level. Then, for every l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},

(2.12) NA0<​(l⁡(l+1))≤l2,𝒩A0​(l⁡(l+1))≤(l+1)2.\displaystyle N_{A_{0}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr)\leq l^{2},\quad\quad\mathcal{N}_{A_{0}}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr)\leq(l+1)^{2}.

If equality holds in the closed-counting estimate in (2.12), then all conclusions of Proposition 2.6 hold with

ρm=2​m+1,0≤m≤l.\displaystyle\rho_{m}=2m+1,\qquad 0\leq m\leq l.
Proof.

Proposition 2.5 and the identities

∑m=0l−1(2​m+1)=l2,∑m=0l(2​m+1)=(l+1)2\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}(2m+1)=l^{2},\qquad\sum_{m=0}^{l}(2m+1)=(l+1)^{2}

give (2.12). The eigenvalue statement is the strict-counting formulation of the first inequality. The equality assertion follows from Proposition 2.6. ∎

Remark 2.8 (Dictionary for the four geometric realizations).

The abstract results above will be used through the following identifications.

  1. (1)

    In the rotationally symmetric proof, 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}, the spaces HmH_{m} are the radial Hilbert spaces, Bm=𝐁mB_{m}=\mathbf{B}_{m}, and αm=m⁡(m+n−2)\alpha_{m}=m(m+n-2). The geometric work is the identification of the correct pole-compatible domains, the one-dimensional kernel computation rm=1r_{m}=1, and the radial curvature form inequality. Proposition 2.5 then supplies the spectral recursion.

  2. (2)

    In the smooth Riemannian proof, 𝔽=ℂ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{C}, Hm=L2​(Em)H_{m}=L^{2}(E_{m}), BmB_{m} is the closed bundle operator, and αm=m⁡(m+1)\alpha_{m}=m(m+1). The bundle construction, the curvature identity, and the kernel dimension rm=2​m+1r_{m}=2m+1 are the geometric inputs. Corollary 2.7 supplies the counting argument.

  3. (3)

    In the complex-geometric proof, the same ladder is written on the anticanonical powers K−mK^{-m}. Riemann–Roch and Serre duality provide the kernel information, while the Bochner–Kodaira identity provides the form inequality. The Hilbert-space conclusion is again Corollary 2.7.

  4. (4)

    In the Alexandrov proof, Hm=HmXH_{m}=H_{m}^{X} and Bm=BmXB_{m}=B_{m}^{X} are the singular closed operators with their maximal Hilbert-space domains. The singular analysis establishes compactness, the weak form inequality, and the cohomological estimate rm≤2​m+1r_{m}\leq 2m+1. The closed-counting part of Corollary 2.7 gives the finite bound, while Proposition 2.6 gives the full top-rung equality space when the round count is saturated.

Thus the later sections need only verify the geometric and domain-theoretic hypotheses appropriate to their setting; the partner-spectrum algebra, the index shift, the min–max recursion, and the equality propagation will not be repeated.

Part I Rotationally symmetric case

3. Rotationally symmetric model and notation

This part deals with the rotationally symmetric model in arbitrary dimension. Its purpose is not to reduce the general theorem to a symmetric case, but to display the geometric input to the abstract ladder mechanism of Section 2 in the elementary language of separated variables.

Definition 3.1.

Let n≥3n\geq 3. A smooth metric gg on Sn−1S^{n-1} is called rotationally symmetric if

g=d​r2+f​(r)2​g𝕊n−2,0≤r≤a,\displaystyle g=dr^{2}+f(r)^{2}g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}},\qquad 0\leq r\leq a,

where g𝕊n−2g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}} is the unit round metric. Smoothness at the two poles means that ff is smooth on [0,a][0,a], positive on (0,a)(0,a), and

f⁡(0)=f⁡(a)=0,f′​(0)=1,f′​(a)=−1,\displaystyle f(0)=f(a)=0,\qquad f^{\prime}(0)=1,\qquad f^{\prime}(a)=-1,

together with the usual even-order compatibility conditions at the poles.

Notation 3.2.

Throughout this part,

g=d​r2+f​(r)2​g𝕊n−2.\displaystyle g=dr^{2}+f(r)^{2}g_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}}.

All Hilbert spaces, inner products, forms, and dimensions are taken over the real field. For m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, let ℋm​(ℝn−1)\mathcal{H}_{m}(\mathbb{R}^{n-1}) denote the restrictions to 𝕊n−2\mathbb{S}^{n-2} of the homogeneous harmonic polynomials of degree mm on ℝn−1\mathbb{R}^{n-1}, and set

dn−2,m\displaystyle d_{n-2,m} :=dimℝℋm​(ℝn−1),\displaystyle:=\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\mathcal{H}_{m}(\mathbb{R}^{n-1}), λm\displaystyle\lambda_{m} :=m⁡(m+n−3).\displaystyle:=m(m+n-3).

Thus λm\lambda_{m} is the Laplace eigenvalue corresponding to the space of degree-mm spherical harmonics on 𝕊n−2\mathbb{S}^{n-2}.

We define

𝒟m:={u∈C∞([0,a]):\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{m}:=\Bigl\{u\in C^{\infty}([0,a]):\ u⁡(r)=rm​ψ​(r2)=(a−r)m​φ​((a−r)2)\displaystyle u(r)=r^{m}\psi(r^{2})=(a-r)^{m}\varphi\bigl((a-r)^{2}\bigr)
for some ψ,φ∈C∞(ℝ)}.\displaystyle\text{for some }\psi,\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})\Bigr\}.

The radial Hilbert space is

(3.1) H:=L2​((0,a),fn−2​𝑑r,ℝ),⟨u,v⟩H:=∫0au​v​fn−2​𝑑r.\displaystyle H:=L^{2}\bigl((0,a),f^{n-2}\,dr;\mathbb{R}\bigr),\qquad\langle u,v\rangle_{H}:=\int_{0}^{a}uvf^{n-2}\,dr.

For later use, write

Krad:=−f′′f,Ktan:=1−(f′)2f2on (0,a).\displaystyle K_{\mathrm{rad}}:=-\frac{f^{\prime\prime}}{f},\qquad K_{\mathrm{tan}}:=\frac{1-(f^{\prime})^{2}}{f^{2}}\qquad\text{on }(0,a).

When n≥4n\geq 4, these are respectively the radial and tangential sectional curvatures. When n=3n=3, KtanK_{\mathrm{tan}} is the auxiliary radial quantity which occurs in the separated form comparison. The pole compatibility of ff implies that both quantities extend smoothly to the poles.

Definition 3.3.

For m≥0m\geq 0, define on 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m} the densely defined nonnegative symmetric form

𝔩m​[u,v]:=∫0a(u′​v′+λmf2​u​v)​fn−2​𝑑r.\displaystyle\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,v]:=\int_{0}^{a}\left(u^{\prime}v^{\prime}+\frac{\lambda_{m}}{f^{2}}uv\right)f^{n-2}\,dr.

For m=0m=0, the angular term is identically zero; in particular, this definition does not involve a product of zero with a potentially divergent integral. Lemma 4.3 below shows that this form is closable in HH. We denote its closure, again, by 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m}, and 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m} denotes the nonnegative self-adjoint operator associated with the closed form 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m}. Thus

Dom(𝐋m):={u∈Dom(𝔩m):\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{L}_{m}):=\Bigl\{u\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m}):\ there exists ​w∈H​ such that\displaystyle\text{there exists }w\in H\text{ such that}
(3.2) 𝔩m[u,v]=⟨w,v⟩H for every v∈Dom(𝔩m)},\displaystyle\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,v]=\langle w,v\rangle_{H}\text{ for every }v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m})\Bigr\},

and 𝐋m​u=w\mathbf{L}_{m}u=w. On the smooth core its formal expression is

ℒm​u:=−u′′−(n−2)​f′f​u′+m⁡(m+n−3)f2​u.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{m}u:=-u^{\prime\prime}-(n-2)\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}u^{\prime}+\frac{m(m+n-3)}{f^{2}}u.
Definition 3.4.

For m≥0m\geq 0, define

(3.3) ℬm​u:=u′−m​f′f​u,u∈𝒟m.\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}u:=u^{\prime}-m\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}u,\qquad u\in\mathscr{D}_{m}.

We first regard this as the densely defined operator

ℬm:𝒟m⊂H⟶H.\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}:\mathscr{D}_{m}\subset H\longrightarrow H.

Its formal adjoint expression with respect to (3.1) is

(3.4) ℬm†​v:=−v′−(m+n−2)​f′f​v.\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\dagger}v:=-v^{\prime}-(m+n-2)\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}v.

For v∈𝒟m+1v\in\mathscr{D}_{m+1}, the pole conditions imply that ℬm†​v∈H\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\dagger}v\in H. Moreover, for u∈𝒟mu\in\mathscr{D}_{m} and v∈𝒟m+1v\in\mathscr{D}_{m+1}, integration by parts gives

⟨ℬm​u,v⟩H=⟨u,ℬm†​v⟩H.\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{B}_{m}u,v\rangle_{H}=\langle u,\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\dagger}v\rangle_{H}.

Since 𝒟m+1\mathscr{D}_{m+1} is dense in HH, ℬm\mathcal{B}_{m} is closable. We set

𝐁m:=ℬm¯:Dom⁡(𝐁m)⊂H⟶H,\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{m}:=\overline{\mathcal{B}_{m}}:\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m})\subset H\longrightarrow H,

where

Dom(𝐁m)=𝒟m¯∥⋅∥𝐁m,∥u∥𝐁m2:=∥u∥H2+∥ℬmu∥H2.\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m})=\overline{\mathscr{D}_{m}}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{\mathbf{B}_{m}}},\qquad\|u\|_{\mathbf{B}_{m}}^{2}:=\|u\|_{H}^{2}+\|\mathcal{B}_{m}u\|_{H}^{2}.

Its Hilbert-space adjoint is denoted by

𝐁m∗:Dom⁡(𝐁m∗)⊂H⟶H.\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}:\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*})\subset H\longrightarrow H.

Thus v∈Dom⁡(𝐁m∗)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}) exactly when there exists w∈Hw\in H such that

⟨𝐁m​u,v⟩H=⟨u,w⟩H,u∈Dom⁡(𝐁m),\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{B}_{m}u,v\rangle_{H}=\langle u,w\rangle_{H},\qquad u\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m}),

and then 𝐁m∗​v=w\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}v=w. On 𝒟m+1\mathscr{D}_{m+1}, 𝐁m∗\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*} agrees with the expression in (3.4).

4. Frequency decomposition and the radial ladder

Theorem 4.1.

Let d≥2d\geq 2. For j≥0j\geq 0, let 𝒫j​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the homogeneous polynomials of degree jj, and let

ℋj​(ℝd):={P∈𝒫j​(ℝd):Δℝd​P=0}.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{j}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):=\{P\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\mathbb{R}^{d}):\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}P=0\}.

Every Pj∈𝒫j​(ℝd)P_{j}\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) has a unique decomposition

Pj​(x)=Hj​(x)+|x|2​Hj−2​(x)+⋯+|x|2​q​Hj−2​q​(x),q=⌊j/2⌋,\displaystyle P_{j}(x)=H_{j}(x)+|x|^{2}H_{j-2}(x)+\cdots+|x|^{2q}H_{j-2q}(x),\qquad q=\lfloor j/2\rfloor,

where Hj−2​ℓ∈ℋj−2​ℓ​(ℝd)H_{j-2\ell}\in\mathcal{H}_{j-2\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Consequently,

(4.1) Pj|𝕊d−1∈ℋj​(𝕊d−1)⊕ℋj−2​(𝕊d−1)⊕⋯.\displaystyle P_{j}|_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\in\mathcal{H}_{j}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\oplus\mathcal{H}_{j-2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})\oplus\cdots.

In particular, if Y∈ℋm​(𝕊d−1)Y\in\mathcal{H}_{m}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}), then

(4.2) ∫𝕊d−1Pj​(θ)​Y​(θ)​d​V𝕊d−1​(θ)=0\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}P_{j}(\theta)Y(\theta)\,dV_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}(\theta)=0

unless j=m+2​ℓj=m+2\ell for some ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0.

Proof.

The decomposition is the standard Fischer decomposition; see [3, Proposition 5.5 and Theorem 5.7, pp. 76–77]. Restriction to the unit sphere and orthogonality of spherical harmonics of different degrees give (4.1) and (4.2). ∎

Lemma 4.2.

Let w∈C∞​(Sn−1,ℝ)w\in C^{\infty}(S^{n-1};\mathbb{R}), let m≥0m\geq 0, and let φ∈ℋm​(ℝn−1)|𝕊n−2\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{m}(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})|_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}}. Then

u⁡(r):=∫𝕊n−2w⁡(r,θ)​φ​(θ)​d​V𝕊n−2∈𝒟m.\displaystyle u(r):=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}}w(r,\theta)\varphi(\theta)\,dV_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}}\in\mathscr{D}_{m}.
Proof.

Smoothness on (0,a)(0,a) follows by differentiation under the integral sign. Near r=0r=0, use smooth normal coordinates x=r​θ∈ℝn−1x=r\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1} and write w⁡(r,θ)=W0​(r​θ)w(r,\theta)=W_{0}(r\theta) with W0W_{0} smooth. For every NN,

W0​(r​θ)=∑j=0m+2​N+1rj​Pj​(θ)+O⁡(rm+2​N+2),\displaystyle W_{0}(r\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{m+2N+1}r^{j}P_{j}(\theta)+O(r^{m+2N+2}),

where PjP_{j} is homogeneous of degree jj. By Theorem 4.1, the integral of PjP_{j} against the degree-mm harmonic φ\varphi vanishes unless j=m+2​ℓj=m+2\ell. Hence

u⁡(r)=∑ℓ=0Ncℓ​rm+2​ℓ+O⁡(rm+2​N+2)\displaystyle u(r)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{N}c_{\ell}r^{m+2\ell}+O(r^{m+2N+2})

for every NN. Therefore r−m​u​(r)r^{-m}u(r) extends smoothly across r=0r=0 and has only even Taylor coefficients. It follows that, near r=0r=0,

u⁡(r)=rm​ψ0​(r2)\displaystyle u(r)=r^{m}\psi_{0}(r^{2})

for a smooth function ψ0\psi_{0}.

The same argument in normal coordinates at the other pole gives

u⁡(r)=(a−r)m​φ0​((a−r)2)\displaystyle u(r)=(a-r)^{m}\varphi_{0}\bigl((a-r)^{2}\bigr)

near r=ar=a. The functions r−m​u​(r)r^{-m}u(r) and (a−r)−m​u​(r)(a-r)^{-m}u(r), viewed respectively as functions of r2r^{2} and (a−r)2(a-r)^{2}, are smooth on their compact half-intervals and therefore admit smooth extensions to ℝ\mathbb{R}. This is exactly the definition of u∈𝒟mu\in\mathscr{D}_{m}. ∎

Lemma 4.3.

For every m≥0m\geq 0:

  1. (1)

    the form 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m} initially defined on 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m} is closable, and, with 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m} denoting its closure, the embedding

    (4.3) Dom⁡(𝔩m)↪H\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m})\hookrightarrow H

    is compact;

  2. (2)

    𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m} is nonnegative, self-adjoint, and has compact resolvent;

  3. (3)

    every eigenfunction of 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m} belongs to 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m}.

Proof.

Fix a real L2​(𝕊n−2)L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{n-2})-normalized spherical harmonic YmY_{m} of degree mm and define

Jm:H⟶L2​(Sn−1,g,ℝ),Jm​u​(r,θ):=u⁡(r)​Ym​(θ).\displaystyle J_{m}:H\longrightarrow L^{2}(S^{n-1},g;\mathbb{R}),\qquad J_{m}u(r,\theta):=u(r)Y_{m}(\theta).

Then JmJ_{m} is an isometry and, for u,v∈𝒟mu,v\in\mathscr{D}_{m},

⟨Jm​u,Jm​v⟩L2​(Sn−1,g)\displaystyle\langle J_{m}u,J_{m}v\rangle_{L^{2}(S^{n-1},g)} =⟨u,v⟩H,\displaystyle=\langle u,v\rangle_{H},
(4.4) ∫Sn−1⟨∇(Jm​u),∇(Jm​v)⟩g​d​Vg\displaystyle\int_{S^{n-1}}\langle\nabla(J_{m}u),\nabla(J_{m}v)\rangle_{g}\,dV_{g} =𝔩m​[u,v].\displaystyle=\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,v].

The pole conditions defining 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m} imply Jm​𝒟m⊂C∞​(Sn−1)J_{m}\mathscr{D}_{m}\subset C^{\infty}(S^{n-1}). Thus

(4.5) ‖Jm​u‖H1​(Sn−1,g)2=‖u‖H2+𝔩m​[u,u],u∈𝒟m.\displaystyle\|J_{m}u\|_{H^{1}(S^{n-1},g)}^{2}=\|u\|_{H}^{2}+\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,u],\qquad u\in\mathscr{D}_{m}.

If uj→0u_{j}\to 0 in HH and 𝔩m​[uj−uk,uj−uk]→0\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u_{j}-u_{k},u_{j}-u_{k}]\to 0, then Jm​ujJ_{m}u_{j} converges in H1H^{1} and converges to 00 in L2L^{2}; hence its H1H^{1} limit is 00. This proves closability. After taking closures, (4.5) identifies Dom⁡(𝔩m)\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m}) isometrically with a closed subspace of H1​(Sn−1,g)H^{1}(S^{n-1},g). Rellich compactness on the closed manifold therefore gives (4.3).

The representation theorem for closed nonnegative forms gives the nonnegative self-adjoint operator 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m} characterized by (3.2); see [26, Proposition 3.1.7, p. 25]. The compactness of the form-domain embedding implies that (I+𝐋m)−1(I+\mathbf{L}_{m})^{-1} is compact.

It remains to prove the last assertion. Let 𝐋m​u=λ​u\mathbf{L}_{m}u=\lambda u. For Φ∈C∞​(Sn−1)\Phi\in C^{\infty}(S^{n-1}), set

vΦ​(r):=∫𝕊n−2Φ⁡(r,θ)​Ym​(θ)​𝑑θ.\displaystyle v_{\Phi}(r):=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-2}}\Phi(r,\theta)Y_{m}(\theta)\,d\theta.

Lemma 4.2 gives vΦ∈𝒟mv_{\Phi}\in\mathscr{D}_{m}. Approximating uu by elements of 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m} in the form norm and using (4.4), we obtain

∫Sn−1⟨∇(Jm​u),∇Φ⟩g​d​Vg=𝔩m​[u,vΦ]=λ​⟨u,vΦ⟩H=λ​∫Sn−1Jm​u​Φ​d​Vg.\displaystyle\int_{S^{n-1}}\langle\nabla(J_{m}u),\nabla\Phi\rangle_{g}\,dV_{g}=\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,v_{\Phi}]=\lambda\langle u,v_{\Phi}\rangle_{H}=\lambda\int_{S^{n-1}}J_{m}u\,\Phi\,dV_{g}.

Thus Jm​uJ_{m}u is a weak eigenfunction of −Δg-\Delta_{g}. Elliptic regularity gives

Jm​u∈C∞​(Sn−1);\displaystyle J_{m}u\in C^{\infty}(S^{n-1});

see [5, Theorem 44, p. 68]. Projecting onto YmY_{m} and applying Lemma 4.2 yields u∈𝒟mu\in\mathscr{D}_{m}. ∎

Lemma 4.4.

For every Λ∈ℝ\Lambda\in\mathbb{R},

N−Δg<​(Λ)=∑m=0∞dn−2,m​N𝐋m<​(Λ).\displaystyle N_{-\Delta_{g}}^{<}(\Lambda)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_{n-2,m}N_{\mathbf{L}_{m}}^{<}(\Lambda).

The same identity holds with N<N^{<} replaced by the closed counting function 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Proof.

For each mm, choose a real orthonormal basis of ℋm​(𝕊n−2)\mathcal{H}_{m}(\mathbb{S}^{n-2}), denoted by

{φm,α}α=1dn−2,m.\displaystyle\{\varphi_{m,\alpha}\}_{\alpha=1}^{d_{n-2,m}}.

The spherical-harmonic decomposition

L2​(𝕊n−2,ℝ)=⨁^m=0∞​ℋm​(𝕊n−2)\displaystyle L^{2}(\mathbb{S}^{n-2};\mathbb{R})=\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m=0}^{\infty}\mathcal{H}_{m}(\mathbb{S}^{n-2})

induces the unitary decomposition

L2​(Sn−1,g,ℝ)≅⨁^m=0∞​⨁^α=1dn−2,m​H,{um,α}⟼∑m,αum,α​(r)​φm,α​(θ).\displaystyle L^{2}(S^{n-1},g;\mathbb{R})\cong\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m=0}^{\infty}\widehat{\bigoplus}_{\alpha=1}^{d_{n-2,m}}H,\qquad\{u_{m,\alpha}\}\longmapsto\sum_{m,\alpha}u_{m,\alpha}(r)\varphi_{m,\alpha}(\theta).

For a finite family with um,α∈𝒟mu_{m,\alpha}\in\mathscr{D}_{m}, orthogonality and integration by parts on 𝕊n−2\mathbb{S}^{n-2} give

∫Sn−1|∇w|g2​d​Vg=∑m,α𝔩m​[um,α,um,α].\displaystyle\int_{S^{n-1}}|\nabla w|_{g}^{2}\,dV_{g}=\sum_{m,\alpha}\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u_{m,\alpha},u_{m,\alpha}].

Conversely, Lemma 4.2 shows that the angular coefficients of every smooth function lie in the corresponding 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m}. Finite spherical-harmonic truncations of smooth functions converge in H1H^{1}, so closure of the preceding identity gives an orthogonal direct-sum decomposition of the Dirichlet form. Hence

−Δg≅⨁^m=0∞​⨁^α=1dn−2,m​𝐋m.\displaystyle-\Delta_{g}\cong\widehat{\bigoplus}_{m=0}^{\infty}\widehat{\bigoplus}_{\alpha=1}^{d_{n-2,m}}\mathbf{L}_{m}.

The strict and closed counting identities follow, including multiplicities. The sums are finite at each fixed threshold because

𝐋m≥m⁡(m+n−3)max[0,a]⁡f2​I,\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{m}\geq\frac{m(m+n-3)}{\max_{[0,a]}f^{2}}\,I,

so only finitely many angular degrees can contribute below a prescribed number. ∎

Lemma 4.5.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

(4.6) ℬm​𝒟m⊂𝒟m+1.\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}\mathscr{D}_{m}\subset\mathscr{D}_{m+1}.

Near r=0r=0, smoothness of the warping function gives

ℬm​u=rm+1​(2​ψ′​(r2)−m​H0​(r2)​ψ​(r2)).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}u=r^{m+1}\bigl(2\psi^{\prime}(r^{2})-mH_{0}(r^{2})\psi(r^{2})\bigr).

Lemma 4.6.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

Dom(𝐁m∗)=𝒟m+1¯∥⋅∥𝐁m∗,∥v∥𝐁m∗2:=∥v∥H2+∥𝐁m∗v∥H2.\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*})=\overline{\mathscr{D}_{m+1}}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}}},\qquad\|v\|_{\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}}^{2}:=\|v\|_{H}^{2}+\|\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}v\|_{H}^{2}.

Let v∈Dom⁡(𝐁m∗)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}) and set w=𝐁m∗​vw=\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}v. On compact subintervals of (0,a)(0,a),

−v′−(m+n−2)​f′f​v=w\displaystyle-v^{\prime}-(m+n-2)\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}v=w

(4.7) (fm+n−2​v)′=−fm+n−2​w.\displaystyle\bigl(f^{m+n-2}v\bigr)^{\prime}=-f^{m+n-2}w.

The integration constant at either endpoint is zero: otherwise v∼c​f−(m+n−2)v\sim cf^{-(m+n-2)}, which is not in L2​((0,a),fn−2​d​r)L^{2}((0,a),f^{n-2}dr) for n≥3n\geq 3.

Near r=0r=0, (4.7) and Cauchy–Schwarz imply

Choose a cutoff χε\chi_{\varepsilon} which vanishes in the two ε\varepsilon-neighborhoods of the endpoints, equals one outside the two 2​ε2\varepsilon-neighborhoods, and satisfies |χε′|≤C​ε−1|\chi_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}|\leq C\varepsilon^{-1}. Then χε​v→v\chi_{\varepsilon}v\to v in HH and, by (4.8),

ℬm†​(χε​v)=χε​w−χε′​v⟶win ​H.\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}^{\dagger}(\chi_{\varepsilon}v)=\chi_{\varepsilon}w-\chi_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}v\longrightarrow w\qquad\text{in }H.

After cutting off, ordinary mollification on compact subintervals produces a sequence in Cc∞​(0,a)⊂𝒟m+1C_{c}^{\infty}(0,a)\subset\mathscr{D}_{m+1} converging to vv in the graph norm of 𝐁m∗\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}. ∎

Lemma 4.7.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

(4.9) Dom⁡(𝐁m)=Dom⁡(𝔩m).\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{B}_{m})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m}).

Moreover, the graph norm of ℬm\mathcal{B}_{m} and the 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m}-form norm are equivalent on 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m}.

Proof.

For u∈𝒟mu\in\mathscr{D}_{m}, expanding the square and integrating the mixed term by parts gives

(4.10) ‖ℬm​u‖H2−𝔩m​[u,u]=m​∫0au2​fn−2​[(m+n−3)​((f′)2−1)+f​f′′f2]​𝑑r.\displaystyle\|\mathcal{B}_{m}u\|_{H}^{2}-\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,u]=m\int_{0}^{a}u^{2}f^{n-2}\left[\frac{(m+n-3)((f^{\prime})^{2}-1)+ff^{\prime\prime}}{f^{2}}\right]dr.

The pole compatibility conditions make the coefficient in brackets smooth at both endpoints: its numerator is O⁡(f2)O(f^{2}). Hence the right-hand side of (4.10) is bounded in absolute value by a constant times ‖u‖H2\|u\|_{H}^{2}. Therefore

‖u‖H2+‖ℬm​u‖H2≍‖u‖H2+𝔩m​[u,u]on ​𝒟m.\displaystyle\|u\|_{H}^{2}+\|\mathcal{B}_{m}u\|_{H}^{2}\asymp\|u\|_{H}^{2}+\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,u]\qquad\text{on }\mathscr{D}_{m}.

The two completions of 𝒟m\mathscr{D}_{m} inside HH consequently coincide, proving (4.9). ∎

Lemma 4.8 (Radial ladder identity).

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

(4.11) 𝐋0\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{0} =𝐁0∗𝐁0on 𝒟0,\displaystyle=\mathbf{B}_{0}^{*}\mathbf{B}_{0}\qquad\text{on }\mathscr{D}_{0},
(4.12) 𝐁m​𝐁m∗−𝐁m+1∗​𝐁m+1\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{m}\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}-\mathbf{B}_{m+1}^{*}\mathbf{B}_{m+1} =(2m+n−1)Kradon 𝒟m+1.\displaystyle=(2m+n-1)K_{\mathrm{rad}}\qquad\text{on }\mathscr{D}_{m+1}.
Proof.

Using (3.3) and (3.4), one obtains on the indicated cores

𝐁m∗​𝐁m\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}\mathbf{B}_{m} =−d2d​r2−(n−2)​f′f​dd​r+m⁡(m+n−3)​(f′)2f2+m​f′′f,\displaystyle=-\frac{d^{2}}{dr^{2}}-(n-2)\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}\frac{d}{dr}+m(m+n-3)\frac{(f^{\prime})^{2}}{f^{2}}+m\frac{f^{\prime\prime}}{f},

5. Radial curvature and application of the abstract recursion

Lemma 5.1.

Assume Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g. Then, on (0,a)(0,a),

(5.1) f′′+f\displaystyle f^{\prime\prime}+f ≤0,\displaystyle\leq 0,
(5.2) f2+(f′)2\displaystyle f^{2}+(f^{\prime})^{2} ≤1.\displaystyle\leq 1.

Consequently,

Krad≥1,Ktan≥1.\displaystyle K_{\mathrm{rad}}\geq 1,\qquad K_{\mathrm{tan}}\geq 1.

Moreover, Krad≡1K_{\mathrm{rad}}\equiv 1 if and only if (Sn−1,g)(S^{n-1},g) is the unit round sphere.

Proof.

For a unit vector XX tangent to a principal orbit,

Rcg(∂r,∂r)\displaystyle\Rc_{g}(\partial_{r},\partial_{r}) =(n−2)​Krad,\displaystyle=(n-2)K_{\mathrm{rad}},
Rcg⁡(X,X)\displaystyle\Rc_{g}(X,X) =Krad+(n−3)​Ktan.\displaystyle=K_{\mathrm{rad}}+(n-3)K_{\mathrm{tan}}.

The radial component of the Ricci lower bound gives Krad≥1K_{\mathrm{rad}}\geq 1, equivalently (5.1).

Since f′′≤−f<0f^{\prime\prime}\leq-f<0, f′f^{\prime} decreases from 11 to −1-1 and vanishes at a unique point. For

E⁡(r):=f​(r)2+f′​(r)2,\displaystyle E(r):=f(r)^{2}+f^{\prime}(r)^{2},

one has

E′​(r)=2​f′​(r)​(f⁡(r)+f′′​(r)).\displaystyle E^{\prime}(r)=2f^{\prime}(r)(f(r)+f^{\prime\prime}(r)).

Thus EE decreases before the zero of f′f^{\prime} and increases after it. Since E⁡(0)=E⁡(a)=1E(0)=E(a)=1, one obtains E≤1E\leq 1, which is (5.2) and gives Ktan≥1K_{\mathrm{tan}}\geq 1.

If Krad≡1K_{\mathrm{rad}}\equiv 1, then f′′+f=0f^{\prime\prime}+f=0, f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, and f′​(0)=1f^{\prime}(0)=1, so f⁡(r)=sin⁡rf(r)=\sin r. The conditions at the second pole force a=πa=\pi. The converse is immediate. ∎

Lemma 5.2.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

(5.3) Dom⁡(𝔞m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m}) =Dom⁡(𝔩m),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m}),
(5.4) Dom⁡(𝔠m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}) =Dom⁡(𝔞m+1)=Dom⁡(𝔩m+1).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m+1}).

On this common domain,

(5.5) 𝔠m​[v,v]−𝔞m+1​[v,v]=(2​m+n−1)​∫0a(Krad−1)​v2​fn−2​𝑑r.\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}[v,v]-\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}[v,v]=(2m+n-1)\int_{0}^{a}(K_{\mathrm{rad}}-1)v^{2}f^{n-2}\,dr.

The common form domains in (5.3) and (5.4) embed compactly into HH when equipped with any of the indicated form norms. Consequently, the operators 𝐀m\mathbf{A}_{m} and 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m} have compact resolvent. In addition, every eigenfunction of 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m} belongs to 𝒟m+1\mathscr{D}_{m+1}.

Proof.

The first domain identity is Lemma 4.7. On 𝒟m+1\mathscr{D}_{m+1}, the radial ladder identity (4.12), together with

(m+1)​(m+n−1)−m⁡(m+n−2)=2​m+n−1,\displaystyle(m+1)(m+n-1)-m(m+n-2)=2m+n-1,

gives (5.5). Since KradK_{\mathrm{rad}} is bounded on [0,a][0,a], the 𝔠m\mathfrak{c}_{m}- and 𝔞m+1\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}-form norms are equivalent on 𝒟m+1\mathscr{D}_{m+1}. Lemma 4.6 identifies the first completion with Dom⁡(𝔠m)\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}), while the definition of 𝐁m+1\mathbf{B}_{m+1} identifies the second with Dom⁡(𝔞m+1)\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}). This proves (5.4) and extends (5.5) to the closed domains.

By Lemma 4.7 and Definition 3.5, the 𝔞m\mathfrak{a}_{m}-form norm is equivalent to the 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m}-form norm on their common domain. The bounded-potential identity (5.5) likewise makes the 𝔠m\mathfrak{c}_{m}- and 𝔞m+1\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}-form norms equivalent. Therefore (4.3), applied at levels mm and m+1m+1, gives the asserted compact embeddings. The standard closed-form resolvent argument then gives compact resolvent for both 𝐀m\mathbf{A}_{m} and 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m}.

For the regularity assertion, polarizing the calculation in Lemma 4.7 gives

(5.6) 𝔩m+1​[v,ϕ]−𝔠m​[v,ϕ]=(m+n−2)​∫0a((m+1)​(Ktan−1)−(Krad−1))​v​ϕ​fn−2​𝑑r.\displaystyle\mathfrak{l}_{m+1}[v,\phi]-\mathfrak{c}_{m}[v,\phi]=(m+n-2)\int_{0}^{a}\bigl((m+1)(K_{\mathrm{tan}}-1)-(K_{\mathrm{rad}}-1)\bigr)v\phi f^{n-2}\,dr.

The coefficient is smooth and bounded on [0,a][0,a]. If 𝐂m​v=γ​v\mathbf{C}_{m}v=\gamma v, then (5.6) shows that v∈Dom⁡(𝐋m+1)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathbf{L}_{m+1}) and that Jm+1​vJ_{m+1}v satisfies a second-order elliptic equation with smooth coefficients on Sn−1S^{n-1}. Elliptic regularity and Lemma 4.2 give v∈𝒟m+1v\in\mathscr{D}_{m+1}. ∎

Lemma 5.3 (Comparison with the separated Laplacian).

Assume Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g. Then

𝐋m≥𝐀m\displaystyle\mathbf{L}_{m}\geq\mathbf{A}_{m}

in the quadratic-form sense. Consequently, for every j≥0j\geq 0 and every Λ∈ℝ\Lambda\in\mathbb{R},

(5.7) λj​(𝐋m)\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{L}_{m}) ≥λj​(𝐀m),\displaystyle\geq\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{A}_{m}),
(5.8) N𝐋m<​(Λ)\displaystyle N_{\mathbf{L}_{m}}^{<}(\Lambda) ≤N𝐀m<​(Λ).\displaystyle\leq N_{\mathbf{A}_{m}}^{<}(\Lambda).
Proof.

By Lemma 4.7, equivalently by (5.3), the closed forms 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m} and 𝔞m\mathfrak{a}_{m} have the same domain. For u∈𝒟mu\in\mathscr{D}_{m}, direct calculation gives

(5.9) 𝔩m​[u,u]−𝔞m​[u,u]=m​∫0a((m+n−3)​(Ktan−1)+(Krad−1))​u2​fn−2​𝑑r.\displaystyle\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,u]-\mathfrak{a}_{m}[u,u]=m\int_{0}^{a}\bigl((m+n-3)(K_{\mathrm{tan}}-1)+(K_{\mathrm{rad}}-1)\bigr)u^{2}f^{n-2}\,dr.

The coefficient is bounded, so this identity extends to every u∈Dom⁡(𝔩m)=Dom⁡(𝔞m)u\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m}); it also shows that the two form norms on the common domain are equivalent. Lemma 5.1 makes the right-hand side nonnegative. The min–max principle for the self-adjoint operators associated with 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m} and 𝔞m\mathfrak{a}_{m}, namely 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m} and 𝐀m\mathbf{A}_{m}, gives (5.7), and the counting inequality is equivalent to it. ∎

Lemma 5.4.

Assume Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g. Then, for every m≥0m\geq 0,

ker⁡𝐁m=ℝ​fm,dimℝker⁡𝐁m=1,ker⁡𝐁m∗={0}.\displaystyle\ker\mathbf{B}_{m}=\mathbb{R}f^{m},\qquad\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\ker\mathbf{B}_{m}=1,\qquad\ker\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}=\{0\}.

u′=m​f′f​u\displaystyle u^{\prime}=m\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}u

in the distributional, hence classical, sense. Thus (f−m​u)′=0(f^{-m}u)^{\prime}=0, so u=c​fmu=cf^{m}. Conversely, the pole expansions of ff show that fm∈𝒟mf^{m}\in\mathscr{D}_{m}, and (3.3) gives 𝐁m​fm=0\mathbf{B}_{m}f^{m}=0.

The preceding lemmas verify all hypotheses needed to use the separated radial result from Section 2. Explicitly, for every ladder level mm we take

(5.11) 𝔽=ℝ,Hm=H,Bm=𝐁m,αm=m⁡(m+n−2).\displaystyle\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R},\qquad H_{m}=H,\qquad B_{m}=\mathbf{B}_{m},\qquad\alpha_{m}=m(m+n-2).

Proposition 5.5.

Assume Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g. For every l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},

N𝐋m<​(l⁡(l+n−2))≤l−m,0≤m<l,\displaystyle N_{\mathbf{L}_{m}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)\leq l-m,\qquad 0\leq m<l,

and gives zero for m≥lm\geq l. The comparison (5.8) transfers these bounds from 𝐀m\mathbf{A}_{m} to 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m}. ∎

6. The rotational comparison theorem and rigidity

Lemma 6.1.

For every l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},

∑m=0l−1dn−2,m​(l−m)=N−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2)).\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}d_{n-2,m}(l-m)=N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr).
Proof.

The standard dimension formula is

(6.1) dn−2,m=(n+m−2n−2)−(n+m−4n−2),\displaystyle d_{n-2,m}=\binom{n+m-2}{n-2}-\binom{n+m-4}{n-2},

with the convention that the binomial coefficient vanishes when the upper index is smaller than n−2n-2. The branching identity

∑s=0mdn−2,s=dn−1,m\displaystyle\sum_{s=0}^{m}d_{n-2,s}=d_{n-1,m}

follows by summing (6.1). Therefore

∑m=0l−1dn−2,m​(l−m)\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}d_{n-2,m}(l-m) =∑k=0l−1∑m=0kdn−2,m=∑k=0l−1dn−1,k=N−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2)).\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{l-1}\sum_{m=0}^{k}d_{n-2,m}=\sum_{k=0}^{l-1}d_{n-1,k}=N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr).

∎

Proposition 6.2.

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let (Sn−1,g)(S^{n-1},g) be rotationally symmetric with Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g. Then, for every l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},

N−Δg<​(l⁡(l+n−2))≤N−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2)).\displaystyle N_{-\Delta_{g}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)\leq N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr).
Proof.

By Lemma 4.4 and Proposition 5.5,

N−Δg<​(l⁡(l+n−2))\displaystyle N_{-\Delta_{g}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr) =∑m=0∞dn−2,m​N𝐋m<​(l⁡(l+n−2))≤∑m=0l−1dn−2,m​(l−m).\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_{n-2,m}N_{\mathbf{L}_{m}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)\leq\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}d_{n-2,m}(l-m).

Lemma 6.1 identifies the last expression with the round strict counting function. ∎

Lemma 6.3.

Let 𝔰\mathfrak{s} and 𝔱\mathfrak{t} be lower-bounded closed forms in the radial Hilbert space HH defined in (3.1), with common form domain 𝒱:=Dom⁡(𝔰)=Dom⁡(𝔱).\mathcal{V}:=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{s})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{t}).

Let SS and TT be the self-adjoint operators associated with 𝔰\mathfrak{s} and 𝔱\mathfrak{t}, respectively. Suppose that

𝔰⁡[v,v]=𝔱⁡[v,v]+∫0aP​|v|2​fn−2,v∈𝒱,\displaystyle\mathfrak{s}[v,v]=\mathfrak{t}[v,v]+\int_{0}^{a}P|v|^{2}f^{n-2},\qquad v\in\mathcal{V},

for a bounded function P≥0P\geq 0. Assume that the inclusion 𝒱↪ℋ\mathcal{V}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{H} is compact and that PP is positive on a nonempty open set U⊆(0,a)U\subseteq(0,a). Assume also that, for every j≥0j\geq 0, no nonzero element of the span of the first j+1j+1 eigenfunctions of SS vanishes identically on UU. Then

(6.2) λj(S)>λj(T),j=0,1,2,….\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(S)>\lambda_{j}(T),\qquad j=0,1,2,\ldots.
Proof.

Let FjF_{j} be the span of the first j+1j+1 eigenfunctions of SS, counted with multiplicity. For every 0≠v∈Fj0\neq v\in F_{j},

𝔰⁡[v,v]‖v‖2≤λj​(S),\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{s}[v,v]}{\|v\|^{2}}\leq\lambda_{j}(S),

and the spectral-subspace hypothesis gives∫0aP​|v|2​fn−2>0.\int_{0}^{a}P|v|^{2}f^{n-2}>0.

Hence

𝔱⁡[v,v]‖v‖2<λj​(S)(0≠v∈Fj).\displaystyle\frac{\mathfrak{t}[v,v]}{\|v\|^{2}}<\lambda_{j}(S)\qquad(0\neq v\in F_{j}).

The unit sphere of FjF_{j} is compact, so the supremum of the left-hand side over Fj∖{0}F_{j}\setminus\{0\} is still strictly smaller than λj​(S)\lambda_{j}(S). The min–max principle for TT gives (6.2). ∎

In the radial applications below, the spectral-subspace nonvanishing hypothesis follows from Lemmas 4.3 and 5.2. Indeed, after decomposing a finite spectral sum into its distinct eigenvalue components by polynomial spectral projections, each component satisfies a second-order ordinary differential equation with smooth coefficients on (0,a)(0,a); vanishing on an open interval therefore forces that component to vanish identically. The same argument, with elliptic unique continuation, applies to the smooth bundle operators used later in the paper.

Lemma 6.4.

Assume that (Sn−1,g)(S^{n-1},g) is rotationally symmetric, Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g, and gg is not round. Then

(6.3) λj​(𝐋m)>(m+j)​(m+j+n−2)whenever ​(m,j)≠(0,0).\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{L}_{m})>(m+j)(m+j+n-2)\qquad\text{whenever }(m,j)\neq(0,0).
Proof.

Step (1). By Lemma 5.1, nonroundness implies that there is a nonempty open interval U⊂(0,a)U\subset(0,a) on which

Krad>1.\displaystyle K_{\mathrm{rad}}>1.

We first compare the two consecutive partner operators. Apply Lemma 6.3 in the Hilbert space HH with

𝔰=𝔠m,𝔱=𝔞m+1,S=𝐂m,T=𝐀m+1.\displaystyle\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{c}_{m},\qquad\mathfrak{t}=\mathfrak{a}_{m+1},\qquad S=\mathbf{C}_{m},\qquad T=\mathbf{A}_{m+1}.

The operators 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m} and 𝐀m+1\mathbf{A}_{m+1} are, by Definition 3.5, the self-adjoint operators associated with 𝔠m\mathfrak{c}_{m} and 𝔞m+1\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}, respectively. By (5.4), their forms have the common domain

Dom⁡(𝔠m)=Dom⁡(𝔞m+1)=Dom⁡(𝔩m+1).\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m+1}).

The identity (5.5) holds on the common closed form domain and has the bounded potential

P=(2​m+n−1)​(Krad−1).\displaystyle P=(2m+n-1)(K_{\mathrm{rad}}-1).

Hence (4.3), applied at level m+1m+1, shows that the common form domain embeds compactly into HH. The displayed potential PP is nonnegative everywhere and positive on UU.

Finally, the regularity assertion in Lemma 5.2, followed by the ordinary-differential-equation argument stated after Lemma 6.3, verifies that no nonzero element of a finite 𝐂m\mathbf{C}_{m}-spectral subspace can vanish identically on UU.

Thus all hypotheses of Lemma 6.3 are satisfied, and

(6.4) λj​(𝐂m)>λj​(𝐀m+1),m,j≥0.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{C}_{m})>\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{A}_{m+1}),\qquad m,j\geq 0.

We next use the exact partner shift from Section 2. Apply Lemma 2.2 with Hm=HH_{m}=H, Bm=𝐁mB_{m}=\mathbf{B}_{m}, and αm=m⁡(m+n−2)\alpha_{m}=m(m+n-2). Lemma 5.4 gives rm=1r_{m}=1 and sm=0s_{m}=0, so (2.1) becomes

λj​(𝐀m)=λj−1​(𝐂m),j≥1.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{A}_{m})=\lambda_{j-1}(\mathbf{C}_{m}),\qquad j\geq 1.

Combining this with (6.4) and iterating yields

λj​(𝐀m)\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{A}_{m}) >λj−1​(𝐀m+1)>⋯>λ0​(𝐀m+j)\displaystyle>\lambda_{j-1}(\mathbf{A}_{m+1})>\cdots>\lambda_{0}(\mathbf{A}_{m+j})
(6.5) =(m+j)​(m+j+n−2),j≥1,\displaystyle=(m+j)(m+j+n-2),\qquad j\geq 1,

where the last equality is (5.10).

Step (2). For m=0m=0, (5.3) and (5.9) show that the closed forms 𝔩0\mathfrak{l}_{0} and 𝔞0\mathfrak{a}_{0} coincide. Since 𝐋0\mathbf{L}_{0} and 𝐀0\mathbf{A}_{0} are their associated self-adjoint operators, respectively, one has 𝐋0=𝐀0\mathbf{L}_{0}=\mathbf{A}_{0}, and (6.5) proves the assertion for j≥1j\geq 1.

Step (3). Assume now that m≥1m\geq 1. We again apply Lemma 6.3 in HH, this time with

𝔰=𝔩m,𝔱=𝔞m,S=𝐋m,T=𝐀m.\displaystyle\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{l}_{m},\qquad\mathfrak{t}=\mathfrak{a}_{m},\qquad S=\mathbf{L}_{m},\qquad T=\mathbf{A}_{m}.

By Definition 3.3, 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m} is the self-adjoint operator associated with 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m}, while Definition 3.5 identifies 𝐀m\mathbf{A}_{m} as the self-adjoint operator associated with 𝔞m\mathfrak{a}_{m}. The form-domain identity (5.3) gives

Dom⁡(𝔩m)=Dom⁡(𝔞m),\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{l}_{m})=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m}),

On this common closed form domain, (5.9) reads

𝔩m​[u,u]\displaystyle\mathfrak{l}_{m}[u,u] =𝔞m​[u,u]\displaystyle=\mathfrak{a}_{m}[u,u]
+m∫0a((m+n−3)(Ktan−1)+(Krad−1))u2fn−2dr.\displaystyle\quad+m\int_{0}^{a}\bigl((m+n-3)(K_{\mathrm{tan}}-1)+(K_{\mathrm{rad}}-1)\bigr)u^{2}f^{n-2}\,dr.

The coefficient is bounded, so the 𝔩m\mathfrak{l}_{m}- and 𝔞m\mathfrak{a}_{m}-form norms are equivalent.

Consequently, (4.3), applied at level mm, shows that their common form domain embeds compactly into HH. Lemma 5.1 makes the potential nonnegative, and, because m≥1m\geq 1, it is strictly positive on UU.

By Lemma 4.3 and the ordinary-differential-equation argument stated after Lemma 6.3, no nonzero element of a finite 𝐋m\mathbf{L}_{m}-spectral subspace vanishes identically on UU.

Hence Lemma 6.3 gives

λj​(𝐋m)>λj​(𝐀m),j≥0.\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{L}_{m})>\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{A}_{m}),\qquad j\geq 0.

Together with (5.10) and (6.5), this proves (6.3) in all cases except (m,j)=(0,0)(m,j)=(0,0), where both sides are zero. ∎

Theorem 6.5.

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let (Sn−1,g)(S^{n-1},g) be a smooth rotationally symmetric Riemannian manifold with Rcg≥(n−2)​g\Rc_{g}\geq(n-2)g. Then

(6.6) λi​(Sn−1,g)≥λi​(𝕊n−1,ground),i≥1.\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{n-1},g)\geq\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1},g_{\mathrm{round}}),\qquad i\geq 1.

Consequently,

(6.7) 𝒩−Δg​(l⁡(l+n−2))≤𝒩−Δ𝕊n−1​(l⁡(l+n−2)),l∈ℤ≥0.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{g}}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr),\qquad l\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Moreover, if equality holds in (6.6) for some i≥1i\geq 1, or if equality holds in (6.7) for some l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, then (Sn−1,g)(S^{n-1},g) is isometric to the unit round sphere.

Proof.

Step (1). Fix i≥1i\geq 1, and choose the unique l≥1l\geq 1 such that the ii-th round eigenvalue is l⁡(l+n−2)l(l+n-2). Equivalently,

N−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2))≤i<N−Δ𝕊n−1<​((l+1)​(l+n−1)).\displaystyle N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)\leq i<N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl((l+1)(l+n-1)\bigr).

Proposition 6.2 gives

λN−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2))​(Sn−1,g)≥l⁡(l+n−2).\displaystyle\lambda_{N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}(l(l+n-2))}(S^{n-1},g)\geq l(l+n-2).

Since the eigenvalues are nondecreasing and ii is not smaller than this index,

λi​(Sn−1,g)≥l⁡(l+n−2)=λi​(𝕊n−1,ground).\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{n-1},g)\geq l(l+n-2)=\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1},g_{\mathrm{round}}).

This proves (6.6). The closed-counting comparison (6.7) follows immediately; for l=0l=0, both connected manifolds have exactly one eigenvalue at zero.

Step (2). For rigidity, suppose that gg is not round. If

λj​(𝐋m)≤l⁡(l+n−2),\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(\mathbf{L}_{m})\leq l(l+n-2),

then Lemma 6.4 implies m+j≤l−1m+j\leq l-1. Hence Lemmas 4.4 and 6.1 give, for every l≥1l\geq 1,

𝒩−Δg​(l⁡(l+n−2))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{g}}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr) =∑m=0∞dn−2,m​𝒩𝐋m​(l⁡(l+n−2))≤∑m=0l−1dn−2,m​(l−m)\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_{n-2,m}\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{L}_{m}}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)\leq\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}d_{n-2,m}(l-m)
(6.8) =N−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2))\displaystyle=N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr)
<𝒩−Δ𝕊n−1​(l⁡(l+n−2)).\displaystyle<\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr).

Thus equality in (6.7) is impossible for a nonround metric.

Step (3). The same estimate also makes every positive ordered comparison strict. Indeed, if the ii-th round eigenvalue equals l⁡(l+n−2)l(l+n-2), then

i≥N−Δ𝕊n−1<​(l⁡(l+n−2)),\displaystyle i\geq N_{-\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+n-2)\bigr),

whereas (6.8) shows that at most that many eigenvalues of −Δg-\Delta_{g} are less than or equal to l⁡(l+n−2)l(l+n-2). Therefore

λi​(Sn−1,g)>l⁡(l+n−2)=λi​(𝕊n−1,ground).\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{n-1},g)>l(l+n-2)=\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{n-1},g_{\mathrm{round}}).

Equality in (6.6) is likewise impossible unless gg is round. ∎

Part II Smooth Riemannian 22-Spheres with K≥1K\geq 1

Throughout this part, m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. The basic objects are the line bundles Em=(T1,0​S2)⊗mE_{m}=(T^{1,0}S^{2})^{\otimes m}, the Hilbert spaces Hm=L2​(Em)H_{m}=L^{2}(E_{m}), and the closed first-order operators Bm:Hm⊃Dom⁡(Bm)→Hm+1B_{m}:H_{m}\supset\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m})\to H_{m+1}. They are constructed in Section 7. The shifted forms 𝔞m,𝔠m\mathfrak{a}_{m},\mathfrak{c}_{m} and their operators Am,CmA_{m},C_{m} are fixed at the beginning of Section 9.

In this part, we always assume that (S2,g)(S^{2},g) is a smooth Riemannian sphere satisfying Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1 unless otherwise mentioned.

7. Riemannian ladder identity

The purpose of this section is to remove the artificial symmetry from Section 3 for S2S^{2}. In the rotational case, mm measured angular frequency. For a general metric there is no distinguished angular coordinate, but there is still a canonical rotation group acting on oriented orthonormal frames.

Fix the standard orientation on S2S^{2}. The metric and the orientation define the bundle map J:T​S2⟶T​S2J:TS^{2}\longrightarrow TS^{2} by the rule that, for every local oriented orthonormal frame e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} with respect to gg,

J​e1=e2,J​e2=−e1.\displaystyle Je_{1}=e_{2},\qquad Je_{2}=-e_{1}.

Thus J2=−IdJ^{2}=-\Id. Let

Tℂ​S2:=T​S2⊗ℝℂ.\displaystyle T_{\mathbb{C}}S^{2}:=TS^{2}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}.

Since S2S^{2} is oriented, let d​AgdA_{g} denote the Riemannian area form of gg.

Definition 7.1.

Extend ℂ\mathbb{C}-linearly J:T​S2⟶T​S2J:TS^{2}\longrightarrow TS^{2} to Tℂ​S2T_{\mathbb{C}}S^{2}, we define the +i+i-eigenbundle of JJ by

T1,0​S2:=ker⁡(J−i​Id)={W∈Tℂ​S2:J​W=i​W}.\displaystyle T^{1,0}S^{2}:=\ker(J-i\Id)=\{W\in T_{\mathbb{C}}S^{2}:JW=iW\}.

For each integer m≥0m\geq 0, define

Em:=(T1,0​S2)⊗m,E0:=S2×ℂ.\displaystyle E_{m}:=(T^{1,0}S^{2})^{\otimes m},\qquad E_{0}:=S^{2}\times\mathbb{C}.

The replacement of the mm-th Fourier mode is realized geometrically as the line bundle Em=(T1,0​S2)⊗mE_{m}=(T^{1,0}S^{2})^{\otimes m}. This is the first conceptual upgrade in the paper.

In a local oriented orthonormal frame, set

Z:=12​(e1−i​e2).\displaystyle Z:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(e_{1}-ie_{2}).

If another local oriented orthonormal frame is written as

e1′=cos⁡α​e1+sin⁡α​e2,e2′=−sin⁡α​e1+cos⁡α​e2,\displaystyle e_{1}^{\prime}=\cos\alpha\,e_{1}+\sin\alpha\,e_{2},\qquad e_{2}^{\prime}=-\sin\alpha\,e_{1}+\cos\alpha\,e_{2},

then

(7.1) Z′=12​(e1′−i​e2′)=ei​α​Z.\displaystyle Z^{\prime}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(e_{1}^{\prime}-ie_{2}^{\prime})=e^{i\alpha}Z.

In an oriented orthonormal frame, set

Z⊗0:=1,Z⊗m:=Z⊗⋯⊗Zwith m tensor factors, for m≥1.\displaystyle Z^{\otimes 0}:=1,\qquad Z^{\otimes m}:=Z\otimes\cdots\otimes Z\quad\text{with }m\text{ tensor factors, for }m\geq 1.

Under the frame change (7.1), the local tensors satisfy

(Z′)⊗m=ei​m​α​Z⊗m.\displaystyle(Z^{\prime})^{\otimes m}=e^{im\alpha}Z^{\otimes m}.

Thus a local section ss of EmE_{m} is written as s=u⋅Z⊗ms=u\cdot Z^{\otimes m}, where uu is a complex-valued function, and on an overlap the coefficient changes by

u′=e−i​m​α​u.\displaystyle u^{\prime}=e^{-im\alpha}u.

This gives a globally defined rank-one complex vector bundle.

The Hermitian metric hmh_{m} on EmE_{m} is defined by declaring each frame Z⊗mZ^{\otimes m} to be unit:

|u⋅Z⊗m|2=|u|2.\displaystyle|u\cdot Z^{\otimes m}|^{2}=|u|^{2}.

Since |ei​m​α|=1|e^{im\alpha}|=1, this definition is independent of the chosen oriented orthonormal frame.

Notation 7.2.

Let πm:Em→S2\pi_{m}:E_{m}\to S^{2} denote the bundle projection. We use the following spaces of sections:

C∞​(Em)\displaystyle C^{\infty}(E_{m}) :={s:S2→Em:s is smooth and πm∘s=idS2},\displaystyle:=\{s:S^{2}\to E_{m}:\ s\text{ is smooth and }\pi_{m}\circ s=\operatorname{id}_{S^{2}}\},
Γmeas​(Em)\displaystyle\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}}(E_{m}) :={s:S2→Em:s is Borel measurable and πm∘s=idS2a.e.}/∼,\displaystyle:=\{s:S^{2}\to E_{m}:\ s\text{ is Borel measurable and }\pi_{m}\circ s=\operatorname{id}_{S^{2}}\ \text{a.e.}\}/\sim,

where ∼\sim means equality d​AgdA_{g}-almost everywhere. The Hilbert space L2​(Em)L^{2}(E_{m}) is

L2​(Em):={s∈Γmeas​(Em):∫S2|s|hm2​d​Ag<∞}.\displaystyle L^{2}(E_{m}):=\left\{s\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{meas}}(E_{m}):\int_{S^{2}}|s|_{h_{m}}^{2}\,dA_{g}<\infty\right\}.

Its Hermitian inner product is

⟨s,t⟩L2​(Em):=∫S2hm​(s,t)​d​Ag.\displaystyle\langle s,t\rangle_{L^{2}(E_{m})}:=\int_{S^{2}}h_{m}(s,t)\,dA_{g}.

We use the convention that the inner product is linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second variable. Since S2S^{2} is compact and EmE_{m} is smooth, C∞​(Em)C^{\infty}(E_{m}) is dense in L2​(Em)L^{2}(E_{m}).

Let ω\omega be the Levi-Civita connection one-form in the oriented orthonormal frame e1,e2e_{1},e_{2}, defined by

(7.2) ∇e1=ω⊗e2,∇e2=−ω⊗e1.\displaystyle\nabla e_{1}=\omega\otimes e_{2},\qquad\nabla e_{2}=-\omega\otimes e_{1}.

Then ∇Z=i​ω⊗Z\nabla Z=i\omega\otimes Z.

With the sign convention in (7.2), the curvature equation is

d​ω=−Kg​d​Ag.\displaystyle d\omega=-K_{g}\,dA_{g}.

For instance, on the unit round sphere 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} with e1=∂re_{1}=\partial_{r} and e2=(sinr)−1∂θe_{2}=(\sin r)^{-1}\partial_{\theta}, one has ω=cos⁡r​d​θ\omega=\cos r\,d\theta, hence d​ω=−sin⁡r​d​r∧d​θ=−d​Ad\omega=-\sin r\,dr\wedge d\theta=-dA.

The connection induced on EmE_{m} is defined as follows:

∇(m)(u⋅Z⊗m)=(d​u+i​m​ω​u)⊗Z⊗m.\displaystyle\nabla^{(m)}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes m})=(du+im\omega u)\otimes Z^{\otimes m}.

For k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, define Hk​(Em)H^{k}(E_{m}) to be the Sobolev space of sections obtained by completing C∞​(Em)C^{\infty}(E_{m}) for the norm

‖s‖Hk​(Em)2:=∑r=0k∫S2|(∇(m))r​s|2​d​Ag.\displaystyle\|s\|_{H^{k}(E_{m})}^{2}:=\sum_{r=0}^{k}\int_{S^{2}}\left|\big(\nabla^{(m)}\big)^{r}s\right|^{2}\,dA_{g}.

In particular, H0​(Em)=L2​(Em)H^{0}(E_{m})=L^{2}(E_{m}).

Notation 7.3.

For a vector field XX on (S2,g)(S^{2},g) and any complex-valued function uu defined on (S2,g)(S^{2},g), define

DX(m)​u:=X​u+i​m​ω​(X)​u,∀m∈ℤ≥0.\displaystyle D_{X}^{(m)}u:=Xu+im\omega(X)u,\quad\quad\forall m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

The first-order differential expression is

(7.3) ℬm:C∞​(Em)⟶C∞​(Em+1),ℬm​(u⋅Z⊗m):=(De1(m)​u+i​De2(m)​u)​Z⊗(m+1).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{m}:C^{\infty}(E_{m})\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(E_{m+1}),\quad\quad\mathcal{B}_{m}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes m}):=\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m)}u+iD_{e_{2}}^{(m)}u\bigr)Z^{\otimes(m+1)}.

Bm(0):Dom⁡(Bm(0))=C∞​(Em)⊂L2​(Em)⟶L2​(Em+1),Bm(0)​s:=ℬm​s.\displaystyle B_{m}^{(0)}:\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{(0)})=C^{\infty}(E_{m})\subset L^{2}(E_{m})\longrightarrow L^{2}(E_{m+1}),\qquad B_{m}^{(0)}s:=\mathcal{B}_{m}s.

Bm:=Bm(0)¯:Dom⁡(Bm)⊂L2​(Em)⟶L2​(Em+1)\displaystyle B_{m}:=\overline{B_{m}^{(0)}}:\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m})\subset L^{2}(E_{m})\longrightarrow L^{2}(E_{m+1})

Bm:Dom⁡(Bm)=H1​(Em)⊂L2​(Em)⟶L2​(Em+1).\displaystyle B_{m}:\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m})=H^{1}(E_{m})\subset L^{2}(E_{m})\longrightarrow L^{2}(E_{m+1}).

This is a global operator. Indeed, under the frame change (7.1), the connection form changes by

Remark 7.6 (The rotationally symmetric ladder as a symmetry reduction).

The intrinsic construction above contains the rotationally symmetric two-sphere as a special case. More precisely, this literal identification concerns the case n=3n=3 in the rotationally symmetric part, beginning with Section 3.

Let

g=d​r2+f​(r)2​d​θ2\displaystyle g=dr^{2}+f(r)^{2}\,d\theta^{2}

be a rotationally symmetric metric on S2S^{2}, and use the adapted oriented orthonormal frame

e1=∂r,e2=1f⁡(r)∂θ.\displaystyle e_{1}=\partial_{r},\qquad e_{2}=\frac{1}{f(r)}\partial_{\theta}.

Its Levi-Civita connection form is

ω=f′​(r)​d​θ,ω⁡(e1)=0,ω⁡(e2)=f′f.\displaystyle\omega=f^{\prime}(r)\,d\theta,\qquad\omega(e_{1})=0,\qquad\omega(e_{2})=\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}.

Consequently, for a local section s=u⁡(r,θ)​Z⊗ms=u(r,\theta)Z^{\otimes m} of EmE_{m}, the general operator BmB_{m} takes the form

(7.5) Bm​s=(∂ru+if​∂θu−m​f′f​u)​Z⊗(m+1).\displaystyle B_{m}s=\left(\partial_{r}u+\frac{i}{f}\partial_{\theta}u-m\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}u\right)Z^{\otimes(m+1)}.

In the adapted moving frame Z⊗mZ^{\otimes m}, the mm-th rotational weight is carried by the frame itself. Hence the complexification of the mm-th Fourier sector is represented by sections whose coefficient is radial. Restricting (7.5) to u=u⁡(r)u=u(r) gives

Bm​(u​Z⊗m)\displaystyle B_{m}\bigl(uZ^{\otimes m}\bigr) =(u′−m​f′f​u)​Z⊗(m+1)=(𝐁m​u)​Z⊗(m+1),\displaystyle=\left(u^{\prime}-m\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}u\right)Z^{\otimes(m+1)}=(\mathbf{B}_{m}u)Z^{\otimes(m+1)},

where 𝐁m\mathbf{B}_{m} is exactly the radial operator in (3.3).

On the pole-compatible radial graph core {v​Z⊗(m+1):v∈𝒟m+1⊗ℝℂ}\left\{vZ^{\otimes(m+1)}:v\in\mathscr{D}_{m+1}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}\right\}, the adjoint satisfies

Bm∗​(v​Z⊗(m+1))\displaystyle B_{m}^{*}\bigl(vZ^{\otimes(m+1)}\bigr) =(−v′−(m+1)​f′f​v)​Z⊗m=(𝐁m∗​v)​Z⊗m,\displaystyle=\left(-v^{\prime}-(m+1)\frac{f^{\prime}}{f}v\right)Z^{\otimes m}=(\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}v)Z^{\otimes m},

which agrees with the formal adjoint expression (3.4) when n=3n=3.

The Hilbert-space structures also agree. For a radial coefficient,

‖u​Z⊗m‖L2​(Em)2=2​π​∫0a|u⁡(r)|2​f​(r)​𝑑r.\displaystyle\bigl\|uZ^{\otimes m}\bigr\|_{L^{2}(E_{m})}^{2}=2\pi\int_{0}^{a}|u(r)|^{2}f(r)\,dr.

Thus, up to the harmless factor 2​π2\pi, this is the complexification of the radial space HH from Section 3. Moreover, smooth extension across the two poles imposes precisely the complexified pole conditions

u∈𝒟m⊗ℝℂ.\displaystyle u\in\mathscr{D}_{m}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}.

Taking graph closures therefore identifies the restriction of the closed bundle operator BmB_{m} with the complexification of the closed radial operator 𝐁m\mathbf{B}_{m}, and similarly for their adjoints.

Finally, since

Kg=−f′′f=Krad,\displaystyle K_{g}=-\frac{f^{\prime\prime}}{f}=K_{\mathrm{rad}},

the Riemannian ladder identity (7.7), when restricted to these radial-coefficient subspaces, becomes

𝐁m​𝐁m∗−𝐁m+1∗​𝐁m+1=2​(m+1)​Krad,\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{m}\mathbf{B}_{m}^{*}-\mathbf{B}_{m+1}^{*}\mathbf{B}_{m+1}=2(m+1)K_{\mathrm{rad}},

which is exactly the radial ladder identity (4.12) for n=3n=3.

Thus the rotationally symmetric proof on S2S^{2} is the separated-variable, symmetry-reduced realization of the intrinsic Riemannian construction. For a general metric there is no global angular coordinate, and the bundles EmE_{m} provide the invariant replacement for the Fourier-mode decomposition.

The key identity is the following Weitzenbock-type formula.

Lemma 7.7 (Riemannian ladder identity).

On C∞​(S2,ℂ)C^{\infty}(S^{2};\mathbb{C}),

(7.6) B0∗​B0=−Δg\displaystyle B_{0}^{*}B_{0}=-\Delta_{g}

B0​u=(e1​u+i​e2​u)​Z.\displaystyle B_{0}u=(e_{1}u+ie_{2}u)Z.

B0∗​(v​Z)=−(De1(1)​v−i​De2(1)​v),\displaystyle B_{0}^{*}(vZ)=-\left(D_{e_{1}}^{(1)}v-iD_{e_{2}}^{(1)}v\right),

Expanding,

(e1−i​e2)​(e1​u+i​e2​u)=e1​e1​u+e2​e2​u+i⁡[e1,e2]​u.\displaystyle(e_{1}-ie_{2})(e_{1}u+ie_{2}u)=e_{1}e_{1}u+e_{2}e_{2}u+i[e_{1},e_{2}]u.

(e1−i​e2+i​ω1+ω2)​(e1​u+i​e2​u)=e1​e1​u+e2​e2​u+ω2​e1​u−ω1​e2​u.\displaystyle\left(e_{1}-ie_{2}+i\omega_{1}+\omega_{2}\right)(e_{1}u+ie_{2}u)=e_{1}e_{1}u+e_{2}e_{2}u+\omega_{2}e_{1}u-\omega_{1}e_{2}u.
