div⁡e1=ω2,div⁡e2=−ω1.\displaystyle\operatorname{div}e_{1}=\omega_{2},\qquad\operatorname{div}e_{2}=-\omega_{1}.

B0∗​B0​u=−Δg​u.\displaystyle B_{0}^{*}B_{0}u=-\Delta_{g}u.

Step (2). The assertion is local. Fix a point p∈S2p\in S^{2}, and choose the oriented orthonormal frame so that

Bm−1​Bm−1∗−Bm∗​Bm=2​m​Kgon ​Em.\displaystyle B_{m-1}B_{m-1}^{*}-B_{m}^{*}B_{m}=2mK_{g}\qquad\text{on }E_{m}.

Replacing mm by m+1m+1 proves (7.7). ∎

8. The Vanishing Theorem

The ladder identity alone is not enough for a finite eigenvalue comparison. The counting recursion also needs the exact size of the unpaired kernel and the absence of an adjoint kernel. In the rotational proof, these facts were endpoint facts for the one-dimensional equation Bm​u=0B_{m}u=0. Globally, endpoint analysis is replaced by the geometry of holomorphic sections.

This section is therefore the bridge between the Riemannian ladder and complex analysis. We need two facts:

dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1,ker⁡Bm∗={0}.\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1,\qquad\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\}.

The identity dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1 is first proved in an elementary way: conformal invariance reduces the problem to the round conformal sphere, and stereographic coordinates identify the kernel with polynomials of degree at most 2​m2m.

The adjoint vanishing ker⁡Bm∗=0\ker B_{m}^{*}=0 is a Bochner consequence of the curvature term in the ladder identity.

Lemma 8.1.

Let g^=e2​φ​g\widehat{g}=e^{2\varphi}g, where φ∈C∞​(S2)\varphi\in C^{\infty}(S^{2}). Define B^m\widehat{B}_{m} from g^\widehat{g} in the same way as BmB_{m} is defined from gg. Then

ker⁡B^m=ker⁡Bm.\displaystyle\ker\widehat{B}_{m}=\ker B_{m}.
Proof.

Let e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} be a local oriented gg-orthonormal frame and put

(8.1) u^=em​φ​u.\displaystyle\widehat{u}=e^{m\varphi}u.

In components, if φj=ej​φ\varphi_{j}=e_{j}\varphi, then

ω^​(e1)=ω⁡(e1)−φ2,ω^​(e2)=ω⁡(e2)+φ1.\displaystyle\widehat{\omega}(e_{1})=\omega(e_{1})-\varphi_{2},\qquad\widehat{\omega}(e_{2})=\omega(e_{2})+\varphi_{1}.

Using (8.1) and (8.2), we compute

D^e^1(m)​u^+i​D^e^2(m)​u^\displaystyle\widehat{D}_{\widehat{e}_{1}}^{(m)}\widehat{u}+i\widehat{D}_{\widehat{e}_{2}}^{(m)}\widehat{u} =e(m−1)​φ​(De1(m)​u+i​De2(m)​u).\displaystyle=e^{(m-1)\varphi}\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m)}u+iD_{e_{2}}^{(m)}u\bigr).

B^m​s\displaystyle\widehat{B}_{m}s =e(m−1)​φ​(De1(m)​u+i​De2(m)​u)​Z^⊗(m+1)\displaystyle=e^{(m-1)\varphi}\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m)}u+iD_{e_{2}}^{(m)}u\bigr)\widehat{Z}^{\otimes(m+1)}
=e(m−1)​φ​(De1(m)​u+i​De2(m)​u)​e−(m+1)​φ​Z⊗(m+1)=e−2​φ​Bm​s.\displaystyle=e^{(m-1)\varphi}\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m)}u+iD_{e_{2}}^{(m)}u\bigr)e^{-(m+1)\varphi}Z^{\otimes(m+1)}=e^{-2\varphi}B_{m}s.

This implies the conclusion. ∎

Lemma 8.2.

For every m≥0m\geq 0, dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1.

Proof.

By the uniformization theorem, every smooth metric on S2S^{2} is conformal, after an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, to the round metric [15].

The construction of EmE_{m} and BmB_{m} is natural under diffeomorphisms, and Lemma 8.1 shows that ker⁡Bm\ker B_{m} is unchanged by a conformal change of metric.

Hence it is enough to compute ker⁡Bm\ker B_{m} for the round metric.

Let z=x+i​yz=x+iy be the stereographic coordinate on 𝕊2∖{∞}\mathbb{S}^{2}\setminus\{\infty\}. The round metric is

ground=e2​ψ​(d​x2+d​y2),eψ=21+|z|2.\displaystyle g_{\mathrm{round}}=e^{2\psi}(dx^{2}+dy^{2}),\qquad e^{\psi}=\frac{2}{1+|z|^{2}}.

e1=e−ψ∂x,e2=e−ψ∂y.\displaystyle e_{1}=e^{-\psi}\partial_{x},\qquad e_{2}=e^{-\psi}\partial_{y}.

Then

(8.3) ω=−ψy​d​x+ψx​d​y.\displaystyle\omega=-\psi_{y}\,dx+\psi_{x}\,dy.

Let s=u⋅Z⊗ms=u\cdot Z^{\otimes m} be a section on 𝕊2∖{∞}\mathbb{S}^{2}\setminus\{\infty\}. Since

∂z¯:=12(∂x+i∂y),\displaystyle\partial_{\bar{z}}:=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}+i\partial_{y}),

formulas (7.3) and (8.3) give

Bm​s=0\displaystyle B_{m}s=0 ⟺∂z¯u−m⁡(∂z¯ψ)​u=0⟺∂z¯(e−m​ψ​u)=0.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\partial_{\bar{z}}u-m(\partial_{\bar{z}}\psi)u=0\Longleftrightarrow\partial_{\bar{z}}(e^{-m\psi}u)=0.

Thus P⁡(z):=e−m​ψ​u​(z)P(z):=e^{-m\psi}u(z) is an entire complex analytic function on ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Now write the section itself in the coordinate vector frame. Since

Z=12(e1−ie2)=2e−ψ∂z,∂z:=12(∂x−i∂y),\displaystyle Z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(e_{1}-ie_{2})=\sqrt{2}\,e^{-\psi}\partial_{z},\qquad\partial_{z}:=\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}-i\partial_{y}),

we have

(8.4) s=u⋅Z⊗m=em​ψP(z)(2e−ψ∂z)⊗m=2m/2P(z)(∂z)⊗m.\displaystyle s=u\cdot Z^{\otimes m}=e^{m\psi}P(z)\bigl(\sqrt{2}\,e^{-\psi}\partial_{z}\bigr)^{\otimes m}=2^{m/2}P(z)(\partial_{z})^{\otimes m}.

Near infinity, use the coordinate w=1/zw=1/z. Then

∂z=−w2∂w.\displaystyle\partial_{z}=-w^{2}\partial_{w}.

Therefore (8.4) becomes

s=2m/2(−1)mw2​mP(1/w)(∂w)⊗m.\displaystyle s=2^{m/2}(-1)^{m}w^{2m}P(1/w)(\partial_{w})^{\otimes m}.

The section ss is smooth at w=0w=0 if and only if the coefficient

w2​m​P​(1/w)\displaystyle w^{2m}P(1/w)

has no negative powers in its Laurent expansion at w=0w=0. Since PP is entire, this is equivalent to saying that PP is a polynomial of degree at most 2​m2m:

P⁡(z)=a0+a1​z+⋯+a2​m​z2​m.\displaystyle P(z)=a_{0}+a_{1}z+\cdots+a_{2m}z^{2m}.

Conversely, every such polynomial gives a smooth global section satisfying Bm​s=0B_{m}s=0. Hence

kerBm={2m/2P(z)(∂z)⊗m:P is a polynomial of degree ≤2m}.\displaystyle\ker B_{m}=\{2^{m/2}P(z)(\partial_{z})^{\otimes m}:\ P\text{ is a polynomial of degree }\leq 2m\}.

The complex dimension is therefore 2​m+12m+1. ∎

Lemma 8.3.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

ker⁡Bm∗={0}.\displaystyle\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\}.
Proof.

We apply Lemma 2.3 to the concrete Hilbert spaces

Hm=L2​(Em),Hm+1=L2​(Em+1),\displaystyle H_{m}=L^{2}(E_{m}),\qquad H_{m+1}=L^{2}(E_{m+1}),

9. The comparison theorem and rigidity

For the remainder of Part II we use the following notation. For every m≥0m\geq 0, let

Hm:=L2​(Em),αm:=m⁡(m+1),\displaystyle H_{m}:=L^{2}(E_{m}),\qquad\alpha_{m}:=m(m+1),

and define the closed forms

𝔞m​(s,t)\displaystyle\mathfrak{a}_{m}(s,t) :=⟨Bm​s,Bm​t⟩Hm+1+m⁡(m+1)​⟨s,t⟩Hm,\displaystyle:=\langle B_{m}s,B_{m}t\rangle_{H_{m+1}}+m(m+1)\langle s,t\rangle_{H_{m}}, Dom⁡(𝔞m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m}) =H1​(Em),\displaystyle=H^{1}(E_{m}),
𝔠m​(s,t)\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}(s,t) :=⟨Bm∗​s,Bm∗​t⟩Hm+m⁡(m+1)​⟨s,t⟩Hm+1,\displaystyle:=\langle B_{m}^{*}s,B_{m}^{*}t\rangle_{H_{m}}+m(m+1)\langle s,t\rangle_{H_{m+1}}, Dom⁡(𝔠m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}) =H1​(Em+1).\displaystyle=H^{1}(E_{m+1}).

Let AmA_{m} and CmC_{m} be their associated self-adjoint operators. Thus

Am\displaystyle A_{m} =Bm∗Bm+m(m+1)Iin Hm,\displaystyle=B_{m}^{*}B_{m}+m(m+1)I\quad\text{in }H_{m},
Cm\displaystyle C_{m} =BmBm∗+m(m+1)Iin Hm+1.\displaystyle=B_{m}B_{m}^{*}+m(m+1)I\quad\text{in }H_{m+1}.

Elliptic regularity and Rellich compactness on the closed surface show that both operators have compact resolvent. Their eigenvalues are counted with complex multiplicity and are denoted by λj​(Am)\lambda_{j}(A_{m}) and λj​(Cm)\lambda_{j}(C_{m}), starting at j=0j=0.

The geometric content of the comparison is the following exact form identity: for every t∈H1​(Em+1)t\in H^{1}(E_{m+1}),

(9.1) 𝔠m​(t,t)−𝔞m+1​(t,t)=2​(m+1)​∫S2(Kg−1)​|t|2​d​Ag.\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}(t,t)-\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}(t,t)=2(m+1)\int_{S^{2}}(K_{g}-1)|t|^{2}\,dA_{g}.

It follows from Lemma 7.7 on smooth sections and extends to H1​(Em+1)H^{1}(E_{m+1}) by density. In particular,

Dom⁡(𝔠m)\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{c}_{m}) =Dom⁡(𝔞m+1),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}),
(9.2) 𝔠m​(t,t)\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}(t,t) ≥𝔞m+1​(t,t)when ​Kg≥1.\displaystyle\geq\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}(t,t)\qquad\text{when }K_{g}\geq 1.
Proposition 9.1.

For every m,j≥0m,j\geq 0,

(9.3) λj+2​m+1​(Am)=λj​(Cm)≥λj​(Am+1).\displaystyle\lambda_{j+2m+1}(A_{m})=\lambda_{j}(C_{m})\geq\lambda_{j}(A_{m+1}).

Consequently, for every l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},

NAm<​(l⁡(l+1))≤(2​m+1)+NAm+1<​(l⁡(l+1)).\displaystyle N_{A_{m}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr)\leq(2m+1)+N_{A_{m+1}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr).

The same assertion holds for the closed counting functions 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Proof.

Apply Proposition 2.4 to the concrete spaces Hm=L2​(Em)H_{m}=L^{2}(E_{m}), the closed operator BmB_{m}, and the shift αm=m⁡(m+1)\alpha_{m}=m(m+1). The compact-resolvent assumption in Notation 2.1 was verified above. The required form-domain inclusion and form order are exactly (9.2). Finally, Lemma 8.2 gives rm=dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1r_{m}=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1. Formula (9.3) and both counting recursions are therefore the specialization of (2.4) and (2.5). ∎

Theorem 9.2.

Let (S2,g)(S^{2},g) be a smooth Riemannian two-sphere with Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1. Then, for every l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+},

(9.4) N−Δg<​(l⁡(l+1))\displaystyle N_{-\Delta_{g}}^{<}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr) ≤l2,\displaystyle\leq l^{2},
(9.5) 𝒩−Δg​(l​(l+1))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{g}}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr) ≤(l+1)2.\displaystyle\leq(l+1)^{2}.

Equivalently,

(9.6) λi​(S2,g)≥λi​(𝕊2,ground),i≥1.\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{2},g)\geq\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}}),\qquad i\geq 1.
Proof.

We apply Corollary 2.7 to

Hm=L2​(Em),Bm,αm=m⁡(m+1).\displaystyle H_{m}=L^{2}(E_{m}),\qquad B_{m},\qquad\alpha_{m}=m(m+1).

The form order is (9.2), compact resolvent was recorded above, and Lemma 8.2 gives the required exact kernel dimensions 2​m+12m+1. Lemma 7.7 gives A0=B0∗​B0=−ΔgA_{0}=B_{0}^{*}B_{0}=-\Delta_{g}. Hence (2.12) is precisely (9.4)– (9.5).

For (9.6), choose l≥1l\geq 1 so that l2≤i≤l2+2​ll^{2}\leq i\leq l^{2}+2l. The round eigenvalue at every index in this cluster is l⁡(l+1)l(l+1), while the strict-counting estimate gives λl2​(g)≥l⁡(l+1)\lambda_{l^{2}}(g)\geq l(l+1). Monotonicity of the ordered spectrum gives the claim. ∎

Lemma 9.3.

Assume Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1 and Kg≢1K_{g}\not\equiv 1. Then, for every m,j≥0m,j\geq 0,

λj​(Cm)>λj​(Am+1).\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(C_{m})>\lambda_{j}(A_{m+1}).
Proof.

Fix mm and set

V:=2​(m+1)​(Kg−1).\displaystyle V:=2(m+1)(K_{g}-1).

By (9.1), Cm=Am+1+VC_{m}=A_{m+1}+V in the quadratic-form sense. The smooth function VV is nonnegative and is positive on a nonempty open set Ω\Omega.

Let SjS_{j} be the direct sum of the eigenspaces of CmC_{m} belonging to its first j+1j+1 eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity. We claim that

∫S2V​|s|2​d​Ag>0for every ​0≠s∈Sj.\displaystyle\int_{S^{2}}V|s|^{2}\,dA_{g}>0\qquad\text{for every }0\neq s\in S_{j}.

Otherwise ss vanishes on Ω\Omega. Decompose ss into the finite sum of its components corresponding to the distinct eigenvalues of CmC_{m}.

Because ss vanishes on Ω\Omega, so do Cmq​sC_{m}^{q}s for all q≥0q\geq 0. A Vandermonde argument therefore shows that each individual eigencomponent vanishes on Ω\Omega.

The unique-continuation theorem for second-order elliptic operators with smooth coefficients forces each such component to vanish identically, a contradiction.

The unit sphere of the finite-dimensional space SjS_{j} is compact, so there is δj>0\delta_{j}>0 such that

∫S2V​|s|2​d​Ag≥δj​‖s‖2(s∈Sj).\displaystyle\int_{S^{2}}V|s|^{2}\,dA_{g}\geq\delta_{j}\|s\|^{2}\qquad(s\in S_{j}).

Consequently,

sup0≠s∈Sj𝔞m+1​(s,s)‖s‖2≤λj​(Cm)−δj.\displaystyle\sup_{0\neq s\in S_{j}}\frac{\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}(s,s)}{\|s\|^{2}}\leq\lambda_{j}(C_{m})-\delta_{j}.

The min–max principle for Am+1A_{m+1} now gives λj​(Am+1)<λj​(Cm)\lambda_{j}(A_{m+1})<\lambda_{j}(C_{m}). ∎

Theorem 9.4.

Let (S2,g)(S^{2},g) be a smooth Riemannian two-sphere with Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1. If

(9.7) λi​(S2,g)=λi​(𝕊2,ground)\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{2},g)=\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}})

for some i≥1i\geq 1, or if

(9.8) 𝒩−Δg​(l⁡(l+1))=(l+1)2\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{g}}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr)=(l+1)^{2}

holds for some l∈ℤ+l\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, then (S2,g)(S^{2},g) is isometric to the unit round sphere.

Proof.

Suppose first that Kg≢1K_{g}\not\equiv 1. Combining Proposition 9.1 with Lemma 9.3 gives

λj+2​m+1​(Am)>λj​(Am+1)(m,j≥0).\displaystyle\lambda_{j+2m+1}(A_{m})>\lambda_{j}(A_{m+1})\qquad(m,j\geq 0).

For fixed l≥1l\geq 1, iterate this inequality for m=0,1,…,l−1m=0,1,\ldots,l-1. Since ∑m=0l−1(2​m+1)=l2\sum_{m=0}^{l-1}(2m+1)=l^{2}, one obtains

λl2​(g)=λl2​(A0)>λ0​(Al)=l⁡(l+1);\displaystyle\lambda_{l^{2}}(g)=\lambda_{l^{2}}(A_{0})>\lambda_{0}(A_{l})=l(l+1);

the last equality uses any nonzero element of ker⁡Bl\ker B_{l}, whose existence follows from Lemma 8.2. If (9.7) holds and l2≤i≤l2+2​ll^{2}\leq i\leq l^{2}+2l, then

λi​(g)≥λl2​(g)>l⁡(l+1)=λi​(𝕊2,ground),\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(g)\geq\lambda_{l^{2}}(g)>l(l+1)=\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}}),

a contradiction. Thus individual eigenvalue equality forces Kg≡1K_{g}\equiv 1.

Now assume (9.8), and set i=(l+1)2−1=l2+2​li=(l+1)^{2}-1=l^{2}+2l. The counting equality implies λi​(S2,g)≤l⁡(l+1)\lambda_{i}(S^{2},g)\leq l(l+1), whereas the ordered comparison (9.6) gives

λi​(S2,g)≥λi​(𝕊2,ground)=l⁡(l+1).\displaystyle\lambda_{i}(S^{2},g)\geq\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\mathrm{round}})=l(l+1).

Thus (9.7) holds at the index ii, and the preceding argument gives Kg≡1K_{g}\equiv 1.

In either case, a complete simply connected surface of constant curvature 11 is the unit round sphere. Hence (S2,g)(S^{2},g) is round. ∎

Theorems 9.2 and 9.4 prove the smooth comparison and rigidity assertions of Theorem 1.8. The role of Section 2 is now explicit: the present part supplies the bundle operator, the curvature form order, and the kernel dimension; Section 2 supplies the partner spectra, index shifts, counting recursion, and equality propagation.

The proof is genuinely two-dimensional. Section 16 shows that the direct S3S^{3} analogue with Ric≥2\operatorname{Ric}\geq 2 is false, and the higher-dimensional examples in [2] show that a Ricci lower bound alone does not yield the same finite-index rigidity.

10. A complex-geometric proof

This section gives a complex-geometric proof of Theorem 1.8. The point is that the bundles appearing in the ladder are powers of the anticanonical bundle on the Riemann surface underlying the oriented Riemannian sphere, and the first-order operators are Dolbeault operators after a metric identification.

We use Griffiths–Harris as the standard reference for the complex-geometric background: Dolbeault’s theorem, the correspondence between divisor classes and holomorphic line bundles on compact Riemann surfaces, Riemann–Roch for compact Riemann surfaces, global duality, Hermitian holomorphic bundles, Chern connections, curvature; see [13, Ch. 0, §3, p. 45; Ch. 0, §5, pp. 66–79; Ch. 0, §7, pp. 106–122; Ch. 1, §1, pp. 129–139; Ch. 2, §3, pp. 240–246; Ch. 5, §4, pp. 705–707].

The one-dimensional Bochner–Kodaira formula needed below is proved explicitly for the reader’s convenience.

If L→ΣL\to\Sigma is a holomorphic line bundle over a compact Riemann surface, let 𝒪⁡(L)\mathcal{O}(L) denote the sheaf of holomorphic sections of LL, and set

hq(L):=dimℂHq(Σ,𝒪(L)),q=0,1.\displaystyle h^{q}(L):=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}H^{q}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(L)),\qquad q=0,1.

Let KΣ:=Λ1,0​T∗​ΣK_{\Sigma}:=\Lambda^{1,0}T^{*}\Sigma be the canonical holomorphic line bundle, then KΣ−1=T1,0​Σ.K_{\Sigma}^{-1}=T^{1,0}\Sigma.

For each integer m≥0m\geq 0, define

Lm:=KΣ−m=(T1,0​Σ)⊗m,L0:=Σ×ℂ.\displaystyle L_{m}:=K_{\Sigma}^{-m}=(T^{1,0}\Sigma)^{\otimes m},\qquad L_{0}:=\Sigma\times\mathbb{C}.

Thus LmL_{m} is the same smooth complex line bundle as the bundle EmE_{m} used in Sections 7–9, now equipped with its natural holomorphic structure.

Theorem 10.1 (Dolbeault, Riemann–Roch, Serre duality).

Let Σ\Sigma be a compact Riemann surface of genus 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, and let L→ΣL\to\Sigma be a holomorphic line bundle. Then

H∂¯0,q(Σ,L)≃Hq(Σ,𝒪(L)),q=0,1.\displaystyle H^{0,q}_{\bar{\partial}}(\Sigma,L)\simeq H^{q}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(L)),\qquad q=0,1.
h0​(L)−h1​(L)=deg⁡L+1−𝔤,\displaystyle h^{0}(L)-h^{1}(L)=\deg L+1-\mathfrak{g},
H1​(Σ,𝒪⁡(L))≃H0​(Σ,𝒪⁡(KΣ⊗L−1))∗.\displaystyle H^{1}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(L))\simeq H^{0}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(K_{\Sigma}\otimes L^{-1}))^{*}.
Proof.

These are standard results. For Dolbeault’s theorem, see Griffiths–Harris [13, Ch. 0, §3, p. 45]. For Riemann–Roch on compact Riemann surfaces, see [13, Ch. 2, §3, pp. 240–246]. The divisor–line-bundle correspondence used to write the statement for holomorphic line bundles is recalled in [13, Ch. 1, §1, pp. 129–139]. The Serre-duality statement used here is the one-dimensional line-bundle case of global duality; see [13, Ch. 5, §4, pp. 705–707]. ∎

Lemma 10.2 (Anticanonical powers on the conformal sphere).

Let Σ\Sigma be a compact Riemann surface biholomorphic to ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1}. Then

(10.1) h0​(Lm)=dimℂH0​(Σ,Lm)=2​m+1,\displaystyle h^{0}(L_{m})=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}H^{0}(\Sigma,L_{m})=2m+1,

and

(10.2) H1​(Σ,𝒪⁡(Lm))=0.\displaystyle H^{1}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(L_{m}))=0.

Finally, for every p∈Σp\in\Sigma, the evaluation map

evp:H0​(Σ,Lm)⟶(Lm)p\displaystyle\operatorname{ev}_{p}:H^{0}(\Sigma,L_{m})\longrightarrow(L_{m})_{p}

is surjective. Consequently,

(10.3) dimℂ{s∈H0​(Σ,Lm):s⁡(p)=0}=2​m.\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\{s\in H^{0}(\Sigma,L_{m}):s(p)=0\}=2m.
Proof.

Step (1). Equivalently, Σ\Sigma has genus 𝔤=0\mathfrak{g}=0. The canonical bundle of a compact Riemann surface of genus 𝔤\mathfrak{g} has degree

deg⁡KΣ=2​𝔤−2;\deg K_{\Sigma}=2\mathfrak{g}-2;

see [15, §5.4, Lemma 5.4.4, p. 215]. Hence, by additivity of degree under tensor products and dualization,

deg⁡Lm\displaystyle\deg L_{m} =deg⁡(KΣ−m)=−m​deg⁡KΣ=2​m.\displaystyle=\deg\bigl(K_{\Sigma}^{-m}\bigr)=-m\,\deg K_{\Sigma}=2m.

Theorem 10.1 gives

(10.4) h0​(Lm)−h0​(KΣ⊗Lm−1)=2​m+1.\displaystyle h^{0}(L_{m})-h^{0}(K_{\Sigma}\otimes L_{m}^{-1})=2m+1.

But

KΣ⊗Lm−1=KΣm+1,deg⁡(KΣm+1)=−2​(m+1)<0.\displaystyle K_{\Sigma}\otimes L_{m}^{-1}=K_{\Sigma}^{m+1},\qquad\deg(K_{\Sigma}^{m+1})=-2(m+1)<0.

A holomorphic line bundle of negative degree has no nonzero holomorphic section: if s≢0s\not\equiv 0 is holomorphic, then its zero divisor is effective and has degree equal to the degree of the line bundle, which is impossible when the degree is negative. Thus

H0​(Σ,KΣm+1)=0.\displaystyle H^{0}(\Sigma,K_{\Sigma}^{m+1})=0.

Consequently, (10.4) gives (10.1). Serre duality gives

H1​(Σ,𝒪⁡(Lm))≃H0​(Σ,KΣ⊗Lm−1)∗=H0​(Σ,KΣm+1)∗=0,\displaystyle H^{1}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(L_{m}))\simeq H^{0}(\Sigma,K_{\Sigma}\otimes L_{m}^{-1})^{*}=H^{0}(\Sigma,K_{\Sigma}^{m+1})^{*}=0,

which proves (10.2).

Step (2). Since

Kℂ​ℙ1≃𝒪ℂ​ℙ1​(−2),\displaystyle K_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}(-2),

one has

(10.5) Lm≃𝒪ℂ​ℙ1​(2​m).\displaystyle L_{m}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}(2m).

Moreover,

By (10.5), LmL_{m} is identified with 𝒪ℂ​ℙ1​(2​m)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}(2m), and 𝒪ℂ​ℙ1​(2​m)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}(2m) is globally generated for m≥0m\geq 0.

Therefore for every p∈Σp\in\Sigma there exists a holomorphic section of LmL_{m} which does not vanish at pp. Since the target (Lm)p(L_{m})_{p} is one-dimensional, evp\operatorname{ev}_{p} is surjective. Its kernel has codimension one in H0​(Σ,Lm)H^{0}(\Sigma,L_{m}), and (10.1) gives (10.3). ∎

Let (S2,g)(S^{2},g) be oriented. The orientation and metric define the complex structure

J:T​S2⟶T​S2,J​e1=e2,J​e2=−e1\displaystyle J:TS^{2}\longrightarrow TS^{2},\qquad Je_{1}=e_{2},\qquad Je_{2}=-e_{1}

for every local oriented gg-orthonormal frame e1,e2e_{1},e_{2}. Denote the resulting compact Riemann surface by

Σ:=(S2,J).\displaystyle\Sigma:=(S^{2},J).

For a holomorphic line bundle L→ΣL\to\Sigma, write

Ω0,q(Σ,L):=C∞(Λ0,qT∗Σ⊗L),q=0,1.\displaystyle\Omega^{0,q}(\Sigma,L):=C^{\infty}\bigl(\Lambda^{0,q}T^{*}\Sigma\otimes L\bigr),\qquad q=0,1.

The Dolbeault operator is

∂¯L:Ω0,0​(Σ,L)⟶Ω0,1​(Σ,L),\displaystyle\bar{\partial}_{L}:\Omega^{0,0}(\Sigma,L)\longrightarrow\Omega^{0,1}(\Sigma,L),

and for L=LmL=L_{m} we write ∂¯m:=∂¯Lm\bar{\partial}_{m}:=\bar{\partial}_{L_{m}}.

Let e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} be a local oriented orthonormal frame, with dual coframe θ1,θ2\theta^{1},\theta^{2}. Set

Z:=12​(e1−i​e2),ζ:=12​(θ1+i​θ2),ζ¯:=12​(θ1−i​θ2).\displaystyle Z:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(e_{1}-ie_{2}),\qquad\zeta:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\theta^{1}+i\theta^{2}),\qquad\bar{\zeta}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\theta^{1}-i\theta^{2}).

Then ZZ is a local unitary frame of T1,0​Σ=KΣ−1T^{1,0}\Sigma=K_{\Sigma}^{-1}, ζ\zeta is the dual local unitary frame of KΣK_{\Sigma}, and ζ¯\bar{\zeta} is a local unitary frame of Λ0,1​T∗​Σ\Lambda^{0,1}T^{*}\Sigma.

The metric gives a unitary bundle isomorphism

ℐm:Λ0,1​T∗​Σ⊗Lm⟶Lm+1,ℐm​(ζ¯⊗Z⊗m)=Z⊗(m+1).\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{m}:\Lambda^{0,1}T^{*}\Sigma\otimes L_{m}\longrightarrow L_{m+1},\quad\quad\mathcal{I}_{m}(\bar{\zeta}\otimes Z^{\otimes m})=Z^{\otimes(m+1)}.

This definition is independent of the oriented orthonormal frame: if Z′=ei​α​ZZ^{\prime}=e^{i\alpha}Z, then ζ¯′=ei​α​ζ¯\bar{\zeta}^{\prime}=e^{i\alpha}\bar{\zeta}, and both sides acquire the same factor ei⁡(m+1)​αe^{i(m+1)\alpha}. In particular, ℐm∗=ℐm−1.\mathcal{I}_{m}^{*}=\mathcal{I}_{m}^{-1}.

Define

(10.6) BmDol:=2​ℐm∘∂¯m:C∞​(Lm)⟶C∞​(Lm+1).\displaystyle B_{m}^{\mathrm{Dol}}:=\sqrt{2}\,\mathcal{I}_{m}\circ\bar{\partial}_{m}:C^{\infty}(L_{m})\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(L_{m+1}).

Let ω\omega be the Levi-Civita connection one-form defined by

∇e1=ω⊗e2,∇e2=−ω⊗e1.\displaystyle\nabla e_{1}=\omega\otimes e_{2},\qquad\nabla e_{2}=-\omega\otimes e_{1}.

The induced Chern connection on LmL_{m} is

∇(m)(u⋅Z⊗m)=(d​u+i⋅m​u​ω)⊗Z⊗m.\displaystyle\nabla^{(m)}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes m})=(du+i\cdot mu\omega)\otimes Z^{\otimes m}.

The complexified cotangent bundle splits as

T∗​Σ⊗ℝℂ=Λ1,0​T∗​Σ⊕Λ0,1​T∗​Σ.\displaystyle T^{*}\Sigma\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}=\Lambda^{1,0}T^{*}\Sigma\oplus\Lambda^{0,1}T^{*}\Sigma.

Let

Π1,0:T∗​Σ⊗ℝℂ→Λ1,0​T∗​Σ,Π0,1:T∗​Σ⊗ℝℂ→Λ0,1​T∗​Σ\displaystyle\Pi^{1,0}:T^{*}\Sigma\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}\to\Lambda^{1,0}T^{*}\Sigma,\qquad\Pi^{0,1}:T^{*}\Sigma\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C}\to\Lambda^{0,1}T^{*}\Sigma

be the corresponding projections. Equivalently, for a complex-valued one-form α\alpha,

Π1,0​α=12​(α−i​α∘J),Π0,1​α=12​(α+i​α∘J),\displaystyle\Pi^{1,0}\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\alpha-i\,\alpha\circ J\bigr),\qquad\Pi^{0,1}\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(\alpha+i\,\alpha\circ J\bigr),

where (α∘J)​(X)=α​(J​X)(\alpha\circ J)(X)=\alpha(JX).

We define

(∇(m))′:=(Π1,0⊗IdLm)∘∇(m),(∇(m))′′:=(Π0,1⊗IdLm)∘∇(m).\displaystyle(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime}:=(\Pi^{1,0}\otimes\operatorname{Id}_{L_{m}})\circ\nabla^{(m)},\qquad(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime}:=(\Pi^{0,1}\otimes\operatorname{Id}_{L_{m}})\circ\nabla^{(m)}.

Thus

∇(m)=(∇(m))′+(∇(m))′′,\displaystyle\nabla^{(m)}=(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime}+(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime},

with

(∇(m))′:C∞​(Lm)→Ω1,0​(Σ,Lm),(∇(m))′′:C∞​(Lm)→Ω0,1​(Σ,Lm).\displaystyle(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime}:C^{\infty}(L_{m})\to\Omega^{1,0}(\Sigma,L_{m}),\qquad(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime}:C^{\infty}(L_{m})\to\Omega^{0,1}(\Sigma,L_{m}).

Writing

Dej(m)u:=eju+imuω(ej),j=1,2,\displaystyle D^{(m)}_{e_{j}}u:=e_{j}u+imu\omega(e_{j}),\qquad j=1,2,

One obtains

(10.7) ∂¯m​(u⋅Z⊗m)=12​(De1(m)​u+i​De2(m)​u)​ζ¯⊗Z⊗m.\displaystyle\bar{\partial}_{m}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes m})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m)}u+iD_{e_{2}}^{(m)}u\bigr)\bar{\zeta}\otimes Z^{\otimes m}.

Combining (10.6) and (10.7),

BmDol​(u⋅Z⊗m)=(De1(m)​u+i​De2(m)​u)​Z⊗(m+1),\displaystyle B_{m}^{\mathrm{Dol}}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes m})=\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m)}u+iD_{e_{2}}^{(m)}u\bigr)Z^{\otimes(m+1)},

which is exactly the operator BmB_{m} from (7.3). Hence we write simply

Bm=BmDol.\displaystyle B_{m}=B_{m}^{\mathrm{Dol}}.

As before, BmB_{m} denotes the closed operator initially defined on C∞​(Lm)C^{\infty}(L_{m}):

Bm:Dom⁡(Bm)=H1​(Lm)⊂L2​(Lm)⟶L2​(Lm+1),\displaystyle B_{m}:\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m})=H^{1}(L_{m})\subset L^{2}(L_{m})\longrightarrow L^{2}(L_{m+1}),

and Bm∗B_{m}^{*} denotes its Hilbert-space adjoint.

For m=0m=0, L0L_{0} is trivial, and B0∗​B0=−ΔgB_{0}^{*}B_{0}=-\Delta_{g} is exactly (7.6) from Lemma 7.7.

We now apply the metric-independent cohomology from Section 10. Since Σ\Sigma is a compact Riemann surface of genus zero, Σ≃ℂ​ℙ1\Sigma\simeq\mathbb{CP}^{1}. By construction,

ker⁡Bm=ker⁡∂¯m=H0​(Σ,Lm).\displaystyle\ker B_{m}=\ker\bar{\partial}_{m}=H^{0}(\Sigma,L_{m}).

Applying Lemma 10.2 gives

(10.8) dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1.\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1.

For the adjoint-kernel vanishing, the same lemma gives

H1​(Σ,𝒪⁡(Lm))=0.\displaystyle H^{1}(\Sigma,\mathcal{O}(L_{m}))=0.

By Dolbeault’s theorem, this is equivalent to

(10.9) H∂¯0,1​(Σ,Lm)=0.\displaystyle H^{0,1}_{\bar{\partial}}(\Sigma,L_{m})=0.

Let Ψ∈Dom⁡(Bm∗)\Psi\in\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{*}) satisfy Bm∗​Ψ=0B_{m}^{*}\Psi=0. By elliptic regularity for ∂¯m∗\bar{\partial}_{m}^{*}, it is enough to argue in the smooth category. Put

η:=ℐm−1​Ψ∈Ω0,1​(Σ,Lm).\displaystyle\eta:=\mathcal{I}_{m}^{-1}\Psi\in\Omega^{0,1}(\Sigma,L_{m}).

Since Bm=2​ℐm​∂¯mB_{m}=\sqrt{2}\,\mathcal{I}_{m}\bar{\partial}_{m}, the equation Bm∗​Ψ=0B_{m}^{*}\Psi=0 is equivalent to

∂¯m∗​η=0.\displaystyle\bar{\partial}_{m}^{*}\eta=0.

Because Σ\Sigma has complex dimension one, there are no (0,2)(0,2)-forms, so automatically

∂¯m​η=0.\displaystyle\bar{\partial}_{m}\eta=0.

Thus η\eta defines a Dolbeault cohomology class in H∂¯0,1​(Σ,Lm)H^{0,1}_{\bar{\partial}}(\Sigma,L_{m}). By (10.9), this class is zero, so there exists s∈Ω0,0​(Σ,Lm)s\in\Omega^{0,0}(\Sigma,L_{m}) such that

η=∂¯m​s.\displaystyle\eta=\bar{\partial}_{m}s.

Then

‖η‖L22=⟨η,∂¯m​s⟩L2=⟨∂¯m∗​η,s⟩L2=0.\displaystyle\|\eta\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\langle\eta,\bar{\partial}_{m}s\rangle_{L^{2}}=\langle\bar{\partial}_{m}^{*}\eta,s\rangle_{L^{2}}=0.

Hence η=0\eta=0, and therefore Ψ=0\Psi=0. We have proved

(10.10) ker⁡Bm∗={0}.\displaystyle\ker B_{m}^{*}=\{0\}.

This is the complex-geometric replacement for Lemma 8.3.

Remark 10.3.

The proof of (10.8) and (10.10) uses only the complex geometry of ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1}, together with the smooth Hilbert adjoint after the metric is chosen. It does not use the curvature lower bound Kg≥1K_{g}\geq 1.

It remains to recover the curvature ladder. This is the one place where the Hermitian metric and the above Chern connections ∇(m)\nabla^{(m)} are essential.

Let ωΣ:=d​Ag\omega_{\Sigma}:=dA_{g} be the Kähler form of (Σ,g,J)(\Sigma,g,J). For m≥0m\geq 0, set

Θm:=(∇(m))2.\displaystyle\Theta_{m}:=(\nabla^{(m)})^{2}.

and on LmL_{m}-valued zero-forms define

Δm′=((∇(m))′)∗​(∇(m))′,Δm′′=((∇(m))′′)∗​(∇(m))′′.\displaystyle\Delta_{m}^{\prime}=((\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime})^{*}(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime},\qquad\Delta_{m}^{\prime\prime}=((\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime})^{*}(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime}.

By (10.7),

(10.11) (∇(m))′′=∂¯m.\displaystyle(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime}=\bar{\partial}_{m}.
Theorem 10.4 (One-dimensional Bochner–Kodaira identity).

For every m≥0m\geq 0, on smooth sections of LmL_{m},

(10.12) Δm′−Δm′′=ΛωΣ​(i​Θm).\displaystyle\Delta_{m}^{\prime}-\Delta_{m}^{\prime\prime}=\Lambda_{\omega_{\Sigma}}(i\Theta_{m}).

Equivalently, if i​Θm=f​ωΣi\Theta_{m}=f\omega_{\Sigma}, then

Δm′−Δm′′=f.\displaystyle\Delta_{m}^{\prime}-\Delta_{m}^{\prime\prime}=f.
Remark 10.5.

This is the one-dimensional line-bundle case of the classical Bochner–Kodaira identity, specialized here to the bundles LmL_{m} and to the Chern connections ∇(m)\nabla^{(m)} already introduced above. The differential-geometric method goes back to Bochner and Kodaira; see Kodaira’s 1953 paper [17]. The vector-bundle form is closely related to the Akizuki–Nakano/Nakano identities [1, 25]. We include the proof in this special case to fix the sign convention.

Proof.

The identity is local. Fix p∈Σp\in\Sigma, and choose a local oriented orthonormal frame so that the associated unitary (1,0)(1,0)-coframe ζ\zeta, the dual vector ZZ, and the unitary frame Z⊗mZ^{\otimes m} of LmL_{m} are normal at pp. Thus

ωΣ=i​ζ∧ζ¯\displaystyle\omega_{\Sigma}=i\zeta\wedge\bar{\zeta}

at pp, the first-order frame-connection terms vanish at pp, and [Z,Z¯]​(p)=0[Z,\bar{Z}](p)=0. For a smooth section ss of LmL_{m},

(∇(m))′​s=(∇Z(m)s)​ζ,(∇(m))′′​s=(∇Z¯(m)s)​ζ¯.\displaystyle(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime}s=(\nabla^{(m)}_{Z}s)\zeta,\qquad(\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime}s=(\nabla^{(m)}_{\bar{Z}}s)\bar{\zeta}.

At pp, the formal adjoints satisfy

((∇(m))′)∗​(a​ζ)=−∇Z¯(m)a,((∇(m))′′)∗​(b​ζ¯)=−∇Z(m)b.\displaystyle((\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime})^{*}(a\zeta)=-\nabla^{(m)}_{\bar{Z}}a,\qquad((\nabla^{(m)})^{\prime\prime})^{*}(b\bar{\zeta})=-\nabla^{(m)}_{Z}b.

Therefore

Δm′​s=−∇Z¯(m)​∇Z(m)s,Δm′′​s=−∇Z(m)​∇Z¯(m)s.\displaystyle\Delta_{m}^{\prime}s=-\nabla^{(m)}_{\bar{Z}}\nabla^{(m)}_{Z}s,\qquad\Delta_{m}^{\prime\prime}s=-\nabla^{(m)}_{Z}\nabla^{(m)}_{\bar{Z}}s.

Subtracting gives

(Δm′−Δm′′)​s=(∇Z(m)∇Z¯(m)−∇Z¯(m)∇Z(m))​s=Θm​(Z,Z¯)​s.\displaystyle(\Delta_{m}^{\prime}-\Delta_{m}^{\prime\prime})s=(\nabla^{(m)}_{Z}\nabla^{(m)}_{\bar{Z}}-\nabla^{(m)}_{\bar{Z}}\nabla^{(m)}_{Z})s=\Theta_{m}(Z,\bar{Z})s.

Write i​Θm=f​ωΣi\Theta_{m}=f\omega_{\Sigma}. Since ωΣ​(Z,Z¯)=i\omega_{\Sigma}(Z,\bar{Z})=i, one has

Θm​(Z,Z¯)=f.\displaystyle\Theta_{m}(Z,\bar{Z})=f.

Thus

(Δm′−Δm′′)​s=f​s=ΛωΣ​(i​Θm)​s.\displaystyle(\Delta_{m}^{\prime}-\Delta_{m}^{\prime\prime})s=fs=\Lambda_{\omega_{\Sigma}}(i\Theta_{m})s.

Since pp was arbitrary, the identity holds globally. ∎

The next identity is not a new curvature formula; it is the preceding one-dimensional Bochner–Kodaira identity rewritten in the ladder notation of this paper.

Lemma 10.6 (Dolbeault curvature ladder).

For every m≥0m\geq 0, as operators on C∞​(Lm+1)C^{\infty}(L_{m+1}),

Bm​Bm∗−Bm+1∗​Bm+1=2​(m+1)​Kg.\displaystyle B_{m}B_{m}^{*}-B_{m+1}^{*}B_{m+1}=2(m+1)K_{g}.
Proof.

By (10.11) and the definition of Δm+1′′\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime\prime},

Δm+1′′=∂¯m+1∗​∂¯m+1.\displaystyle\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime\prime}=\bar{\partial}_{m+1}^{*}\bar{\partial}_{m+1}.

By (10.6) and the unitarity of ℐm+1\mathcal{I}_{m+1},

(10.13) Bm+1∗​Bm+1=2​∂¯m+1∗​∂¯m+1=2​Δm+1′′on ​C∞​(Lm+1).\displaystyle B_{m+1}^{*}B_{m+1}=2\bar{\partial}_{m+1}^{*}\bar{\partial}_{m+1}=2\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime\prime}\qquad\text{on }C^{\infty}(L_{m+1}).

For the (∇(m+1))′(\nabla^{(m+1)})^{\prime}-part, define the unitary metric identification

𝒥m:Λ1,0​T∗​Σ⊗Lm+1⟶Lm,𝒥m​(ζ⊗Z⊗(m+1))=Z⊗(m).\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{m}:\Lambda^{1,0}T^{*}\Sigma\otimes L_{m+1}\longrightarrow L_{m},\qquad\mathcal{J}_{m}(\zeta\otimes Z^{\otimes(m+1)})=Z^{\otimes(m)}.

The local formula for ∇(m+1)\nabla^{(m+1)} gives

(∇(m+1))′​(u⋅Z⊗(m+1))=12​(De1(m+1)​u−i​De2(m+1)​u)​ζ⊗Z⊗(m+1).\displaystyle(\nabla^{(m+1)})^{\prime}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes(m+1)})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m+1)}u-iD_{e_{2}}^{(m+1)}u\bigr)\zeta\otimes Z^{\otimes(m+1)}.

The formal adjoint of BmB_{m} is locally

Bm∗​(u⋅Z⊗(m+1))=−(De1(m+1)​u−i​De2(m+1)​u)​Z⊗(m).\displaystyle B_{m}^{*}(u\cdot Z^{\otimes(m+1)})=-\bigl(D_{e_{1}}^{(m+1)}u-iD_{e_{2}}^{(m+1)}u\bigr)Z^{\otimes(m)}.

Hence

Bm∗=−2​𝒥m​(∇(m+1))′.\displaystyle B_{m}^{*}=-\sqrt{2}\,\mathcal{J}_{m}(\nabla^{(m+1)})^{\prime}.

Since 𝒥m\mathcal{J}_{m} is unitary,

(10.14) Bm​Bm∗=2​((∇(m+1))′)∗​(∇(m+1))′=2​Δm+1′on ​C∞​(Lm+1).\displaystyle B_{m}B_{m}^{*}=2((\nabla^{(m+1)})^{\prime})^{*}(\nabla^{(m+1)})^{\prime}=2\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime}\qquad\text{on }C^{\infty}(L_{m+1}).

Combining (10.13) and (10.14),

(10.15) Bm​Bm∗−Bm+1∗​Bm+1=2​(Δm+1′−Δm+1′′).\displaystyle B_{m}B_{m}^{*}-B_{m+1}^{*}B_{m+1}=2(\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime}-\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime\prime}).

It remains to evaluate Θm+1\Theta_{m+1}. We use the curvature convention

d​ω=−Kg​d​Ag.\displaystyle d\omega=-K_{g}\,dA_{g}.

By the local formula for ∇(m+1)\nabla^{(m+1)},

Θm+1=(∇(m+1))2=i⁡(m+1)​d​ω=−i⁡(m+1)​Kg​ωΣ,i​Θm+1=(m+1)​Kg​ωΣ.\displaystyle\Theta_{m+1}=(\nabla^{(m+1)})^{2}=i(m+1)\,d\omega=-i(m+1)K_{g}\omega_{\Sigma},\qquad i\Theta_{m+1}=(m+1)K_{g}\omega_{\Sigma}.

Therefore

ΛωΣ​(i​Θm+1)=(m+1)​Kg.\displaystyle\Lambda_{\omega_{\Sigma}}(i\Theta_{m+1})=(m+1)K_{g}.

By (10.12),

Δm+1′−Δm+1′′=(m+1)​Kg.\displaystyle\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime}-\Delta_{m+1}^{\prime\prime}=(m+1)K_{g}.

Substituting this into (10.15) gives

Bm​Bm∗−Bm+1∗​Bm+1=2​(m+1)​Kgon ​C∞​(Lm+1).\displaystyle B_{m}B_{m}^{*}-B_{m+1}^{*}B_{m+1}=2(m+1)K_{g}\qquad\text{on }C^{\infty}(L_{m+1}).

∎

We now apply the abstract mechanism of Section 2. For the present Dolbeault realization, take

Hm=L2​(Lm),Bm=2​ℐm​∂¯m,αm=m⁡(m+1).\displaystyle H_{m}=L^{2}(L_{m}),\qquad B_{m}=\sqrt{2}\,\mathcal{I}_{m}\bar{\partial}_{m},\qquad\alpha_{m}=m(m+1).

The associated forms and self-adjoint operators are precisely the forms 𝔞m,𝔠m\mathfrak{a}_{m},\mathfrak{c}_{m} and operators Am,CmA_{m},C_{m} introduced in Section 9. Ellipticity on the compact smooth surface gives compact resolvent. Lemma 10.2 gives

dimℂker⁡Bm=2​m+1,\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{m}=2m+1,

and the Bochner–Kodaira identity, in the form of Lemma 10.6, gives, for every t∈H1​(Lm+1)t\in H^{1}(L_{m+1}),

𝔠m​(t,t)−𝔞m+1​(t,t)=2​(m+1)​∫S2(Kg−1)​|t|2​d​Ag≥0.\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{m}(t,t)-\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}(t,t)=2(m+1)\int_{S^{2}}(K_{g}-1)|t|^{2}\,dA_{g}\geq 0.

Thus the hypotheses of Corollary 2.7 hold on the concrete spaces Hm=L2​(Lm)H_{m}=L^{2}(L_{m}) for the concrete closed operators BmB_{m}. That corollary gives the counting and eigenvalue comparison in Theorem 9.2. The equality cases are then handled by the strict form comparison and by Proposition 2.6, exactly as in the proof of Theorem 9.4.

Part III Alexandrov 22-Spheres with Curvature ≥1\geq 1

Throughout this part, XX is a compact Alexandrov surface homeomorphic to S2S^{2} and with Alexandrov curvature bounded below by 11.

11. Preliminary results on Alexandrov 22-spheres

This section collects the external Alexandrov-surface, conformal-metric, and spectral-convergence results used later.

From [31, Proposition A.13], we know XX is a surface of bounded integral curvature.

Note

Pot⁡(ℂ​ℙ1,g0):={w∈L1​(ℂ​ℙ1,d​A0):Δ0​w∈ℳ⁡(ℂ​ℙ1)},\operatorname{Pot}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},g_{0}):=\left\{w\in L^{1}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},dA_{0}):\Delta_{0}w\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{CP}^{1})\right\},

where ℳ⁡(ℂ​ℙ1)\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{CP}^{1}) denotes the space of finite signed Radon measures on ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1}. The condition Δ0​w∈ℳ⁡(ℂ​ℙ1)\Delta_{0}w\in\mathcal{M}(\mathbb{CP}^{1}) is understood in the distributional sense: there exists a finite signed Radon measure μw\mu_{w} such that

∫ℂ​ℙ1w​Δ0​φ​d​A0=∫ℂ​ℙ1φ​d​μwfor every ​φ∈C∞​(ℂ​ℙ1).\int_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}w\,\Delta_{0}\varphi\,dA_{0}=\int_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}\varphi\,d\mu_{w}\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{CP}^{1}).

where Δ0\Delta_{0} is the Laplacian of unit round sphere 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}.

Then by Troyanov [35, Theorem 7.3(b)], there exist a smooth metric hh on XX and v∈Pot⁡(X,h)v\in\operatorname{Pot}(X,h) such that dX=dh,vd_{X}=d_{h,v}; where

dh,v​(x,y):=infγ∫01ev⁡(γ⁡(t))​|γ˙​(t)|h​𝑑t,d_{h,v}(x,y):=\inf_{\gamma}\int_{0}^{1}e^{v(\gamma(t))}|\dot{\gamma}(t)|_{h}\,dt,

and the infimum is over absolutely continuous curves γ:[0,1]→X\gamma:[0,1]\to X joining xx to yy.

Notation 11.1 (Fixed conformal parametrization of XX).

Fix a conformal homeomorphism

F:ℂ​ℙ1⟶X.F:\mathbb{CP}^{1}\longrightarrow X.

If hh and vv are the smooth metric and potential on XX given above, write

F∗​h=e2​ψ​g0,v~:=v∘F,u:=v~+ψ=v∘F+ψ.F^{*}h=e^{2\psi}g_{0},\qquad\widetilde{v}:=v\circ F,\qquad u:=\widetilde{v}+\psi=v\circ F+\psi.

Define the pulled-back distance

dXF​(p,q):=dX​(F⁡(p),F⁡(q)).d_{X}^{F}(p,q):=d_{X}(F(p),F(q)).

Then

dXF=dg0,u.d_{X}^{F}=d_{g_{0},u}.

After this declaration only, one may identify XX with ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} and suppress the superscript FF.

Thus, in the sense of singular conformal metrics,

(11.1) gX=e2​u​g0,d​AX=e2​u​d​A0.\displaystyle g_{X}=e^{2u}g_{0},\qquad dA_{X}=e^{2u}\,dA_{0}.

Let ωX\omega_{X} denote the Alexandrov curvature measure. In the fixed round conformal model,

ωX:=d​A0−Δ0​u.\displaystyle\omega_{X}:=dA_{0}-\Delta_{0}u.

in the distributional sense. In a local coordinate in which gX=e2​U​|d​z|2g_{X}=e^{2U}|dz|^{2}, the same formula is

ωX=−Δeuc​U\displaystyle\omega_{X}=-\Delta_{\mathrm{euc}}U

as a Radon measure (see [30, Theorem 7.1.1, §7.3, pp. 112–119]).

Recall [22, Theorem 2.0] identifies the synthetic lower bound with the measure inequality

(11.2) ωX≥d​AX=e2​u​d​A0.\displaystyle\omega_{X}\geq dA_{X}=e^{2u}dA_{0}.
Lemma 11.2.

u≥−Cu\geq-C.

Proof: Let GG be the Green kernel of −Δ0-\Delta_{0}, normalized to have zero mean. Since −Δ0​u=ωX−d​A0-\Delta_{0}u=\omega_{X}-dA_{0}, the Green representation is

u⁡(x)=u¯+∫ℂ​ℙ1G⁡(x,y)​d​ωX​(y)−∫ℂ​ℙ1G⁡(x,y)​d​A0​(y).\displaystyle u(x)=\overline{u}+\int_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}G(x,y)\,d\omega_{X}(y)-\int_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}G(x,y)\,dA_{0}(y).

limi→∞‖e2​ui−e2​u‖L1​(d​A0)\displaystyle\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}\|e^{2u_{i}}-e^{2u}\|_{L^{1}(dA_{0})} ≤limi→∞‖eui−eu‖L2​(d​A0)​(‖eui‖L2​(d​A0)+‖eu‖L2​(d​A0))=0.\displaystyle\leq\lim_{i\rightarrow\infty}\|e^{u_{i}}-e^{u}\|_{L^{2}(dA_{0})}\bigl(\|e^{u_{i}}\|_{L^{2}(dA_{0})}+\|e^{u}\|_{L^{2}(dA_{0})}\bigr)=0.

In particular Vi→V>0V_{i}\to V>0. Therefore all the hypotheses of Reshetnyak’s convergence theorem are satisfied.

By (11.3), every atom of the limiting curvature measure ωX\omega_{X} has mass strictly less than 2​π2\pi; this is the no-cusp atom condition in Reshetnyak’s convergence theorem.

Thus all hypotheses of [30, Theorem 7.3.17.3.1] are satisfied. The conclusion is exactly (11.28). ∎

Lemma 11.9.

We have

(11.29) limτk→0λj​(S2,gτk)=λj​(X),∀j≥0.\displaystyle\lim_{\tau_{k}\rightarrow 0}\lambda_{j}(S^{2},g_{\tau_{k}})=\lambda_{j}(X),\quad\quad\forall j\geq 0.
Proof.

Lemma 11.8 gives Gromov–Hausdorff convergence. The areas converge by Lemma 11.7, hence the convergence is non-collapse.

Therefore [33, Theorem 1.1] applies and gives (11.29). ∎

Definition 12.1.

Lemma 12.2.

in Hm0⊕Hm+10H_{m}^{0}\oplus H_{m+1}^{0}.

ui:=uτi,Dm:=Bmg0:C∞​(Lm)⟶C∞​(Lm+1),\displaystyle u_{i}:=u_{\tau_{i}},\qquad D_{m}:=B_{m}^{g_{0}}:C^{\infty}(L_{m})\longrightarrow C^{\infty}(L_{m+1}),

Hence, if F=Jm,gτi​s=e(m+1)​ui​sF=J_{m,g_{\tau_{i}}}s=e^{(m+1)u_{i}}s, then

B^mgτi​F\displaystyle\widehat{B}_{m}^{g_{\tau_{i}}}F =Jm+1,gτi​Bmgτi​Jm,gτi−1​F=e(m+2)​ui​e−2​ui​Dm​(e−(m+1)​ui​F)=em​ui​Dm​(e−(m+1)​ui​F),\displaystyle=J_{m+1,g_{\tau_{i}}}B_{m}^{g_{\tau_{i}}}J_{m,g_{\tau_{i}}}^{-1}F=e^{(m+2)u_{i}}e^{-2u_{i}}D_{m}\bigl(e^{-(m+1)u_{i}}F\bigr)=e^{mu_{i}}D_{m}\bigl(e^{-(m+1)u_{i}}F\bigr),

which is equivalent to (12.1).

(12.2) (Fi,Gi)⇀(F,G)weakly in ​Hm0⊕Hm+10.\displaystyle(F_{i},G_{i})\rightharpoonup(F,G)\quad\text{weakly in }H_{m}^{0}\oplus H_{m+1}^{0}.

(12.4) ⟨Gi,e−m​ui​Φ⟩Hm+10=⟨Fi,e−(m+1)​ui​Dm†​Φ⟩Hm0.\displaystyle\left\langle G_{i},e^{-mu_{i}}\Phi\right\rangle_{H_{m+1}^{0}}=\left\langle F_{i},e^{-(m+1)u_{i}}D_{m}^{\dagger}\Phi\right\rangle_{H_{m}^{0}}.

Dm​(e−(m+1)​u​F)=e−m​u​Gin ​𝒟′​(ℂ​ℙ1,Lm+1).\displaystyle D_{m}\bigl(e^{-(m+1)u}F\bigr)=e^{-mu}G\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},L_{m+1}).

By (12.1),

(F,G)∈graph⁡(B^mX).\displaystyle(F,G)\in\operatorname{graph}(\widehat{B}_{m}^{X}).

Step (3). Let

(F,G)∈graph⁡(B^mX).\displaystyle(F,G)\in\operatorname{graph}(\widehat{B}_{m}^{X}).

(12.7) s:=e−(m+1)​u​F,h:=Dm​s=e−m​u​G.\displaystyle s:=e^{-(m+1)u}F,\qquad h:=D_{m}s=e^{-mu}G.

The lower bound u≥−Cu\geq-C implies that ss and hh are locally L2L^{2}, and the second identity in (12.7) is understood distributionally.

e−(m+1)​ui​Fi=s,Dm​s=h=e−m​ui​Gi.\displaystyle e^{-(m+1)u_{i}}F_{i}=s,\qquad D_{m}s=h=e^{-mu_{i}}G_{i}.

Therefore

Here (11.24) controls the positive weights, while F∈Hm0F\in H_{m}^{0} and G∈Hm+10G\in H_{m+1}^{0} provide the required global L2L^{2}-majorants.

and (11.24) gives

ui≤u+τid​A0​-almost everywhere.u_{i}\leq u+\tau_{i}\qquad dA_{0}\text{-almost everywhere}.

Fi\displaystyle F_{i} =e(m+1)​(ui−u)​F,\displaystyle=e^{(m+1)(u_{i}-u)}F, Gi\displaystyle G_{i} =em⁡(ui−u)GdA0-almost everywhere.\displaystyle=e^{m(u_{i}-u)}G\qquad dA_{0}\text{-almost everywhere}.

|Fi−F|hm,02\displaystyle|F_{i}-F|_{h_{m,0}}^{2} =|e(m+1)​(ui−u)−1|2​|F|hm,02≤(1+em+1)2​|F|hm,02,\displaystyle=\left|e^{(m+1)(u_{i}-u)}-1\right|^{2}|F|_{h_{m,0}}^{2}\leq\bigl(1+e^{m+1}\bigr)^{2}|F|_{h_{m,0}}^{2},
|Gi−G|hm+1,02\displaystyle|G_{i}-G|_{h_{m+1,0}}^{2} =|em⁡(ui−u)−1|2​|G|hm+1,02≤(1+em)2​|G|hm+1,02.\displaystyle=\left|e^{m(u_{i}-u)}-1\right|^{2}|G|_{h_{m+1,0}}^{2}\leq\bigl(1+e^{m}\bigr)^{2}|G|_{h_{m+1,0}}^{2}.

The two functions on the right are integrable because

F∈Hm0,G∈Hm+10.F\in H_{m}^{0},\qquad G\in H_{m+1}^{0}.

Dominated convergence in the fixed global bundle norms therefore yields

‖Fi−F‖Hm02\displaystyle\|F_{i}-F\|_{H_{m}^{0}}^{2} =∫ℂ​ℙ1|Fi−F|hm,02​d​A0⟶0,\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}|F_{i}-F|_{h_{m,0}}^{2}\,dA_{0}\longrightarrow 0,

Consequently,

It follows from (12.9) and (12.1) that

If 𝔮\mathfrak{q} is a closed nonnegative form on a Hilbert space, we define the extended quadratic functionals on H0H_{0}:

𝔮⁡[v]\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}[v] :={𝔮⁡(v,v),(v,v)∈Dom⁡(q),+∞,(v,v)∉Dom⁡(q),\displaystyle:=\begin{cases}\mathfrak{q}(v,v),&(v,v)\in\operatorname{Dom}(q),\\[5.69054pt] +\infty,&(v,v)\notin\operatorname{Dom}(q),\end{cases}
Definition 12.3.

Assume 𝔮i,𝔮\mathfrak{q}_{i},\mathfrak{q} are closed nonnegative forms on a Hilbert space HH, we say that 𝔮i\mathfrak{q}_{i} Mosco converge to 𝔮\mathfrak{q} if:

  1. (1)

    whenever vi⇀vv_{i}\rightharpoonup v, 𝔮⁡[v]≤lim¯i⁡𝔮i​[vi]\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}[v]\leq\varliminf_{i}\mathfrak{q}_{i}[v_{i}];

  2. (2)

    for every (v,v)∈Dom⁡(𝔮)(v,v)\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}), there are vi→vv_{i}\to v strongly with 𝔮i​[vi]→𝔮⁡[v]\mathfrak{q}_{i}[v_{i}]\to\mathfrak{q}[v].

Lemma 12.4.

Let H0H_{0} and H1H_{1} be Hilbert spaces, and let

Ti:Dom⁡(Ti)⊂H0⟶H1,T:Dom⁡(T)⊂H0⟶H1\displaystyle T_{i}:\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i})\subset H_{0}\longrightarrow H_{1},\qquad T:\operatorname{Dom}(T)\subset H_{0}\longrightarrow H_{1}

be closed densely defined linear operators. Assume that

graph⁡(Ti)→Moscograph⁡(T)\displaystyle\operatorname{graph}(T_{i})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Mosco}}\operatorname{graph}(T)

as closed subspaces of H0⊕H1H_{0}\oplus H_{1}.

Fix α≥0\alpha\geq 0. Define nonnegative forms on H0H_{0} by

𝔮iα​(v,w)\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}(v,w) :=⟨Ti​v,Ti​w⟩H1+α​⟨v,w⟩H0,Dom⁡(𝔮iα)=Dom⁡(Ti)×Dom⁡(Ti),\displaystyle:=\langle T_{i}v,T_{i}w\rangle_{H_{1}}+\alpha\langle v,w\rangle_{H_{0}},\qquad\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha})=\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i})\times\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i}),
𝔮α​(v,w)\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha}(v,w) :=⟨T​v,T​w⟩H1+α​⟨v,w⟩H0,Dom⁡(𝔮α)=Dom⁡(T)×Dom⁡(T).\displaystyle:=\langle Tv,Tw\rangle_{H_{1}}+\alpha\langle v,w\rangle_{H_{0}},\qquad\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha})=\operatorname{Dom}(T)\times\operatorname{Dom}(T).

Then

𝔮iα→Mosco𝔮αas closed nonnegative forms on ​H0.\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Mosco}}\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha}\qquad\text{as closed nonnegative forms on }H_{0}.
Proof.

Step (1). We first verify that the forms appearing in the statement are indeed densely defined closed nonnegative forms on H0H_{0}.

Since TiT_{i} is densely defined, Dom⁡(𝔮iα)=Dom⁡(Ti)\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha})=\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i}) is dense in H0H_{0}. Since TiT_{i} is closed, its domain is complete with respect to the graph norm

‖v‖graph⁡(Ti)2:=‖v‖H02+‖Ti​v‖H12.\displaystyle\|v\|_{\operatorname{graph}(T_{i})}^{2}:=\|v\|_{H_{0}}^{2}+\|T_{i}v\|_{H_{1}}^{2}.

The form norm associated with 𝔮iα\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha} is

‖v‖𝔮iα2\displaystyle\|v\|_{\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}}^{2} :=‖v‖H02+𝔮iα​[v]=(α+1)​‖v‖H02+‖Ti​v‖H12.\displaystyle:=\|v\|_{H_{0}}^{2}+\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}[v]=(\alpha+1)\|v\|_{H_{0}}^{2}+\|T_{i}v\|_{H_{1}}^{2}.

For v∈Dom⁡(Ti)v\in\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i}),

‖v‖graph⁡(Ti)2≤‖v‖𝔮iα2≤(α+1)​‖v‖graph⁡(Ti)2.\displaystyle\|v\|_{\operatorname{graph}(T_{i})}^{2}\leq\|v\|_{\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}}^{2}\leq(\alpha+1)\|v\|_{\operatorname{graph}(T_{i})}^{2}.

Thus the form norm is equivalent to the graph norm. Consequently Dom⁡(𝔮iα)\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}) is complete in the form norm, so 𝔮iα\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha} is closed. The same argument applies to TT and 𝔮α\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha}.

Step (2). We now prove the two Mosco conditions.

Let

vi⇀vweakly in ​H0.\displaystyle v_{i}\rightharpoonup v\qquad\text{weakly in }H_{0}.

We must prove

(12.11) 𝔮α​[v]≤lim¯i→∞⁡𝔮iα​[vi].\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha}[v]\leq\varliminf_{i\to\infty}\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}[v_{i}].

Put

L:=lim¯i→∞⁡𝔮iα​[vi].\displaystyle L:=\varliminf_{i\to\infty}\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}[v_{i}].

If L=+∞L=+\infty, then (12.11) is automatic. Suppose therefore that L<+∞L<+\infty. Choose a subsequence, denoted by iki_{k}, such that

(12.12) 𝔮ikα​[vik]⟶L.\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}_{i_{k}}^{\alpha}[v_{i_{k}}]\longrightarrow L.

After discarding finitely many terms, all the quantities in (12.12) are finite, and hence

vik∈Dom⁡(Tik).\displaystyle v_{i_{k}}\in\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i_{k}}).

Moreover,

‖Tik​vik‖H12≤𝔮ikα​[vik],\displaystyle\|T_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}}\|_{H_{1}}^{2}\leq\mathfrak{q}_{i_{k}}^{\alpha}[v_{i_{k}}],

so the sequence Tik​vikT_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}} is bounded in H1H_{1}. By weak compactness of bounded subsets of a Hilbert space, after passing to a further subsequence, which we do not relabel, there is w∈H1w\in H_{1} such that

Tik​vik⇀wweakly in ​H1.\displaystyle T_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}}\rightharpoonup w\qquad\text{weakly in }H_{1}.

Therefore

(vik,Tik​vik)⇀(v,w)weakly in ​H0⊕H1.\displaystyle\bigl(v_{i_{k}},T_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}}\bigr)\rightharpoonup(v,w)\qquad\text{weakly in }H_{0}\oplus H_{1}.

For every kk,

(vik,Tik​vik)∈graph⁡(Tik).\displaystyle\bigl(v_{i_{k}},T_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}}\bigr)\in\operatorname{graph}(T_{i_{k}}).

The weak-limit condition in the Mosco convergence of the graphs therefore implies (v,w)∈graph⁡(T)(v,w)\in\operatorname{graph}(T). Thus

(12.13) v∈Dom⁡(T),w=T​v.\displaystyle v\in\operatorname{Dom}(T),\qquad w=Tv.

We have weak convergence

(Tik​vik,α​vik)⇀(T​v,α​v)in ​H1⊕H0.\displaystyle\bigl(T_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}},\sqrt{\alpha}\,v_{i_{k}}\bigr)\rightharpoonup\bigl(Tv,\sqrt{\alpha}\,v\bigr)\qquad\text{in }H_{1}\oplus H_{0}.

Weak lower semicontinuity of the squared norm in H1⊕H0H_{1}\oplus H_{0} now gives

𝔮α​[v]\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha}[v] =‖T​v‖H12+α​‖v‖H02=‖(T​v,α​v)‖H1⊕H02≤lim¯k→∞⁡‖(Tik​vik,α​vik)‖H1⊕H02\displaystyle=\|Tv\|_{H_{1}}^{2}+\alpha\|v\|_{H_{0}}^{2}=\left\|\bigl(Tv,\sqrt{\alpha}\,v\bigr)\right\|_{H_{1}\oplus H_{0}}^{2}\leq\varliminf_{k\to\infty}\left\|\bigl(T_{i_{k}}v_{i_{k}},\sqrt{\alpha}\,v_{i_{k}}\bigr)\right\|_{H_{1}\oplus H_{0}}^{2}
=lim¯k→∞⁡𝔮ikα​[vik]=L.\displaystyle=\varliminf_{k\to\infty}\mathfrak{q}_{i_{k}}^{\alpha}[v_{i_{k}}]=L.

By the definition of LL, this is precisely (12.11).

Step (3). Let

v∈Dom⁡(𝔮α)=Dom⁡(T).\displaystyle v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha})=\operatorname{Dom}(T).

Then

(v,T​v)∈graph⁡(T).\displaystyle(v,Tv)\in\operatorname{graph}(T).

The strong recovery condition in the Mosco convergence of the graphs provides pairs

(vi,wi)∈graph⁡(Ti)\displaystyle(v_{i},w_{i})\in\operatorname{graph}(T_{i})

such that

(12.14) (vi,wi)⟶(v,T​v)strongly in ​H0⊕H1.\displaystyle(v_{i},w_{i})\longrightarrow(v,Tv)\qquad\text{strongly in }H_{0}\oplus H_{1}.

Since (vi,wi)∈graph⁡(Ti)(v_{i},w_{i})\in\operatorname{graph}(T_{i}), we have

vi∈Dom⁡(Ti),wi=Ti​vi.\displaystyle v_{i}\in\operatorname{Dom}(T_{i}),\qquad w_{i}=T_{i}v_{i}.

The strong convergence in (12.14) therefore means

vi⟶vstrongly in ​H0,Ti​vi⟶T​vstrongly in ​H1.\displaystyle v_{i}\longrightarrow v\quad\text{strongly in }H_{0},\qquad T_{i}v_{i}\longrightarrow Tv\quad\text{strongly in }H_{1}.

Consequently,

𝔮iα​[vi]\displaystyle\mathfrak{q}_{i}^{\alpha}[v_{i}] =‖Ti​vi‖H12+α​‖vi‖H02⟶‖T​v‖H12+α​‖v‖H02=𝔮α​[v].\displaystyle=\|T_{i}v_{i}\|_{H_{1}}^{2}+\alpha\|v_{i}\|_{H_{0}}^{2}\longrightarrow\|Tv\|_{H_{1}}^{2}+\alpha\|v\|_{H_{0}}^{2}=\mathfrak{q}^{\alpha}[v].

Thus viv_{i} is a recovery sequence for vv. This proves the strong recovery condition and completes the proof of Mosco convergence. ∎

Lemma 12.5.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 12.4,

graph⁡(Ti∗)→Moscograph⁡(T∗)\displaystyle\operatorname{graph}(T_{i}^{*})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Mosco}}\operatorname{graph}(T^{*})

in H1⊕H0H_{1}\oplus H_{0}.

Proof.

For a closed densely defined TT,

graph⁡(T∗)=𝒰⁡(graph⁡(T)⟂),𝒰⁡(a,b)=(b,−a).\displaystyle\operatorname{graph}(T^{*})=\mathcal{U}(\operatorname{graph}(T)^{\perp}),\qquad\mathcal{U}(a,b)=(b,-a).

Mosco convergence of closed subspaces is equivalent to strong convergence of their orthogonal projections, and is therefore preserved by orthogonal complements and by the fixed unitary 𝒰\mathcal{U}. ∎

(B^mY)∗=Jm,Y​(BmY)∗​Jm+1,Y−1,\displaystyle(\widehat{B}_{m}^{Y})^{*}=J_{m,Y}(B_{m}^{Y})^{*}J_{m+1,Y}^{-1},

so the pulled-back adjoint forms are precisely 𝔠mY\mathfrak{c}_{m}^{Y}. ∎

Proposition 12.7.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

𝔞m+1X​(v,v)≤lim¯i⁡𝔞m+1gτi​(vi,vi)≤limi𝔠mgτi​(vi,vi)=𝔠mX​(v,v).\displaystyle\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}^{X}(v,v)\leq\varliminf_{i}\mathfrak{a}_{m+1}^{g_{\tau_{i}}}(v_{i},v_{i})\leq\lim_{i}\mathfrak{c}_{m}^{g_{\tau_{i}}}(v_{i},v_{i})=\mathfrak{c}_{m}^{X}(v,v).

Lemma 12.8.

For every m≥0m\geq 0,

hm,X=e2​m​u​hm,0,d​AX=e2​u​d​A0.\displaystyle h_{m,X}=e^{2mu}h_{m,0},\qquad dA_{X}=e^{2u}dA_{0}.

(12.16) =∫ℂ​ℙ1|s|hm,02​e2​(m+1)​u​d​A0.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}|s|_{h_{m,0}}^{2}e^{2(m+1)u}\,dA_{0}.

Lemma 11.2 gives

for some finite constant CC. Therefore

|(∂z)⊗m|hm,02=2−me2​m​ψ,dA0=e2​ψdxdy.\displaystyle|(\partial_{z})^{\otimes m}|_{h_{m,0}}^{2}=2^{-m}e^{2m\psi},\qquad dA_{0}=e^{2\psi}\,dx\,dy.

Hence, for every D′⋐DD^{\prime}\Subset D,

(12.19) ∫D′|s|hm,02​d​A0=2−m​∫D′|f|2​e2​(m+1)​ψ​𝑑x​𝑑y.\displaystyle\int_{D^{\prime}}|s|_{h_{m,0}}^{2}\,dA_{0}=2^{-m}\int_{D^{\prime}}|f|^{2}e^{2(m+1)\psi}\,dx\,dy.

Because ψ\psi is smooth, the function e2​(m+1)​ψe^{2(m+1)\psi} is bounded above and bounded away from zero on D′¯\overline{D^{\prime}}. From (12.18) and (12.19), it follows that

f∈L2​(D′,d​x​d​y).\displaystyle f\in L^{2}(D^{\prime},dx\,dy).

f∈L1​(D′,d​x​d​y).\displaystyle f\in L^{1}(D^{\prime},dx\,dy).

As D′⋐DD^{\prime}\Subset D was arbitrary,

(12.20) f∈Lloc2​(D)⊂Lloc1​(D).\displaystyle f\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\subset L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D).

We next use the kernel equation. By the maximal definition of BmXB_{m}^{X}, the distribution ∂¯m​s\bar{\partial}_{m}s is represented by a measurable LmL_{m}-valued (0,1)(0,1)-form η\eta, and

BmX​s=2​ℐm,X​η.\displaystyle B_{m}^{X}s=\sqrt{2}\,\mathcal{I}_{m,X}\eta.

Since BmX​s=0B_{m}^{X}s=0 and ℐm,X\mathcal{I}_{m,X} is a fiberwise isomorphism almost everywhere, one has

Therefore

∂¯m​s=0in ​𝒟′​(D).\displaystyle\bar{\partial}_{m}s=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(D).

Because (∂z)⊗m(\partial_{z})^{\otimes m} is a holomorphic local frame, this equation is exactly

(12.21) ∂z¯f=0in ​𝒟′​(D).\displaystyle\partial_{\bar{z}}f=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(D).

For completeness, we spell out the regularity argument. In distributions,

Δeuc​f=4​∂z∂z¯f=0.\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{euc}}f=4\partial_{z}\partial_{\bar{z}}f=0.

Together with (12.20), the Weyl lemma for the Euclidean Laplacian, applied to the real and imaginary parts of ff, shows that ff agrees almost everywhere with a smooth harmonic function. Equation (12.21) then holds pointwise, and hence ff is holomorphic on DD.

On overlaps of holomorphic coordinate charts, the resulting holomorphic coefficients satisfy the holomorphic transition law of Kℂ​ℙ1−mK_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}^{-m}. Indeed, they already represent the same measurable section almost everywhere, and two holomorphic functions which agree almost everywhere agree everywhere. The local representatives therefore assemble to a global holomorphic section. Hence

Lemma 12.9.

(12.22) ker⁡BrX\displaystyle\ker B_{r}^{X} ⊂H0​(ℂ​ℙ1,Kℂ​ℙ1−r),\displaystyle\subset H^{0}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},K_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}^{-r}), dimℂker⁡BrX\displaystyle\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\ker B_{r}^{X} ≤2​r+1.\displaystyle\leq 2r+1.

Since αr+1−αr=2​(r+1)>0\alpha_{r+1}-\alpha_{r}=2(r+1)>0, one has t=0t=0.

We next compare the essential spectra of the two partners at one level. Let

be the polar decomposition. By (12.23),

Ran⁡BrX¯=(ker⁡(BrX)∗)⟂=Hr+1X.\displaystyle\overline{\operatorname{Ran}B_{r}^{X}}=\bigl(\ker(B_{r}^{X})^{*}\bigr)^{\perp}=H_{r+1}^{X}.

Hence the partial isometry UrU_{r} restricts to a unitary map

Ur:(ker⁡BrX)⟂⟶Hr+1X.\displaystyle U_{r}:(\ker B_{r}^{X})^{\perp}\longrightarrow H_{r+1}^{X}.

Set

Tr:=(BrX)∗​BrX|(ker⁡BrX)⟂.\displaystyle T_{r}:=(B_{r}^{X})^{*}B_{r}^{X}\big|_{(\ker B_{r}^{X})^{\perp}}.

The polar-decomposition functional calculus gives

BrX​(BrX)∗=Ur​Tr​Ur∗.\displaystyle B_{r}^{X}(B_{r}^{X})^{*}=U_{r}T_{r}U_{r}^{*}.

Moreover, (ker⁡BrX)⟂(\ker B_{r}^{X})^{\perp} is a reducing subspace for (BrX)∗​BrX(B_{r}^{X})^{*}B_{r}^{X}, and therefore

ArX\displaystyle A_{r}^{X} =αr​Iker⁡BrX⊕(Tr+αr​I),\displaystyle=\alpha_{r}I_{\ker B_{r}^{X}}\oplus(T_{r}+\alpha_{r}I),
CrX\displaystyle C_{r}^{X} =Ur​(Tr+αr​I)​Ur∗.\displaystyle=U_{r}(T_{r}+\alpha_{r}I)U_{r}^{*}.

The first summand of ArXA_{r}^{X} acts on the finite-dimensional space ker⁡BrX\ker B_{r}^{X} by (12.22). A finite-dimensional direct summand has empty essential spectrum, while unitary equivalence preserves essential spectrum. Hence

(12.24) σess​(ArX)=σess​(CrX).\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{r}^{X})=\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C_{r}^{X}).

For a self-adjoint operator TT bounded from below on a Hilbert space HH, define

Λess​(T):={infσess​(T),σess​(T)≠∅,+∞,σess​(T)=∅.\displaystyle\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(T):=\begin{cases}\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T),&\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)\neq\varnothing,\\ +\infty,&\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)=\varnothing.\end{cases}

If 𝔮T\mathfrak{q}_{T} is the closed form of TT, the max–min principle and its form-domain version imply

(12.25) Λess​(T)=supL⊂HdimL<∞infv∈Dom⁡(𝔮T)∩L⟂‖v‖H=1𝔮T​(v,v).\displaystyle\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(T)=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}L\subset H\\ \dim L<\infty\end{subarray}}\ \inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{T})\cap L^{\perp}\\ \|v\|_{H}=1\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{q}_{T}(v,v).

Indeed, for each fixed value of dimL\dim L, the inner variational quantity is the corresponding max–min value; taking the supremum over all finite dimensions gives the bottom of the essential spectrum. See [27, Theorem 8.1.1 and Proposition 8.1.3, pp. 125–127].

It follows in particular that quadratic-form order is monotone at the bottom of the essential spectrum: if S≥TS\geq T in the form sense, then

(12.26) Λess​(S)≥Λess​(T).\displaystyle\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(S)\geq\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(T).

infv∈Dom⁡(𝔮S)∩L⟂‖v‖=1𝔮S​(v,v)≥infv∈Dom⁡(𝔮S)∩L⟂‖v‖=1𝔮T​(v,v)≥infv∈Dom⁡(𝔮T)∩L⟂‖v‖=1𝔮T​(v,v).\displaystyle\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{S})\cap L^{\perp}\\ \|v\|=1\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{q}_{S}(v,v)\geq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{S})\cap L^{\perp}\\ \|v\|=1\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{q}_{T}(v,v)\geq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{q}_{T})\cap L^{\perp}\\ \|v\|=1\end{subarray}}\mathfrak{q}_{T}(v,v).

Taking the supremum over LL proves (12.26).

Apply (12.26) to the form order

CrX≥Ar+1X\displaystyle C_{r}^{X}\geq A_{r+1}^{X}

from Proposition 12.7, and then use (12.24). This yields

(12.27) Λess​(ArX)=Λess​(CrX)≥Λess​(Ar+1X)(r≥0).\displaystyle\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{r}^{X})=\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(C_{r}^{X})\geq\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{r+1}^{X})\qquad(r\geq 0).

𝔞NX​(s,s)\displaystyle\mathfrak{a}_{N}^{X}(s,s) =‖BNX​s‖HN+1X2+αN​‖s‖HNX2≥αN​‖s‖HNX2,s∈Dom⁡(𝔞NX).\displaystyle=\|B_{N}^{X}s\|_{H_{N+1}^{X}}^{2}+\alpha_{N}\|s\|_{H_{N}^{X}}^{2}\geq\alpha_{N}\|s\|_{H_{N}^{X}}^{2},\qquad s\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{N}^{X}).

≥N⁡(N+1).\displaystyle\geq N(N+1).

Since this holds for every N>mN>m, it follows that

Λess​(AmX)=+∞,σess​(AmX)=∅.\displaystyle\Lambda_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{m}^{X})=+\infty,\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A_{m}^{X})=\varnothing.

σess​(CmX)=∅,\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(C_{m}^{X})=\varnothing,

so CmXC_{m}^{X} has compact resolvent as well.

Step (2). It remains to prove the compact graph embedding in the statement. By the representation theorem for the closed form 𝔞mX\mathfrak{a}_{m}^{X},

Dom⁡((AmX+I)1/2)=Dom⁡(𝔞mX)=Dom⁡(BmX),\displaystyle\operatorname{Dom}\bigl((A_{m}^{X}+I)^{1/2}\bigr)=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathfrak{a}_{m}^{X})=\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{X}),

and, for s∈Dom⁡(BmX)s\in\operatorname{Dom}(B_{m}^{X}),

‖(AmX+I)1/2​s‖HmX2\displaystyle\bigl\|(A_{m}^{X}+I)^{1/2}s\bigr\|_{H_{m}^{X}}^{2} =𝔞mX​(s,s)+‖s‖HmX2\displaystyle=\mathfrak{a}_{m}^{X}(s,s)+\|s\|_{H_{m}^{X}}^{2}
(12.28) =‖BmX​s‖Hm+1X2+(αm+1)​‖s‖HmX2.\displaystyle=\|B_{m}^{X}s\|_{H_{m+1}^{X}}^{2}+(\alpha_{m}+1)\|s\|_{H_{m}^{X}}^{2}.

fj:=(AmX+I)1/2​sj.\displaystyle f_{j}:=(A_{m}^{X}+I)^{1/2}s_{j}.

The scalar case has the expected interpretation:

(12.29) A0X=(B0X)∗​B0X=−ΔX.\displaystyle A_{0}^{X}=(B_{0}^{X})^{*}B_{0}^{X}=-\Delta_{X}.

Indeed, the form ‖B0X​f‖2\|B_{0}^{X}f\|^{2} is the conformally invariant Dirichlet energy ∫X|∇f|2​d​AX\int_{X}|\nabla f|^{2}dA_{X}, which defines the canonical Alexandrov Laplacian.

Lemma 13.2.

Let l≥1l\geq 1. If

Hm=HmX,Bm=BmX,αm=m⁡(m+1),ρm=2​m+1.\displaystyle H_{m}=H_{m}^{X},\qquad B_{m}=B_{m}^{X},\qquad\alpha_{m}=m(m+1),\qquad\rho_{m}=2m+1.

Lemma 13.3.

Let pp be an atom of νX\nu_{X}, with νX​({p})=2​π​γ\nu_{X}(\{p\})=2\pi\gamma, 0<γ<10<\gamma<1. In a holomorphic coordinate zz centered at pp, write gX=e2​U​|d​z|2g_{X}=e^{2U}|dz|^{2} and

By (13.3) and (13.4), using Lemma 11.2, we obtain

U¯​(r)≥U¯​(rp,ϵ)+12​π​∫rrp,ϵωX​(Bt​(p))t​𝑑t≥−C+ln⁡(rp,ϵr)γ−ϵ.\displaystyle\overline{U}(r)\geq\overline{U}(r_{p,\epsilon})+\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{r}^{r_{p,\epsilon}}\frac{\omega_{X}(B_{t}(p))}{t}dt\geq-C+\ln(\frac{r_{p,\epsilon}}{r})^{\gamma-\epsilon}.

Therefore

eU¯​(r)≥C⋅(rp,ϵ)γ−ϵ⋅r−γ+ϵ≥C⁡(p,ϵ,γ)⋅r−γ+ϵ.\displaystyle e^{\overline{U}(r)}\geq C\cdot(r_{p,\epsilon})^{\gamma-\epsilon}\cdot r^{-\gamma+\epsilon}\geq C(p,\epsilon,\gamma)\cdot r^{-\gamma+\epsilon}.

∎

Lemma 13.4.

Let p∈Xp\in X be an atom of νX\nu_{X}, then

s⁡(p)=0,∀s∈VlX,l≥1.\displaystyle s(p)=0,\quad\quad\quad\forall s\in V_{l}^{X},\ l\geq 1.
Proof.

First, write

Lemma 15.3.

If νX=0\nu_{X}=0, then XX is isometric to the unit round sphere.

Proof.

The Alexandrov Bonnet–Myers diameter theorem [4, Theorem 3.6] gives

diam⁡X≤π.\operatorname{diam}X\leq\pi.

Theorem 15.4 (Alexandrov counting rigidity).

Let XX be a compact Alexandrov two-sphere with curvature at least 11. If, for some l≥1l\geq 1,

𝒩−ΔX​(l⁡(l+1))=(l+1)2,\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{X}}\bigl(l(l+1)\bigr)=(l+1)^{2},

then XX is isometric to the unit round sphere.

Proof.

By Proposition 13.5, the defect measure νX\nu_{X} is atomless. By Lemma 13.2, the concrete application of Proposition 2.6 gives

VlX=ker⁡BlX,dimℂVlX=2​l+1,\displaystyle V_{l}^{X}=\ker B_{l}^{X},\qquad\dim_{\mathbb{C}}V_{l}^{X}=2l+1,

and

𝔠l−1X​(s,s)=𝔞lX​(s,s)(s∈VlX).\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{l-1}^{X}(s,s)=\mathfrak{a}_{l}^{X}(s,s)\qquad(s\in V_{l}^{X}).

(15.2) ∫X|s|hl,X2​d​νX=0for every ​s∈VlX.\displaystyle\int_{X}|s|_{h_{l,X}}^{2}\,d\nu_{X}=0\qquad\text{for every }s\in V_{l}^{X}.

By Lemma 12.8 and the dimension equality,

VlX=H0​(ℂ​ℙ1,Kℂ​ℙ1−l).\displaystyle V_{l}^{X}=H^{0}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},K_{\mathbb{CP}^{1}}^{-l}).

For every p∈ℂ​ℙ1p\in\mathbb{CP}^{1}, the evaluation map is surjective by Lemma 10.2; hence some sp∈VlXs_{p}\in V_{l}^{X} satisfies sp​(p)≠0s_{p}(p)\neq 0.

In a coordinate centered at pp, its holomorphic coefficient is therefore bounded away from zero on a smaller neighborhood. The local conformal factor is bounded from below, so |sp|hl,X2≥cp>0|s_{p}|_{h_{l,X}}^{2}\geq c_{p}>0 almost everywhere on that neighborhood. Equation (15.2) then implies that νX\nu_{X} vanishes there.

Compactness gives finitely many such neighborhoods, and hence νX=0\nu_{X}=0.

Lemma 15.3 now shows that XX is round. ∎

Part IV Eigenvalues comparison and dimension of harmonic functions

16. A counterexample in dimension three

This section explains why the two-dimensional ladder should not be regarded as the shadow of a straightforward higher-dimensional theorem. The obstruction is not only technical. In dimension two, the scalar spherical harmonic multiplicities are reproduced by the line-bundle dimensions dimH0​(ℂ​ℙ1,K−m)=2​m+1\dim H^{0}(\mathbb{CP}^{1},K^{-m})=2m+1, and the curvature commutator has the correct sign under K≥1K\geq 1. In dimension three, a Ricci lower bound does not supply an analogous first-order ladder with the round multiplicities, and the exact eigenvalue comparison is in fact false.

The example below is included to mark the boundary of the method. It gives a completely explicit counterexample to the statement that Ricg≥2​g\Ric_{g}\geq 2g on S3S^{3} should imply λi​(S3,g)≥λi​(𝕊3,ground)\lambda_{i}(S^{3},g)\geq\lambda_{i}(\mathbb{S}^{3},g_{\mathrm{round}}) for every i≥1i\geq 1.

Since E<28E_{<28} is finite dimensional and g^ε→g0\widehat{g}_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow g_{0} smoothly, after shrinking ε>0\varepsilon>0 once more we have

(16.6) sup0≠u∈E<28ℛε​(u)<840.\displaystyle\sup_{0\neq u\in E_{<28}}\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(u)<840.

The conformal factor depends only on qq, and hence is independent of θ\theta and ϕ\phi. Therefore the L2​(g^ε)L^{2}(\widehat{g}_{\varepsilon}) inner product and the Dirichlet form have no cross terms between different ϕ\phi-Fourier frequencies. Every element of E<28E_{<28} has ϕ\phi-Fourier frequencies |m|≤27|m|\leq 27, while f28f_{28} has only the frequencies m=±28m=\pm 28. Define

F:=E<28⊕span⁡{f28}.\displaystyle F:=E_{<28}\oplus\operatorname{span}\{f_{28}\}.

Then

dimF=D+1=7715.\displaystyle\dim F=D+1=7715.

The final min–max test space is depicted in Figure 5: the low-degree harmonic block and the single perturbed degree-2828 test function both lie below the round threshold 840840.

By (16.4), (16.6), and the vanishing of the cross terms,

(16.7) sup0≠u∈Fℛε​(u)<840.\displaystyle\sup_{0\neq u\in F}\mathcal{R}_{\varepsilon}(u)<840.

The min–max principle applied to (16.7) gives

(16.8) λD​(S3,g^ε)<840.\displaystyle\lambda_{D}(S^{3},\widehat{g}_{\varepsilon})<840.

On the round unit S3S^{3}, the degree ll eigenvalue is l⁡(l+2)l(l+2) with multiplicity (l+1)2(l+1)^{2}. By (16.5), the bottom index of the degree 2828 cluster is exactly D=7714D=7714, and therefore

(16.9) λD​(𝕊3,g0)=28⋅30=840.\displaystyle\lambda_{D}(\mathbb{S}^{3},g_{0})=28\cdot 30=840.

Combining (16.8) and (16.9) gives

λ7714​(S3,g^ε)<λ7714​(𝕊3,g0).\displaystyle\lambda_{7714}(S^{3},\widehat{g}_{\varepsilon})<\lambda_{7714}(\mathbb{S}^{3},g_{0}).

This proves the theorem. ∎

Remark 16.2.

The numerical choices are made only to keep the verification short. The curvature check reduces to three quadratics with negative discriminant, and the eigenvalue drop is detected by the single degree 2828 spherical harmonic f28=Re⁡(w28)f_{28}=\operatorname{Re}(w^{28}).

17. The dimension of polynomial growth harmonic functions

This section returns to the original motivation. The eigenvalue comparison on a two-sphere is not merely an isolated compact result; it is the cross-section statement predicted by the sharp dimension problem for polynomial-growth harmonic functions. For a cone C⁡(X)C(X), homogeneous harmonic functions are controlled by the spectrum of the cross-section XX. Thus a finite counting comparison on XX becomes a dimension comparison for harmonic functions on the cone, and, through tangent-cone-at-infinity arguments, for noncompact manifolds.

The smooth theorem proves the needed comparison when the cross-section is a smooth positively curved two-sphere. For a three-manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and positive asymptotic volume ratio, however, the cross-section at infinity is naturally an Alexandrov two-sphere. Hence the equality case forces us to ask for a singular version of the same finite counting rigidity. This is the point where the complex-geometric language becomes more than a simplification: it provides the right framework for curvature measures, singular Hermitian metrics, and holomorphic sections on the conformal sphere.

We now isolate the part of the sharp Yau dimension problem which is genuinely suggested by the two-dimensional eigenvalue comparison proved above.

For k≥0k\geq 0, put ρ⁡(x):=dg​(p,x)\rho(x):=d_{g}(p,x) and define

ℋk(M):={u∈C∞(M):Δgu=0,|u(x)|≤C(ρ(x)k+1) for some C>0},\displaystyle\mathscr{H}_{k}(M):=\{u\in C^{\infty}(M):\Delta_{g}u=0,\ |u(x)|\leq C(\rho(x)^{k}+1)\text{ for some }C>0\},
hk​(M):=dimℋk​(M).\displaystyle h_{k}(M):=\dim\mathscr{H}_{k}(M).

In this section (M3,g)(M^{3},g) is complete with sectional curvature Kg≥0K_{g}\geq 0 and

(17.1) AVR⁡(M):=limr→∞vol⁡Bp​(r)r3>0.\displaystyle\operatorname{AVR}(M):=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{vol}B_{p}(r)}{r^{3}}>0.

The positivity condition (17.1) is what we call maximal volume growth.

For the Euclidean model,

(17.2) hd​(ℝ3)=∑j=0d(2​j+1)=(d+1)2,d∈ℤ≥0.\displaystyle h_{d}(\mathbb{R}^{3})=\sum_{j=0}^{d}(2j+1)=(d+1)^{2},\qquad d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Earlier work of Peter Li–Jiaping Wang [20] gave the corresponding asymptotic upper estimates under nonnegative sectional curvature.

Xian-Tao Huang’s theorem upgrades the asymptotic-cone philosophy to the finite counting inequality under maximal volume growth and uniqueness of the tangent cone.

Theorem 17.1.

Let (Mn,g)(M^{n},g) be a complete noncompact Riemannian manifold with Ricg≥0\Ric_{g}\geq 0 and maximal volume growth. Assume that MM has a unique tangent cone at infinity, denoted by

(C⁡(X),dC⁡(X),mC⁡(X)),\displaystyle(C(X),d_{C(X)},m_{C(X)}),

where C⁡(X)C(X) is the metric cone over the cross-section (X,dX,mX)(X,d_{X},m_{X}). Then, for every k>0k>0,

(17.3) hk​(Mn)≤𝒩−ΔX​(k⁡(k+n−2)).\displaystyle h_{k}(M^{n})\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{X}}\bigl(k(k+n-2)\bigr).
Proof.

This is [14, Theorem 1.6]. ∎

We now prove Theorem 1.12 in the notation of this section.

Proof of Theorem 1.12.

Step (1) For k=0k=0, the Cheng–Yau gradient estimate for bounded harmonic functions under Ricg≥0\operatorname{Ric}_{g}\geq 0 [7] gives h0​(M)=1=h0​(ℝ3)h_{0}(M)=1=h_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{3}). Since Kg≥0K_{g}\geq 0, the metric space (M,dg)(M,d_{g}) is a three-dimensional Alexandrov space with curvature bounded below by 00.

By Shioya’s structure theorem for the limit cone of a noncompact Alexandrov space with nonnegative curvature [32, Proposition 1.1, pp. 209–211], the blow-downs converge, without passing to a subsequence, to the unique tangent cone at infinity:

(17.4) (M,ri−2​g,p)⟶C⁡(X),ri→∞.\displaystyle(M,r_{i}^{-2}g,p)\longrightarrow C(X),\qquad r_{i}\to\infty.

Here X=M⁡(∞)X=M(\infty) is the ideal boundary of MM, and C⁡(X)C(X) is the Euclidean cone over XX. Since (17.1) is positive, the convergence in (17.4) is noncollapsed and the limit cone has Hausdorff dimension 33. Hence XX has Hausdorff dimension 22, and the standard cone criterion gives Alexandrov curvature at least 11 on XX [4, Proposition 4.2.3, pp. 13–14].

Step (2). The pointed form of Perelman’s stability theorem implies that C⁡(X)C(X) is a topological three-manifold near its vertex oo; see [16, Theorem 7.11, pp. 125–126]. Moreover,

Bo​(ε)∖{o}≅(0,ε)×X\displaystyle B_{o}(\varepsilon)\setminus\{o\}\cong(0,\varepsilon)\times X

for every ε>0\varepsilon>0. With integer coefficients, local homology at the vertex therefore satisfies

Hj​(C⁡(X),C⁡(X)∖{o},ℤ)≅Hj​(ℝ3,ℝ3∖{0},ℤ).\displaystyle H_{j}(C(X),C(X)\setminus\{o\};\mathbb{Z})\cong H_{j}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\};\mathbb{Z}).

Because C⁡(X)C(X) is contractible and C⁡(X)∖{o}C(X)\setminus\{o\} deformation retracts onto XX, the long exact sequence of the pair also gives

Hj​(C⁡(X),C⁡(X)∖{o},ℤ)≅H~j−1​(X,ℤ).\displaystyle H_{j}(C(X),C(X)\setminus\{o\};\mathbb{Z})\cong\widetilde{H}_{j-1}(X;\mathbb{Z}).

Thus XX has the reduced integral homology of S2S^{2}. By [4, §12.9.3, p. 52], every compact two-dimensional Alexandrov space is a compact topological surface, possibly with boundary. The identity H2​(X,ℤ)≅ℤH_{2}(X;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z} rules out boundary and gives orientability, while H1​(X,ℤ)=0H_{1}(X;\mathbb{Z})=0. The classification of compact connected surfaces now shows that XX is homeomorphic to S2S^{2}.

Step (3) For k≥1k\geq 1, (17.3) with n=3n=3 and Corollary 15.2 give

hk​(M)≤𝒩−ΔX​(k⁡(k+1))≤(k+1)2=hk​(ℝ3).\displaystyle h_{k}(M)\leq\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{X}}\bigl(k(k+1)\bigr)\leq(k+1)^{2}=h_{k}(\mathbb{R}^{3}).

Together with the case k=0k=0 and (17.2), this proves (1.9).

Step (4) Suppose that hk​(M)=(k+1)2h_{k}(M)=(k+1)^{2} for some k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}. Equality in the preceding chain forces

𝒩−ΔX​(k⁡(k+1))=(k+1)2.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{-\Delta_{X}}\bigl(k(k+1)\bigr)=(k+1)^{2}.

The Alexandrov counting-rigidity theorem, Theorem 15.4, makes XX the unit round sphere. Hence the tangent cone in (17.4) is ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and AVR⁡(M)=ω3\operatorname{AVR}(M)=\omega_{3}. Bishop–Gromov monotonicity says that

r⟼vol⁡Bp​(r)ω3​r3\displaystyle r\longmapsto\frac{\operatorname{vol}B_{p}(r)}{\omega_{3}r^{3}}

is nonincreasing. Its limit as r↓0r\downarrow 0 is 11, and its limit as r→∞r\to\infty is AVR⁡(M)/ω3=1\operatorname{AVR}(M)/\omega_{3}=1; it is therefore identically one. The equality case of Bishop–Gromov implies that (M3,g)(M^{3},g) is isometric to ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. ∎

Remark 17.2 (Why a single-eigenvalue Obata statement is insufficient).

Theorem 15.4 cannot be replaced by a naive Obata-type statement of the form

λj​(X)=λj​(𝕊2,ground)⟹X​ is isometric to ​(𝕊2,ground).\displaystyle\lambda_{j}(X)=\lambda_{j}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\rm round})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X\text{ is isometric to }(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\rm round}).

Indeed, to disprove such a statement it is enough to find one Alexandrov two-sphere XX with curvature ≥1\geq 1, not isometric to the round unit sphere, but satisfying λ1​(X)=2\lambda_{1}(X)=2. The football metrics in Example 17.3 give exactly such examples. Thus the rigidity statement needed in Theorem 15.4 must be formulated as a counting equality at a whole round threshold, not as equality of one eigenvalue.

Example 17.3 (A nonround Alexandrov sphere with λ1=2\lambda_{1}=2).

Let 0<c<10<c<1. On (0,π)×(ℝ/2​π​ℤ)(0,\pi)\times(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}), set

gc=d​r2+c2​sin2⁡r​d​θ2.\displaystyle g_{c}=dr^{2}+c^{2}\sin^{2}r\,d\theta^{2}.

Let XcX_{c} be the metric completion obtained by adding the two endpoints N={r=0}N=\{r=0\} and S={r=π}S=\{r=\pi\}. This is the standard spherical football. The original two-cone classification and construction of spherical metrics of constant curvature on S2S^{2} with two conical singularities is due to Troyanov [34, pp. 296–306]. The explicit Friedrichs spectrum of the spherical football is computed in Mazzeo–Zhu [23, Lemmas 2–3, arXiv version, pp. 24–25]. The metric completion and the eigenfunction responsible for the equality λ1​(Xc)=2\lambda_{1}(X_{c})=2 are shown in Figure 6.

Near r=0r=0, since sin⁡r=r+O⁡(r3)\sin r=r+O(r^{3}), one has

gc=d​r2+c2​r2​d​θ2+O⁡(r4)​d​θ2.\displaystyle g_{c}=dr^{2}+c^{2}r^{2}d\theta^{2}+O(r^{4})d\theta^{2}.

The same expansion holds near r=πr=\pi. Hence NN and SS are conical points with cone angle 2​π​c2\pi c. Since c<1c<1, these cone angles are strictly smaller than 2​π2\pi. On the regular part Xcreg:=Xc∖{N,S}X_{c}^{\rm reg}:=X_{c}\setminus\{N,S\}, the Gaussian curvature is

Kgc=−(c​sin⁡r)′′c​sin⁡r=1.\displaystyle K_{g_{c}}=-\frac{(c\sin r)^{\prime\prime}}{c\sin r}=1.

The curvature measure is therefore

ωXc=d​Agc+2​π​(1−c)​δN+2​π​(1−c)​δS≥d​Agc.\displaystyle\omega_{X_{c}}=dA_{g_{c}}+2\pi(1-c)\delta_{N}+2\pi(1-c)\delta_{S}\geq dA_{g_{c}}.

Thus XcX_{c} is an Alexandrov two-sphere with curvature at least 11. It is not isometric to the round unit sphere because it has two conical points.

By the spectrum formula in [23, Lemmas 2–3, arXiv version, pp. 24–25],

Spec(−ΔXc)={(jc+ℓ)(jc+ℓ+1):j,ℓ∈ℤ≥0},\displaystyle\operatorname{Spec}(-\Delta_{X_{c}})=\left\{\left(\frac{j}{c}+\ell\right)\left(\frac{j}{c}+\ell+1\right):j,\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\right\},

with multiplicity one for j=0j=0 and multiplicity two for j>0j>0. The low-lying part of this spectrum is represented in Figure 7; it separates the meridian mode at eigenvalue 22 from all angular modes when 0<c<10<c<1.

The mode j=0j=0, ℓ=1\ell=1 gives the eigenfunction

u⁡(r,θ)=cos⁡r,−ΔXc​u=2​u.\displaystyle u(r,\theta)=\cos r,\qquad-\Delta_{X_{c}}u=2u.

Since 0<c<10<c<1, every mode with j≥1j\geq 1 has eigenvalue

jc​(jc+1)>2.\displaystyle\frac{j}{c}\left(\frac{j}{c}+1\right)>2.

Also the modes j=0j=0, ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2 have eigenvalues at least 66. Therefore the only eigenvalues not exceeding 22 are 00 and 22, and hence

λ1​(Xc)=2=λ1​(𝕊2,ground).\displaystyle\lambda_{1}(X_{c})=2=\lambda_{1}(\mathbb{S}^{2},g_{\rm round}).

This gives a nonround Alexandrov two-sphere with curvature ≥1\geq 1 and first positive eigenvalue equal to the first positive round eigenvalue. Thus single ordered-eigenvalue equality is not a valid Alexandrov rigidity hypothesis.
